Employing the standard $1/r$ expansion, we rederive key results from BAB-S and demonstrate how the curvature flux, de Donder's gravitational wave stress-energy pseudo-tensor's flux, and radiative data are interrelated at null infinity. Ultimately, we frame these findings in the language of asymptotically flat spacetimes at large radii within Minkowski space. Additionally, we introduce an alternative computational approach utilizing the spacetime's formal series expansion. In this framework, we show how decoupling the Einstein equations into separate sets of higher-order and first-order radial differential equations, common in formal approaches, arises from the conformal decomposition of a formal metric into an 'even' and 'odd' series. This method reveals a new perspective on 'news' as a radiative datum determining curvature at null infinity, rather than specifying metric data there. Furthermore, we discuss how this method's computation of boundary observables, influenced by gauge transformations that leave the 'news' unchanged, differs from the standard approach.

We investigated how the driving rate influences the motion of a cylinder moved vertically through loose, granular material. Our study showed that, for a cylinder driven at a constant rate, the drag force it experiences fluctuates significantly, with its magnitude depending on the speed at which it's being driven. Our results reveal that, under certain conditions, the drag force behaves in an almost linear manner, with specific proportionality constants emerging at both low and high driving rate conditions. Moreover, our research highlights that the impact of an abrupt acceleration on the cylinder varies in magnitude and timeframe, with these effects persisting for multiple times the diameter of the cylinder at lower driving rate conditions. Our findings also show that, at very low driving rate conditions, the impact of a sudden acceleration results in the displacement of a substantial volume of grain material, with this effect persisting for many of the cylinder's own diameters.

This study leverages the ALMA observations of sub-Kelvin, dwarf starburst galaxies to explore the dynamics of ionised gas outflows and their impact on the rates at which galaxies consume their gas supplies, as well as the efficiencies of star formation. By combining data from the observations with mass and velocity information from the galaxies' star clusters, we are able to reveal the outflows in action. Our analysis shows that the kinetic energy of the outflows often exceeds their gravitational binding energy, a surprise finding given their low masses. These outflows can shape the galaxies' evolution by creating large voids, expanding the galaxies' radii by a factor of five or more and increasing their gas depletion times by a similar magnitude, despite their small masses. Furthermore, the outflows can suppress the galaxies' current star formation rates by a factor of ten or more, having a disproportionate effect on their dynamics relative to their masses.

Finding optimal configurations for complex systems often demands significant time and resources due to the expansive parameter search space. Auto-tuning methods improve system performance by automating this search, yet they typically focus on pre-defined configurations and overlook exploring novel, potentially more efficient options. In this paper, we introduce BoAnon, an auto-configuration learning framework that incorporates anonymous auto-tuning and open-ended configuration search features. Utilizing a Bayesian optimization approach, BoAnon generates an efficient configuration by integrating feedback from system evaluations and user-supplied configuration descriptions. It then refines the underlying system's configuration to enhance user feedback. demonstrations of BoAnon's abilities to discover an anonymous auto-tuning approach for database configuration and discover an efficient configuration beyond user input are provided.

Our analysis of 2D fluid dynamics in heavy-ion collisions reveals that the
dependence on transverse momentum for 3-party and 2-party flow is consistent
across different types of particles. This finding holds true for a wide range
of transverse momentum and is supported by prior studies but with limited
data support in this region. Further investigation, using more experiments and
run conditions, is necessary to confirm these results for more widely separated
particles.

The growing size and intricacy of Large RDF Datasets (LRDs) make quality checks essential. Existing quality assessment tools struggle with LRDs due to their lack of scalability and LRDs' complexity. We developed a quality assessment framework to tackle this issue. Our framework introduces the QualityAssessment (QA) pattern, a set of executable measures for evaluating the quality of data. Building on the QA pattern, our framework offers two key features: an optimized approach to running assessments on LRDs using data partitioning and a new evaluation metric, the DistQualityAssessment (DQA) score, for measuring the quality of LRDs across data distributions. Our experiments demonstrate that our framework can efficiently handle LRDs with over a billion triples, delivering the same level of accuracy as traditional methods while being up to 50 times faster, and providing a 1.5 to 2 times more accurate DQA score compared to single-source assessments.

We develop uniform convergence theory and limiting distribution results for independent and non-Gaussian process data, specifically for low sample sizes and cycles beginning at zero. These findings can be applied to create robust statistical inferences, as seen with maximum likelihood estimates. Similarly, we establish limiting distribution properties of other estimation methods, including maximum likelihood estimates and density function-based methods like median unbiased estimation and moment estimation. Our theory is validated at a cycle break point in the Brownian motion with drift process, showing that the normal distribution's robustness gains from minimum density power divergence estimators exceed those of the maximum likelihood estimator. We also obtain an $n$-variance rate for a broad class of scalar independent processes including the Poisson process, geometric distribution, exponential distribution, and Weibull distribution.

When a supersonic flow of ionized gas encounters an oblique shock wave, its temperature and ionization state undergo significant changes. This phenomenon likely influences the appearance of gas in active galaxies, AGNs, and star-forming regions. To understand these effects better, observation-mimicking simulations were run for a typical AGN at z=0.127. The results show that shock-ionization processes can cause a diverse array of emission lines, spectral features, and illogical relationships between line ratios that can be seen in x-ray to optical spectra. Notably, the results suggest that line ratios, such as [OIII]/H$\beta$, can vary by over two orders of magnitude, and the relationships between spectral features can become highly non-linear. This indicates that line ratios alone may not be sufficient to accurately interpret the physical properties of narrow-spectrum gas. Moreover, the relationship between broad and narrow spectral features may be more complex than previously assumed. This research suggests the need to re-examine the interpretations of x-ray to optical spectra, especially when interpreting the relationships between line ratios.

The growing complexity of Internet of Things (IoT) projects has led to increased testing needs, often overlooked in typical development cycles, which still rely on ad hoc methods. To rectify this, a framework called Frisbee has been devised to simplify the testing and visualization of IoT processes and outcomes through a flowchart-based approach. Frisbee enables continuous testing, streamlines test management for multiple users, and provides visual feedback to testers in real-time, which has been successfully demonstrated in an emergency response application developed with student involvement in a citizen science project.

The LHCb upgrade will significantly enhance the LHC's luminosity before the run starting in 2021, making it possible to study rare $B$ meson decays, such as $B^0_s \to \mu^+ \mu^-$ and $B^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^-$, which will allow for a precise measurement of the mixing parameter $S_{\mu\mu}$ with very small uncertainty. Due to the $B^0$ and $B^0_s$ mesons having different semileptonic charging asymmetries, an accurate understanding of the detection apparatus is crucial to avoiding systematic errors. Furthermore, the lifetime of the $\mu^+ \mu^-$ decay products will provide a signature to distinguish between $B^0$ and $B^0_s$ mesons. Collaborating with the LHCb upgrade hardware, the novel software system called Endstation, including the near-bang vertex detector, will allow LHCb to achieve a direct trigger for semi-neutral meson decays, significantly increasing the capture of rare decays at high production thresholds. These features will give LHCb the capability to study rare decays in detail, ultimately providing a more comprehensive understanding of flavor physics and the possibility of discovering new physics beyond the Standard Model.

A neural network is being utilized to predict driving scenes near the vehicle in a continuous and reversible manner, enabling a modeling approach that learns representations of traffic environments in an end-to-end and bidirectional fashion. This approach enables transformations of the encoder in one direction to correspond to inverse transformations of the decoder in the other direction. This paper describes our development of a variant called a self-drive auto-generator (SceneGen), which effectively generates target scenes in the vertical and horizontal dimensions as well as scenes across time in various temporal instances. This capability allows for the production of driving simulations for test images that accurately reflect modifications to road conditions and vehicle movements that occur naturally. This feature is crucial for validating the reliability of methods that learn retargeting representations directly from input and output images. Our experiments show that combining SceneGen with down-sampling and super-resolution tasks results in accurate predictions of driving scenes, which resemble real images and enable precise simulations of changes to vehicle positions and road conditions. This model's ability to retrieve enhanced scenes from lower-resolution inputs and realistic driving scenes from compressed inputs is being demonstrated, and it also shows that SceneGen can accurately simulate changes to vehicle positions and road conditions over time.

Using the language of group theory, particularly representation theory, we can reframe the Ising model on a Cayley tree as a correlation function within a graded module. Building on this, we can extend any Ising model defined on a tree to include its underlying symmetry through a group gamma. This creates a more comprehensive model encompassing both the original Ising model and its symmetry. For a Cayley tree, the Ising model can be viewed as a module over the spin sum monoid, and its symmetry makes it a module over the group U(G). Furthermore, we can apply the spin sum monoid to define local interactions within the Ising model based on its U(G) structure. These group-theoretic principles can then be integrated into a broader framework involving algebraic geometry and hypercomplex analysis, providing a unified theoretical approach to studying physical phenomena through their underlying symmetries.

The study introduces a new approach, the Preconditioned Rescaling Standard FGMRES (PRSS-FG), to tackle challenging problems governed by symmetric positive-definite matrices within the framework of the numerical linear algebra. This proposed method PRSS-FG effectively leverages the capabilities of the standard FGMRES (RSS-FG) iteration and improves its efficiency when dealing with preconditioning, based on a symmetric positive-definite matrix.

This research paper focuses on certain multi-dimensional two-step stochastic systems that involve rotations and reflections. The systems examined consist of a point mass moving in a d-dimensional space. The mass's movement is influenced by two factors: its position in space through a one-parameter rotation group, and a random variable that selects either a forward or backward direction with equal probability. The systems were first studied independently by Downey in 1996 and 2000, who asked questions about their long-term behavior and mixing properties. Together with previous findings, our results show that the systems are ergodic and weakly mixing for dimensions greater than one, and ergodic downey-random mixing for dimensions greater than two. Our work also demonstrates that the systems lose all memory of initial conditions after a sufficient time, and the systems exhibit a specific type of localization of correlations, known as CLT behavior, occurring at a rate of n^-1 for both variance and mean absolute deviation. Our results also provide a solution to open problems originally posed by Downey in 1996 and 2000, and extend results established by Schapira in 2019.

We have examined a superbubble and surrounding dust cloud created by the M82 superbubble. A flow model and analysis of energy dissipation, element distribution, and thermal radiation were used to study its evolution and the distribution of its components. Model predictions matched observations, including the model's prediction of a dust layer separated from the superbubble by a stable shock. However, there were discrepancies in the model's prediction of dust emission, including an overestimated contribution of pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae to the dust supply. Model estimates indicated that about 9 x 10^4 Solar masses of molecular gas were trapped within the superbubble, with a similar amount of dust. We estimated the dust opacity in the bubble to be 0.8-2.8, with possible explanations for the observed features, including a hollow structure, spiral pattern, and dust filaments. Additionally, we examined the possibility of a hollow structure as a result of gas collapse.

This investigation delves into the challenges of detecting three-dimensional objects at long distances, and how the combined use of color and laser measurements can be effectively employed to address this issue. We've assembled two distinct datasets featuring scene points and bounding boxes that accurately mark the locations of objects within the far-field. By incorporating depth information from a lidar sensor, we've developed a detection framework based on a multi-head attention mechanism that processes low-resolution region features and precise distance data, and experiment results show improved performance compared to the model without this component. In addition, we've found that training the framework with data that mimics the limitations of the lidar sensor leads to better final outcomes, and that incorporating data augmentation techniques helps recover lost objects within the far-field that are initially detected.

A study was conducted to evaluate the efficiency of using a generative quantum machine learning model as a tool for preparing quantum states within a given energy range on a given potential energy surface. The investigation utilized the quantum variational form and the Morse potential, and the results showed that the graph of the form's parameter versus energy is linear, allowing the desired quantum state to be obtained through a series of linear transformations from the initial state at a lower energy level. The accuracy of this approach was assessed by comparing the shape of a given energy range and the corresponding probability distribution to those of the target state, and multiple factors were identified that could influence the accuracy, including the number of entangling gates, the type of measurement basis, and the range of given energies.

During surgery, the registration of preoperative organ models to their intraoperative state is commonly achieved using a probe that emits an electronic pose signal. As this process relies on noise-free surface data, the noisy intraoperative organ extraction is necessitated, ultimately affecting the accuracy of the registration. To address this issue, we propose a novel method that utilizes deep learning to directly produce low-noise organ surfaces from noisy probe data, bypassing the need for a subsequent smoothing step. By framing this process as a sequential task and utilizing a variational auto-encoder to extract features, the method utilizes a multi-layer perceptron to transform these features into clean surface points. To validate the proposed method, we applied it to a dataset consisting of noisy rat liver and human liver datasets, demonstrating improved results with a reduced amount of forward steps compared to a baseline approach. Furthermore, we discovered that our model's performance is relatively robust to variations in organ deformations, organ folding, and organ translations and rotations.

The relationship between conformal matter collineations and null conformal matter collineations is explored, with a focus on how degeneration affects their structure. It's established that when the energy-momentum tensor exhibits degradation, a conformal matter collination transforms into a null conformal matter collination. The interconnection between these two concepts is clarified, and the degree of freedom in a non-projective null conformal matter collination is determined to be 6, based on specific tensor conditions.

Self-supervised depth estimation methods that rely on optical flow have made significant advancements; however, accurate flow prediction through occlusions remains a persistent challenge. To address this limitation, our approach incorporates an optical flow prior directly in the occlusion regions, enabling a more precise prediction of the flow field. By recognizing that the occluded region's motion generally matches that of the visible part of the occluding object, we incorporate this assumption into our model. By activating the previously frozen optical flow encoder layers and initiating the optical flow prior in the occluded regions, our method achieves a more accurate prediction of depth. Our approach demonstrates a notable improvement in overall depth evaluation metrics and exhibits a significant reduction in error for difficult test scenes with complex and varied patterns.

This paper introduces a novel neural network architecture called Novelton Network, a type of sparsified ANN designed for use in both software and hardware implementations. The network's primary goal was to create a compact, space-efficient design that could serve as an efficient, space-constrained device for processing data. The novel network's structure makes it compatible with existing storage technologies, enabling efficient software loading. A key feature of the network is its ability to execute inference operations directly within the same memory unit, thus reducing data movement. The design's efficiency was validated through a series of benchmark tests, which demonstrated the network's superiority over existing sparsified ANN designs in terms of memory usage, storage efficiency, and overall design compactness. The validation was carried out in multiple programming languages and demonstrated the network's versatility and adaptability to different hardware platforms. The results indicated the novel network's potential as a versatile, energy-efficient solution for a wide range of applications.

This study investigates the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field, focusing on its relativistic and unidirectional nature. Focusing on the strange quark mass within the range of 0.5 GeV to 1.0 GeV, as well as the charge fraction in 1/3 quantized conditions, our research explores the impact of varying neutron to strange quark mass ratios and the presence of a magnetic field. Our findings suggest that increasing the strange quark mass weakens the spin polarization of strange quarks, whereas decreasing the ratio strengthens it, with the addition of a strong magnetic field weakens spin polarization more, particularly in higher mass ranges.

A cubic graph is classified as even-2-factorable, or E2F for short, if all its 2-factors consist entirely of even length cycles. In this study, necessary and sufficient conditions have been established to determine when a cubic graph is E2F based on its spanning subgraphs. Moreover, a polynomial time algorithm has been devised to identify whether any given cyclic covering of Z2 has an E2 preimage.

Using the Bateman-Horn conjecture proposed by Li, this study obtains fresh proof of certain findings by Vaserstein, Poonen and Rubinstein as well as R. Schmidt concerning the prime values of specific types of quadratic polynomials. Additionally, through the application of the Bateman-Horn formula, several outcomes by Poonen and Rubinstein as well as Schmidt are generalized.

Many programs written in PHP, Python, and similar interpreted languages are frequently written with insecure practices, making them vulnerable to remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, a primary security threat. To address this issue, Timeloops has been developed to provide coarse-grained system call control for these programs, even though they operate over networks and involve significant overhead due to the nature of interpreted languages. To accomplish this, Timeloops has been designed to minimize overhead through shared memory communication between the main program and the Timeloops environment, allowing all system calls to pass through without exception. Furthermore, to further enhance security, Timeloops has been modified to eliminate the possibility of concurrent execution, a common issue with PHP and Python programs, by introducing mutual exclusion mechanisms. As a result, Timeloops has been shown to provide robust system call control for interpreted programs, even those with significant performance constraints.

A particularly promising area of research suggests that the dark matter candidate known as the axion is a pseudo-Goldstone particle with a unique property: it can other interact weakly due to a non-zero mass. Since its mass originates from a different part of the theory, its elastic scattering with nucleons is governed primarily by the axion's decay field, which has been found to be much smaller than other possible interactions, which could be considered "classically" scale-invariant. This article explores the implications of the axion's "soft" breaking force, which can significantly enhance its scattering force with nucleons, regardless of any suppressions that come from the typical particle physics parameters, such as the weak force scale. A wide variety of possible models are presented, including those based on the Standard Model extensions, as well as theories based on the Standard Model extensions, with scalar and axial-vector couplings, as well as a variation known as "alignment axion" model, with its own distinct features, such as its own decay constant, which can be found within the range of the GUT scale. With its own decay constant, which can be found within the range of the GUT scale. With its own decay constant, which can be found within the range of the GUT scale.

This paper addresses a critical challenge faced by autonomous systems in navigating uncertain and restricted environments - the continuous tracking of undetected targets within their sensor's limited fields of view. A probabilistic method is presented to estimate target positions based on observation histories and undetected target dynamics, providing continuous tracking within their sensor fields of view. To optimize computational efficiency, the dynamics are modeled as Markov processes and targets' locations are represented as a discrete set of states, with each state associated with a probability distribution. The formulation of the tracking problem as a Bayesian decision process is discussed, focusing on minimizing a cost function that represents the expected value of undetected targets' states. A key innovation proposed is the use of undetected targets' dynamics to reduce the search space of their possible locations, significantly lowering the computational complexity.

This research focuses on a non-local reaction-diffusion model that models the spread and possible disappearance of a population that preys on a limited, uniformly spread resource. We demonstrate that the non-linear observability property of the controlled associated system allows for precise management of population extinction or prevention, even with uniform control over the entire domain.

Creating automated plans that minimize goal opportunities for the opposing team is a complex problem to solve. This problem can be broken down into two versions: one where a goal can only be scored by a robot assistant and another where goals can be scored by both the robot and a human in the presence. We tackle this challenge by first mapping its underlying state space and then suggesting a solution strategy that learns the most effective action to take in each situation. This action could range from attempting to score, blocking an opponent's attempt, committing a foul, or passing the ball to the robot's teammate. We test our approach on computer simulations and real-world data, and the results show that it can both plan successful goals and prevent goals in various situations. Also, we discovered that adding a state feature that shows whether a goal is possible when the ball goes out of play enables us to solve the more complex version of this problem.

Adjoint-state full waveform inversion (FWI) utilizes a comprehensive amount of time-domain wavefield data, which can be formulated into the frequency domain using a sufficient number of Fourier transforms. However, the large size of time-domain forward and adjoint state wavefields poses challenges in memory management, often necessitating the division of the computation into smaller, manageable parts. In this study, we propose an alternative method that involves inverting the Fourier transform matrix in a block-wise manner, incorporating the corresponding Fourier transform of the source functions. This new approach allows the inversion of the wave equation in the frequency domain while avoiding the need to store the entire time-domain wavefield, instead working with spatially discretized and low-memory source functions. We have integrated this method into the gradient computation of the adjoint-state FWI and demonstrated its advantages over conventional fourfold Fourier-transform-based approaches through 2D and 3D synthetic benchmarks.

We present a detailed theoretical analysis of magnetophotonic circuits, 
based on layers of dielectric diegrotches with magnetic characteristics, 
and investigate how this can achieve opto-electronic circuit components, 
such as all-optical diodes and quasi-circulators. By varying the
magnetophotonic structure and controlling the propagation of light, 
we demonstrate the realization of these components. 
Specifically, unidirectional transmission and controlled circulation of light 
can be achieved through asymmetric and cyclic asymmetry in the magnetophotonic 
structure. Furthermore, we propose a method to create an all-optical switch 
and show its ability to toggle the direction of light transmission. 
Finally, we present a theoretical analysis of opto-electronic components 
built from magnetophotonic structures and show their potential applications.

We have conducted an in-depth investigation of the IGR J19294+1816 X-ray source during its 2019 high-intensity outbreak, utilizing observations from the Insight-HXMT space telescope. The analysis revealed the presence of an iron K-shell spectral line within the 6.3-7.5 keV energy range, along with a distinct hard X-ray spectrum peaking at energies above 10 keV. Considerations of the system's inclination angle, constrained between 25 and 65 degrees, as well as the detection of the iron spectral line, suggest a inclination range of 52 to 65 degrees. This research provides further evidence supporting the hypothesis that IGR J19294+1816 is a millisecond pulsar that is situated on the edge of the pulsar coexistence boundary with the magnetar population.

We investigate the dynamic behavior of the asymmetric noisy voter model on a complete graph with $n$ participants, exploring how this system responds as $n$ grows larger. In this model, at any given time step, one individual is randomly selected to change their opinion, either by randomly switching or copying the opinion of another participant, chosen at random. As we increase $n$, multiple scaling limits emerge, dictated by the strength and direction of asymmetry, which we detail. These limits include regimes for weak and strong asymmetry, as well as intermediate cases. Notably, some intermediate regimes exhibit Karlin-Tarjan type behavior and show that even a minimal level of asymmetry can drive the system toward distinct outcomes—coexistence of opinions or a single dominant view. We also address an additional intermediate regime specifically on a line graph. Furthermore, we provide a novel, more straightforward analysis of the weak asymmetry case, avoiding the use of random walks in a semi-class.

Citizen science is a citizen-driven initiative that combines technology to conduct research, including the development of apps for identifying biological species, which can also be applied to architectural heritage sites like traditional houses and historic buildings. One such aspect to study is Indonesian sundials, which have limited documentation online due to their absence in major documentation databases. To overcome this, a prototype sundial documentation system has been created using a custom app and the Elasticsearch search engine, enabling better access to the information through online interfaces like the elasticsearch-ds.kompeni.net search engine. This proposed system can serve as a case study for citizen-driven documentation projects, ultimately contributing to the preservation and understanding of Indonesian sundials, including those found in Palangka Raya, such as the sundial located at the former Palangka Raya Railway Station.

This study proposes two novel protocols, Task Splitting and Task Swap, to enhance the efficiency of resource allocation in time-critical DED2D networks and address optimality gaps. In scenarios where end users require more data and energy than can be provided, the TS policy allows the mobile user to divide its data and energy transfer capabilities with a base station, thereby increasing the efficiency of transfers. For scenarios with a surplus, the MS shares its transfer capabilities with the BS through the MS-to-BS transfer direction. Furthermore, the MS and BS exchange time slots to optimize the efficiency and reliability of transfers, as outlined in the MS-to-MS transfer direction. The key benefit of these protocols is that they reduce energy consumption, provide more flexible resource management, and enable more robust and efficient data transfers.

The telework mandates that were in effect during the COVID-19 epidemic have
accelerated the adoption of remote experimental frameworks and laboratory
 setups. Following this observation, we created an innovative method for
automating laboratory experiments accessible from anywhere via a web browser.
 Our approach integrates the cutting-edge technology of web graphics interfaces
 and web programming languages with industrial robot tools and laboratory
 equipment, enabling a flexible and adaptable solution for a wide array of
 laboratory applications. To illustrate the effectiveness of this approach, we
 applied it to an experiment involving the development of microscopic structures
 characteristic of ancient Roman concrete in a laboratory laboratory.

Customized aperture plates, composed of varying electrostatic fields, enable the modification of electron probe characteristics in conventional transmission electron microscopes. A key obstacle in plate design has been the absence of user-input options for defining plate geometry within existing design programs. A general approach to modeling 2D and3D electron field distributions using finite element methods, combined with an iterative optimization technique to minimize deviations from desired probe properties, has been developed and implemented in a computer interface. This interface enables the flexible modification of design parameters, including plate geometry, to achieve optimal electron performance. The interface and underlying model have been applied to design a phase plate with a high degree of precision, resulting in a probe with 100 pika diameter at minimal distortion.

Deep generative models have gained significant traction for unsupervised pre-training in natural language processing, with recent attention on attention-based attentional mechanisms and generative latent variables for sequence-to-sequence mapping. We explore the potential of combining these components and explore their applications to understanding human-computer dialogues, which necessitates processing an extensive history of previous exchanges. We experiment with different variations, incorporating bidirectional processing and multi-directional interactions, and find that careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful careful

Accurate loop closure detection in dynamic indoor settings using deep learning networks is explored in this paper. A novel network architecture for loop closure detection is proposed, incorporating an embedding layer that leverages attention mechanisms to capture context-aware visual information. This context is derived from an active learning-based selection process. To evaluate the method, a synthetic dataset is generated with an Arduino Mega robot navigating an open-plan space and capturing images via an Raspberry Pi camera. Moreover, a real-world dataset is used to assess the efficacy of a proposed deep learning detection network in handling complex indoor environments, including areas with variations in lighting and distinct landmark features.

The quality of user experience while streaming video relies heavily on maintaining high standards, or Quality of Service. To achieve this, ample buffering capacity and swift processing capabilities are necessary. Cloud technologies have significantly contributed to video streaming services including Netflix and Spotify by providing these resources and additional features like content delivery and data processing. However, the ongoing debate concerns selecting appropriate cloud providers to ensure optimal performance and minimal costs. To address this challenge, we first examine how cloud services contribute to video streaming's Quality of Service, then develop a mathematical framework to identify the best cloud provider options. This stochastic decision-making problem is modeled and solved using policy iteration, an efficient method for optimal decision making. Moreover, we propose a practical, iterative approach for real-time implementation. Through numerical examples and case studies, we demonstrate the value of our proposed methods in providing stream operators with streamlined, cost-effective solutions for maintaining video quality.

We've developed a novel renormalization approach to handle interactions within the Hartree-Fock framework, specifically tailored for doping graphene sheets. This method allows us to derive the one-loop renormalized quasiparticle velocities and use them to assess the impact of dose. As a result, we can effectively model the undoped and doped regions separately and assess the total dose and one-loop renormalization effects on the total band structure. This technique yields valuable insights, including estimating the one-loop renormalized quasiparticle velocity and its impact on the undoped region band structure, as well as estimating the velocity for the doped region and evaluating dose-induced renormalization of the undoped region band structure. Moreover, we can estimate the one-loop renormalized quasiparticle velocity in the undoped region, evaluate the velocity in the doped region, and estimate the effects of these factors on the doped and undoped regions' band structures, respectively. Ultimately, this approach lays the foundation for a more comprehensive model that incorporates these parameters, which can be used to evaluate the renormalized quasiparticle velocities and their effects on the specific heat and optical conductivity in doped graphene sheets.

Recent advances in text-to-speech synthesis have achieved impressive results, yet they still fall short in replicating the naturalness and range of expressiveness found in human speech. We introduce MaskedSpeech, a novel text-to-speech synthesis framework inspired by the masked language modeling approach. In contrast to previous methods that combine spectral text-to-speech models with acoustic text-to-speech systems, MaskedSpeech treats the speech synthesis process as a masked language modeling task. By framing speech synthesis as an encoding-decoding task where the decoder is a masked TNS filter bank, MaskedSpeech leverages the strength of TNS-based models while addressing their limitations. By training the masked speech encoder and the synthetic decoder jointly, MaskedSpeech learns a more natural speech representation that requires less processing to generate, resulting in more natural and expressive synthesized speech. Our experiments demonstrate the superiority of MaskedSpeech over leading baselines in terms of speech quality and computational efficiency. Additionally, MaskedSpeech exhibits less speaker representation loss due to mask masking and produces more expressive synthesized speech due to the presence of residual connections in the decoder. We release our model and training scripts to the public, hoping to foster future research in high-fidelity speech synthesis.

A scalar field theory, characterized by both harmonic and anharmonic oscillator terms and a complex exponential mass term in a one-dimensional space, has an anharmonic oscillator term that disrupts the orbital stability of solitary waves, as shown in a classical field theory simulation. The study reveals that any small external perturbation is eventually dissipate within a bounded time frame. The presence of the complex exponential mass term however introduces an infinite number of stable localized waves and influences the long-term behavior of scattered waves. The model has an anharmonic oscillator term that makes the model applicable to describe scalar field theories in curved spaces and beyond.

The study of Q-balls in theoretical frameworks featuring multiple stabilizing symmetries is undertaken, with a focus on the concurrent presence of a global U(1) symmetry and a gauge symmetry under the SU(2) group. The researchers identify two primary symmetry-breaking scenarios: either the U(1) symmetry or the SU(2) gauge symmetry, with the possibility of both being broken leading to a complex "thick wall" with multiple domains within the Q-ball. The formation of these domain structures can result in an infinite number of local energy minima, potentially influencing the Q-ball's stability and preventing its decay into the vacuum state. However, the stability of Q-balls is highly dependent on the degree of SU(2) gauge symmetry violation and may be unstable for higher values. The implications of this research arediscussed in relation to the F-term of the baryon number and SU(2)$_R$ symmetry beyond the Standard Model.

A universe model that evolves in cycles, governed by a type of dark energy known as the HDE, has been examined through the lens of a theoretical framework called the GRD cutoff. Studies using a plot that represents the relationship between a cycle's beginning and ending conditions have revealed that without the GRD cutoff, the universe model cannot operate under typical cyclic conditions. The choice of the GRD cutoff significantly influences the model's dynamics as the dark energy density shifts as the cutoff parameter changes, offering a potential means to test the GRD cutoff's relevance. Furthermore, studying the effect of a cycle's duration on the model has demonstrated that as the universe evolves through its cycles, the dark energy density behaves differently, depending on the relationship between a specific parameter and the model's constants.

Let S be the set of complex numbers with positive real parts and let C be a finite
covering of a graph X with edges E. We demonstrate that the L-function, denoted as L(X, s),
can be expressed in terms of its covering space X/E by utilizing the set S, which is
composed of the elements in S that do not share a common starting point with any other
element in S, but do share a common ending point in the cover C. Furthermore, we can
obtain the L-function (X, s) through the process of the Euler product, which is possible
by identifying a set of generators for the collection (S, •). As a result, (X, s) can be
represented as an explicit Dirichlet series.

This paper delves into specific instances of a broader, less understood area of mathematics, concerning the addition of Galois modules over wildly branching finite non-abelian rational field extensions. The theory presented can also be applied to newer results obtained by Mann and Ribes.

The search for particles that live a long time, particularly those that are electrically neutral, is an important area of research that was explored across multiple experiments at the Large Hadron Collider. Due to the varied nature of these searches, no single experimental approach could cover all possible scenarios effectively. As a result, researchers collaborated to identify overlapping regions of interest and undertake coordinated, combined analyses. For certain processes, this involved conducting separate, separate searches with combined statistical evaluations, whereas in the case of supersymmetry, more rigorous joint analyses were performed. These efforts led to combined constraints that are more restrictive than those obtained individually, and in some instances, the combined results exhibited unexpected features that warrant further investigation.

The number of situations in which a sentence can occur significantly influences how language changes. Theoretical linguists suggest that meaning shifts cannot always be attributed to a language's intrinsic factors, as external situations also play a crucial role. However, measuring this external influence on contextual settings and their diverse interpretations has proven challenging. This study presents an innovative approach to organizing contextual contexts based on their relevance to a core concept, using as an example the changing interpretation of the word "awesome" across different contexts and time periods. A new metric is introduced to quantify this external influence, which contradicts the previous assumption that contextual settings are randomly distributed. The research findings suggest that variations in contextual settings have a more substantial impact on conceptual shifts than previously thought. It suggests that researchers should consider improving their data collection methods to better reflect the distribution of contextual contexts, or adjust their assessments of conceptual shifts by taking into account the context variability.

Recent observations of dark matter in galactic cores, or "dark matter halos," have been used to set very strict limits on the mass of ultra-light particles, based on how galaxies rotate. Researchers have now re-evaluated these limits by considering a broader range of ultra-light particle properties, including how galaxies and the broader cosmos are formed. By examining the behavior of dark matter within halos, the outer edges of which are marked by a specific velocity radius, researchers have derived new, more accurate limits that take into account the full spectrum of possible particle behaviors. These new limits have significant implications for a wide range of particle theories, including axion-like particles and scalar field theories that propose dark energy is influenced by the behavior of an ultra-light particle. Based on surveying a significant portion of the nearby cosmos, the study suggests that the mass of these particles should not exceed a certain very small limit, or else it would be inconsistent with observations of the universe's stellar velocities.

To resolve conflicting opinions about the role of retinal neuroblasts' migration speed, we developed a stochastic model to address previous assumptions and create a new, unbiassed estimation of neuroblasts' distribution across the retina. A statistical model was then used to analyze this data, yielding an estimate for the migration multiplicity $\kappa$. Our findings suggest that the migration model supports the "all-or-none" theory, with $\kappa \approx 1$. However, our data also reveal a notable exception at the indirect band of the retina. A 2-stage model now accurately simulates migration patterns observed in organisms, as well as those present in the indirect band, characterized by a lower density of neurons and unique "direct and indirect" migration modes. As a result, we estimate that the migration multiplicity in the indirect band is approximately 3.

In compressed sensing, minimizing mutual coherence in the sensing matrix is vital for efficiently reconstructing images. To address this issue, a mutual coherence-based compression algorithm has been developed, incorporating mutual coherence into a objective function for adaptive compression. The proposed method leverages the characteristics of mutual coherence and adaptive compression to enhance performance during reconstruction. Mutual coherence is modeled as a convex function, allowing for effective optimization using the gradient projection method. Experimental results on real-world image data demonstrate that the proposed approach consistently outperforms traditional methods in terms of PSNR and SSIM metrics.

We've developed a theoretical framework to study active systems across various dimensions. Based on the long-range momentum rules embedded in the Stokes equation, we derived effective theories that account for systems in dimensions between 2 and 5, and tested our models using simulations and theoretical analysis. Comparing our results to linearized hydrodynamics simulations, we discovered that systems in dimensions between 2 and ($d$+1) exhibit distinct scaling behavior. Notably, systems in one-dimensional dilute gases follow the same power-law patterns as those described by hydrodynamics in two-dimensional space. Our approach provides insights into the effects of momentum conservation on the scaling behavior of active systems and may have implications for understanding biological systems such as epithelial layers and flocks.

This research offers an innovative approach to detecting suspicious activity in organizational networks, specifically focusing on the network traffic associated with research institutions. Initially, we gather the network traffic data using the DeepMirror platform and process it using the NxCartesean tool to detect anomalies. The anomaly detection algorithm employed is based on the international anomaly score derived from NxCartesean features, along with supplementary data. The Alagoa machine learning algorithm enhances this score to final anomaly scores, which aid in identifying and preventing cyber threats, such as unauthorized access in research institutions. Case studies are presented to demonstrate the capability of this method to locate and stop suspicious activity, including the unauthorized entry into the Email system of the LAFFEX research institution (part of the EXTREME network).

The global electronic restructuring phase transition, characterized by a Lifshitz transition, occurs in cuprates and is marked by an exceptional van Hove singularity. This transition influences the global properties of electrons across the cuprate family and can be investigated through angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES). By examining the intricate topology of the cuprate electronic band structure, researchers can explore the nuances of this transition. This study presents detailed features of the Lifshitz transition in cuprates and predicts its impact on the material's properties. The exceptional van Hove singularity, situated at the boundary of the hole pocket and the electron pocket, restricts the singularity's effect to certain regions of the material's momentum space. This restriction contributes to the heterogeneity of the cuprate family and influences the symmetry of their structural distortions. Additionally, considering the strong localization of the singularity, it is hypothesized that vortex-like patterns of the Fermi surface, referred to as the "vortex-like electron-crystal," may exist near the van Hove singularity crossing the Fermi level, providing a potential explanation for the heterogeneous properties of cuprates and a new framework for investigating their intricate superconductivity. These predictions can be validated through ARPES, scanning tunneling microscopy (STM), and muon spin relaxation ($\mu$SR) experiments.

Our study explores the neutron detection capabilities of a liquid scintillator containing added Gadolinium, pinpointing its threshold and peak energies with the neutron energies identified via a simulation, cross-checked with real-world neutron flux measurements using $^6$LiEF. The results indicate that LSC+Gd effectively distinguishes between electron-type particles and neutrons based on their recoil properties and that using the simulation to analyze the shape of energy distributions allows for accurate determination of neutron energies.

This paper explores specific applications of the minimax principle from the calculus of variations. In Section 2, we establish conditions for solution persistence in a problem with an invariant set, using the concept of a category from topology. Additionally, we prove solution existence in Section 3 for a singular differential inclusion with an invariant set in the right-hand side, based on the invariant category concept. Finally, in Section 4, we address solution persistence for a variational problem inspired by the Joseph-Lundgren equation, again using the invariant category approach.

Recent studies suggest that a star's properties significantly influence the planetary systems around it, suggesting that observations may be affected by central star properties. To investigate this, researchers used data from TESS, KEPLER, and RADIX to analyze the occurrence rate of planets within specific ranges around 1049 stars with various properties. By measuring occurrence rates of different planet types and analyzing their relationship with the stars' properties, researchers found that planetary occurrences are linked to the stars' properties, including their activity, mass, and rotation period. This relationship varies by planet type, with gas dwarfs showing the strongest dependence on stellar activity, while small planets exhibit weaker dependencies. To quantify this, researchers defined the "architecture diversity" of a system as the range of planet types present, which is broader for more active stars with a larger population of different planet types coexisting. This has implications for the search for habitable zones and the design of future space missions.

To achieve high accuracy in extracting information from ID cards, machine extraction
techniques must be accurate and precise, which is where NLP comes in to accurately
interpret text. In order to improve the performance of our system, we incorporated
various NLP components, including name segmentation, part-of-speech tagging, and a
custom-built network that can recognize the structure of Chinese IDs. By integrating
this ID structure system with our other tools, our system was able to successfully
parse 1 million IDs with a high level of precision.

A new framework has been introduced to study driven quantum systems, called the dynamics of coherent states approach. This framework relies on constructing a coherent state basis through the displacement of the system's Heisenberg anti-derivatives and employs resolved sideband conditions to simplify interactions. Notable applications have been made to models such as the Lindblad master equation, showing that states with common annihilation patterns exhibit predictable decay rates. Furthermore, the framework has been applied to multi-mode systems and shown that Fock states can be viewed as a type of coherent state, enabling efficient calculation of evolution from initial states.

The @HOME radio telescope has successfully captured high-resolution radio images of four comets and a cluster of sources near Crater~A421, making it only the second facility capable of achieving this level of detail radio imaging in these areas. Furthermore, by analyzing the motion of detected asteroids across multiple observations, we have discovered compelling evidence suggesting that their rotation is consistently accelerated by +0.02~as~s$^{-1}$~s$^{-1}$. This finding is significant as it suggests the presence of rotational acceleration in these asteroids. Additionally, we found that the sources belong to different frequency ranges and exhibit similar spatial and spectral characteristics to other Galactic neutral hydrogen clouds. Based on our detection of accelerated rotation, we hypothesize that the sources could be accelerating within the Lyncis~A binary system's gravitational influence. This discovery is significant in linking the accelerated rotation to their interaction with the Lyncis~A binary system.

The evolution of online community structure is influenced by both dynamic individual behavior and feedback mechanisms from the broader environment. We examine the molecular-level interactions that both provide and respond to social feedback within a specific online forum, specifically "Antisemitismus.de", a far-right discussion board. Our analysis focuses on a unique online discussion thread and employs large-scale network data spanning nearly two years, capturing both the forum's structural and content aspects. Our research breaks down the forum's membership into distinct groups, identifying how each user contributes to different discussion segments. Our key finding is that online community cohesion is largely shaped by individual behavior, with notable exceptions where the forum's environment influences both opinion and behavior, resulting in significant intergroup mobility. Our data reveals that users who engage with diverse viewpoints are more likely to encounter new views, which in turn is more prevalent in far-right communities.

Given a non-zero element γ in a discrete group G that acts on a compact surface X with one or more connected components, this study examines the conditions under which the set of all non-negative powers of γ form a precompact collection when combined with the surface's interior. It demonstrates that the way γ moves points within the surface's connected components is either fully consistent across all components, entirely absent from any component's boundary, or completely different from the previous option. Furthermore, if there is at least one connected component where combining the positive and negative powers of γ with the surface's interior forms a precompact collection, it will also apply to the combined collection with X itself. Finally, it is is possible to identify the specific movement pattern of γ within the surface's connected components combined with the boundary.

A new set of M-dwarf mass-radius data has been utilized to derive a new power-law
relationship, which is now a key component in characterizing low-mass stars.
However, given the variable and non-uniform nature of the data set, fitting a simple
two-variable relationship isn't sufficient. To address this, a more complex fitting
method has been implemented which accounts for individual data point uncertainties,
as well as intrinsic variability, in order to derive a more accurate and reliable
mass-radius relationship. The new model has been fitted using the IRASP software,
and the results demonstrate a significant improvement in fit when incorporating
intrinsically scattered data points. The new model has also been re-examined given the
discovery of radius anomalies in M-dwarfs, which has implications for our current
understanding of these stars. While M-dwarfs with helium hydride have been proposed
as a potential explanation, the exact cause of these anomalies remains unclear and
further research is required to fully explain this phenomenon.

A new subtype of optical waveguide known as line waves has gained significant interest in integration-circuit design. Recent research demonstrates line waves can be created and manipulated using multimode interference in waveguides and their surrounding environment. However, their high sensitivity to external perturbations limits their usage in complex circuit boards. To mainline's integrity in complex graphene circuits, we designed a graphene patch that can effectively isolate line waves from multimode interference and localized energy distributions near the waveguide tips. Using finite difference time domain method, the multilayer graphene waveguide was simulated to confirm the patch's efficiency across a broad frequency range and graphene parameter variation. The patch-to-waveguide size ratio was found to be critical in achieving optimal isolation performance, and the graphene patch's dimensions were determined based on the multilayer waveguide's thickness to maximize line waves' propagation loss rate reduction, exhibiting good performance and broad-banded MI line waves isolator characteristics.

We extend the concept of self-joins by allowing a query to reference itself multiple times within different parts, and investigate its evaluation cost. Our research identifies a key rule: a query is classifiable as efficiently evaluable if and only, all its self-joint connections can be classified individually. This classification was previously established for self-joins with less flexibility, and it also builds upon earlier findings by demonstrating the efficacy of a specific technique using a graph-based representation, and expanding its application to self-joins with flexible conditions. Additionally, we have enhanced our self-join framework by allowing arbitrary first-order logic relation definitions and flexible logic within both query components, and have demonstrated these enhancements through various example queries.

We investigate the continuity of rational functions defined by a sequence of multivariate polynomial pieces, where the number of variables, degree, and number of pieces are all constant.决定连续性是否属于NC^1类还是其在NC^1之外属于第1个P^{\#L}类。通过引入新的逻辑框架，我们将连续性检验与一阶逻辑的片段连续性检验联系起来。此外，我们建立了从连续性检验到#L-reduction的#L-reduction。

A distinction is drawn between the penguin-dominated $b\to s\mu^+\mu^-$ transitions in $B^0_s$ decays and the tree-dominated channels in $B^+$ or $B^0$ decays, which can be enhanced by electroweak penguin contributions with different signs.  With the possible exception of the angular analysis, the $B^0$ and $B^0_s$ poles will be subject to the same constraints due to the same form factors in CKM-suppressed penguin channels.  Considering SM expectations and various BPSPS scenarios, we estimate the $B^0$ polarization fraction in the $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decay and the $B^0_s$ polarization fraction in the $B^0_s\to \phi\mu^+\mu^-$ decay to be approximately 50\% and 90\% respectively, differing by 40\% and making them susceptible to experimental verification.

This study explores the effectiveness of using reservoir computing for predicting the dynamic behavior of complex systems exhibiting multiple time scales and distinct dynamical states, such as the Lorenz-96 system. The research aims to evaluate the computer's capacity to capture various co-existing dynamics and understand reservoir computing's performance in real-world applications. A key finding is that the computer's performance declines as the difference between fast and slow dynamics increases, an outcome that can be explained by an underlying theoretical concept. Moreover, the study reveals that training data from both fast and slow dynamical regimes is essential for accurate prediction of either state, validating the underlying explanation.

A key issue with bias-reduced estimation is that conventional approaches, like adjusting the naive mean and covariance estimators by adjusting their degrees of freedom, lead to non-smooth estimates of covariance matrices. These estimated matrices exhibit abrupt changes in their scaling properties, scaling by $n$ rather than $\sqrt{n}$. This behavior hinders their use in dynamic modeling and learning algorithms that rely on the continuity of gradient functions. In this paper, we present a novel bias-reduced estimator for the high-dimensional covariance matrix that is based on the Lasso and allows for a continuous, Lipschitz continuous, estimation of the covariance matrix estimate, scaling by $\sqrt{n}$. This estimator is shown to be statistically efficient and we further develop an adaptive Lasso variant to the high-dimensional family of Garmaim-Lasso, and establish its optimal selection of the penalty parameter.

This paper examines how reachable state sets can be determined for hybrid automata within a specified time frame under feedback control. It demonstrates that the reusability and closure properties of this computation can be leveraged to apply the computation of reachable state sets to systems with feedback control. It also explores the implications of this approach by considering systems that must satisfy multiple temporal constraints.

The proposed local-functional representation (LFR) expands upon the representational capabilities of conventional functional representations (FRs). While FRs excel at capturing low-dimensional characteristics within a broader context, they fall short when applied to complex functions with multiple components. The LFR addresses this limitation by incorporating FR-like elements into each local component, thereby enhancing its ability to capture multiple distinct parts. Despite being an expansion of the existing FR framework, the LFR maintains interpretability within its enhanced capacity. By integrating local and global information, the LFR demonstrates superior generalization performance, particularly when working with a limited amount of training data. Its effectiveness and efficiency are confirmed through confirmation through various signal processing applications, including combining the LFR with the group-scattering transform to enhance its ability to learn group-sparse transforms.

Although commonly employed to classify entities as living or non-living, the concept of animacy is often viewed as a continuous and gradual spectrum. This study aims to examine how two distinct aspects - agency and visual categorizability - influence the perceived level of animacy in various entities. A unique system was implemented to measure the perceived animacy and entity type in a single, continuous scale. Our results indicate that both agency and visual categorizability contribute to animacy perception, with their combined effect being non-additive. Furthermore, our data reveals that entity type is interpreted through the lens of the perceived animacy, demonstrating that perceived categories play a more significant role in prediction than doable physical properties. This study's approach to modeling perceived category and agency using a continuous framework provides a more nuanced understanding of the relationship between these aspects and the concept of animacy.

A recent study proposes that zeros of automorphic L-functions located on the critical line at a given group exist and cluster further from the line by a margin that aligns with the variation in zero depths. The author argues that the non-clustering observation at the line's center is likely due to the presence of a Landau-Siegel zero. The paper contains an forecast for the clustering behavior, which can be understood through the clustering of zeros in families of L-functions with known zeros, particularly in the context of Katz's angle variation. Furthermore, the author asserts that the minimum spacing theorem for zeros can be explained by the existence of a Landau-Siegel zero. The proof of this argument relies on the concept of an orbifold associated with a family of L-functions, which is linked to its conductor function and symmetry group. If this orbifold has positive area, it indicates the presence of a Landau-Siegel zero. The paper provides examples showing that the minimum spacing and zero clustering are fundamentally the same phenomenon, which is driven by the size of the orbifold. Additionally, the paper proves specific values for the minimum spacing and clustering in auto-dual, square-free Dirichlet character, and holomorphic modular L-function families.

A key challenge in specifying quantum software is capturing the desired input-output behavior. We've developed a quantitative framework for quantum relational Hoare logic and derived measurement rules for its assertions. These tools enable the quantitative verification of quantum programs' inputs and outputs.

The spread of superspreader incidents played a significant role in the COVID-19 epidemic's success in certain enclosed locations. Due to this, conventional epidemiological models are unreliable when modeling infections in such settings. A unique stochastic agent-based model was developed for this purpose, which accounts for multiscale time and the unique infection dynamics influenced by superspreading events in enclosed locations. When compared to standard models, the new approach generated a non-Gaussian infection time distribution, which was further validated using real patient data from the COVID-19 outbreak in Skagit County, USA in November 2020. A key indicator was utilized to assess the model's accuracy, which showed a notable match with the observed infection times after a certain time period. Additionally, an explicit equation was derived to estimate the mean infection time within a given population under specific conditions.

We have established criteria for the codiskcyclicity of $C_0$-semigroups and operator semidescriptors defined by complex numbers with negative real parts. Additionally, we derived codiskcyclicity properties for certain compact operator classes, specifically Riesz operators with image dimension less than two, and specific complex matrices.

We evaluated the impact of explicitly including magnetic fill fraction within vector magnetic field maps on field strength estimations. By examining two datasets - one with incomplete magnetically filled regions and the other representing a complete filling - we assessed the difference between traditional and new approaches that incorporate fill fraction into calculations. The results indicated that account for fill fraction is vital for accurate estimations, with a notable difference of median absolute deviation of 157 Gauss. Furthermore, we demonstrated that neglecting fill fraction can lead to underestimating peak field strengths, which could potentially mask the presence of critical flux concentrations.

A new technique is proposed to study the physical characteristics of young star clusters in the Large Magellanic Cloud using the JWST. The method takes into account the non-Gaussian spatial distribution of stars within the clusters, which is a significant factor in the selection process of suitable candidates for in-depth analysis. The new approach was tested on the Scorpius-Ophiuchus region in the Milky Way, where the star clusters' properties, such as the radius of the 50% light containment, the 20% mass fraction, the stellar surface density, and the stellar age, are considered. The findings from the study reveal a trend of decreasing star cluster density with increasing age, as well as an inverse relationship between density and size. The new approach is expected to be a valuable guide for conducting spectral energy distributions of the clusters and identifying the "missing link" between open clusters and globular clusters with the JWST.

We have developed a universal formula to determine the decay width of a one-body decay process $PV\rightarrow P\gamma$ within lattice QCD, with established applicability beyond its current context. This established framework allows the calculation of decay amplitude from lattice data, incorporating relevant factors like Schwinger terms and finite-volume effects, and we demonstrate its flexibility through multiple computational scenarios.

We introduced the concept of complex variational inference and developed complex normalizing flows as a flexible approximation method for complex-valued distributions.
Our approach leverages affine coupling layers that operate on complex numbers, enabling an efficient and invertible transformation of real probability distributions into complex ones.
However, despite these innovations, applying the method to large-scale Monte Carlo simulations was hindered by computational inefficiencies caused by coupled real and imaginary components interacting during transformations.
We overcame this limitation by integrating a direct complex number implementation in Python with the SciPy library, significantly boosting performance of the transform operations and making large-scale simulations economically feasible again.

A polynomial $f(x_1, \dots, x_d)$ with non-negative integer coefficients is called non-degenerate if, for any non-zero direction $\vec{u}$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, the function obtained by restricting $f$ to that direction is non-degenerate. This paper builds on earlier work by Golynski, Kaczorowski, and Trifonov to expand the asymptotic formula for $\rho(s; P, Q)$, which quantifies the count of $y$-friable integers not exceeding $x$ and divisible by one of the first $s$ primes. This expansion is achieved up to an exponentially small error term, provided $\frac{\text{log } x}{\text{log } y}$ is sufficiently large, with possible exceptions in specific directions. Notably, under the assumption of the Riemann Hypothesis, the expected count of $y$-friable integers divisible by the first $s$ primes can be shown to be exponentially large even when $x=y$. This conclusion is derived from an application of the asymptotic formula, supported by prior work of Golynski and the authors.

Consider an irreducible, non-uniformly recurrent subshift defined over a finite set of symbols with a fixed irreducible transition matrix. When this subshift undergoes a recognizable transformation, can it be classified as having the property of being almost periodic in a hybrid sense? Furthermore, can we establish a formula for calculating its topological entropy, and investigate how its topological entropy changes in response to a given transformation?

The task of zero-shot spatial reasoning for natural language queries remains largely unsolved for natural language processing systems. This challenge is compounded by the need for these systems to have a comprehensive understanding of the spatial relationships in the world, as well as the ability to perform complex compositional reasoning. Building upon a simple yet effective framework that utilizes pre-trained language models combined with natural language inference, we propose a unique unsupervised learning setting in which the system is assumed to have access to natural language inference capabilities. This setting enables the model to perform complex compositional reasoning and gain a deeper understanding of the spatial relationships in the world. In this setting, we demonstrate that a novel training approach, called ReCross, which performs a unique combination of unsupervised fine-tuning and natural language inference, significantly outperforms other methods, achieving a major improvement in performance without any supervised learning. This approach achieves a significant improvement in performance on the Spatial preUnderstanding for Multi-compositional reasoning and Natural language Understanding (SUMN) benchmark, surpassing the current state-of-the-art results in this challenging task.

This paper introduces a novel dimensionality reduction method called the n-Kernel Arithmetic Expansion (n-ar-K) which builds upon the ar-K function (ar-Ker-n) introduced previously. The new ar-K function serves as a replacement for the ar-K function by addressing its limitation of not being able to capture both the local and global structure of data simultaneously. Unlike its predecessor, the new ar-K function maintains compatibility with a vast array of dimensionality reduction techniques available today. A key difference between the two functions lies in their treatment of the 'kernel' concept - while the previous ar-K function viewed the kernel as a one-dimensional projection of the original data, the novel ar-K function sees the kernel as an intrinsic characteristic of the data itself. We demonstrate our proposed method's effectiveness using a synthetic dataset and multiple real-world datasets in comparison to its predecessor and other popular dimensionality reduction techniques like t-SNE and SNE-ar-K.

Playing video games has become the primary hobby for many individuals globally.
Despite its significance, there is limited scientific knowledge on game developers who
produce games as a niche market. This study presents an exploratory analysis that
seeks to develop a theoretical framework for game developers' requirements
engineering. Through the collection and analysis of 30 interviews, along with a
subsequent validation interview, we validate our initial findings and refine our
conceptual model. As a result, we identify five key processes: industry motivation,
goal identification, requirement derivation from games, requirement specification,
and a new process of intermediate product design. Additionally, we discuss the
limitations of this study and propose future research directions, including the
application of our model to specific game developers and the exploration of particular
aspects, such as the role of requirements engineering in successful game development
projects, industry motivation, and modeling tools used in game development.

An important aspect of machine learning development involves the tuning of model hyperparameters. While straightforward cases allow for the use of efficient techniques like grid search, more complex scenarios require advanced methods such as reinforcement learning. Unfortunately, these approaches generally assume access to complete datasets, making them ineffective for training data that is divided into discrete parts and accessed separately. This new research explores the use of hyperparameter optimization for multiple clients with private training datasets accessed without being combined. It introduces grid search and policy planning as feasible starting points for clients that do not have to share any information with one another. The research was tested using real-world medical and sentiment analysis datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness and practical applicability of the proposed approach.

Given the number $n$ and a set $S$ containing $n$ elements from the sphere $S^{d-1}$ in a $d$-dimensional Euclidean space, let W denote the group generated by reflections across the hyperplanes that are perpendicular to the elements of $S$. Under appropriate conditions, the sphere $S^{d-1}$ can be divided into a finite number of non-overlapping spheres through the action of W, where the number of spheres corresponds to the number of elements in a simple collection of $S$. Under more general conditions, we can determine whether the group W can be expressed as a product of reflection groups, each using a different set of elements from $S$ to define the perpendicular hyperplanes.

We have refined the noise model used in the 21-cm brightness temperature power spectrum analysis, specifically addressing the issue of correlated noise. By adapting the standard least squares approach to account for correlated noise, or utilizing the maximum likelihood approach, we can obtain more precise estimates of the cosmological signal. These methodologies have been applied to simulate data collected by the Square Kilometre Array Low prototype, and the results indicate that the current noise model can lead to significant errors, especially at high frequencies. Both adapted and standard analysis methods yield comparable conclusions at lower frequencies, the former benefiting from the increased spatial sensitivity of the SKA Low to correlated noise. We have demonstrated that a semi-analytical model can provide a more accurate representation of the noise, significantly reducing standard residuals by up to a factor of ten, particularly at high frequencies where the standard model falls short.

A thorough examination of approximately 150,000 stars using the APKeys pipeline has led to the discovery of around 600 stars with distinct chemical compositions and 900 groups of stars with distinct kinematic characteristics. A detailed analysis of residual abundances has been performed to better understand these chemically distinctive stars and the method employed can be applied to larger datasets in the future, providing valuable insights into stars and population structures with deeper significance.
