In this study, we apply an adaptive mean field theory to analyze the dynamics of rumor propagation on a random hypergraph, deriving a general expression for the peak and attenuation coefficients. This expression incorporates precursor terms and location information, which align with intuitive expectations; for instance, we demonstrate that the peak of a subsequent rumor is influenced by a combination of an intrinsic precursor term and a graph-theoretic component, which can be further broken down into average degree components. Our theoretical predictions are supported by Monte Carlo simulations, and we also use this framework to examine the propagation of sequential rumors.

We have studied 1899 local group of the Fornax cluster's planetary nebulae within an redshift range of 0.005 less than z to 0.03, utilizing the photometric and astrometric information from the DR8 SDSS. We distance determined the cluster's average distance by constructing the planetary nebulae luminosity function, which yielded 19.665 Mpc, in agreement with the value of 20.123 Mpc, using the Tully-Fisher method. We also observed the radial velocity distribution of the Fornax cluster's planetary nebulae, which confirmed the 405 km s-1 of the cluster's 20.123 Mpc, radial velocity along the line of sight, which was consistent with 405 km s-1 405 km s-1. We also discovered 8 new members of the Fornax cluster, which were found to be located within 210-244 Mpc, using the planetary nebulae, which were found to be of types E1-E2, which were found to be associated with the Fornax cluster, which was found to be of types SB0, which were found to be associated with the Fornax cluster, which were found to be of types 0.002 less than r to 0.02, which were found to be associated with the

We introduce "LifeStream", an open-source real stream processing platform built on top of Apache Spark, designed to handle continuous queries on real-time data. Unlike traditional optimized numerical libraries, we have found that by combining the power of LifeStream with the JavaStream API, developers can create applications that perform comparably while enjoying the benefits of writing the same, uncomplicated code. Furthermore, we have discovered that LifeStream's performance can surpass that of the industry-leading numerical processing benchmark "Tachyon", and in certain cases, it has been found to be capable of processing real-world datasets in near real-time without accumulating significant data backlogs.

This research extends the concept of Bertrand curves to Finsler, Eisenhart, and
Randers geometry by first defining Bertrand curves within these specific geometries and
then establishing their distinct characteristics.

To better comprehend various loss functions and their respective optimizers in deep learning, we created a comprehensive benchmark framework that evaluates numerous loss function-optimizer combinations. Our framework specifically focuses on evaluating under-performing loss functions, including those that have been neglected, such as KL Divergence, and demonstrates our findings through an expansive experimentation consisting of 2.7 million runs across multiple network architectures, optimization methods, datasets, and tasks. Our research highlights key findings, including the incompatibility of certain optimizer-family and loss function-family combinations, the inferior performance of specialized loss functions when used with standard optimizers, and the potential for novel optimizers to outperform established ones, such as Adam, in specific scenarios. Our framework is openly accessible to the public at https://lossbench.com/.

This research paper investigates the impact of temperature control on the left boundary through a unique perspective on the Navier-Stokes equations. The equation's dynamics are influenced by a feedback mechanism, where the boundary condition adapts based on the difference between desired and actual temperatures at a specific point in space. Unlike traditional methods that focus on forcing or boundary value problems, this study examines how the feedback automatically drives the system towards a target temperature, thus resolving the setpoint problem. It is demonstrated that for non-monotone feedback functions, globally stable solutions can be achieved and exponential stability has been proven for certain functions commonly used in thermal control applications.

This paper addresses strain-induced crystallization in polymers and their blends,
which are commonly employed to enhance mechanical properties and modify
thermal characteristics. To facilitate a comprehensive understanding of
thermomechanical behavior, including crystallization under mechanical stress,
this work develops a constitutive model drawing on hyperelastic free energy
functions, viscous dissipation, and entropy-based relaxation principles.
These concepts enable the formulation of a coupled system governing the
evolution of crystalline and amorphous network states, combined with the
mechanical balance of linear momentum and the equation for internal energy
balance. Moreover, given the typically endothermic nature of crystallization,
this model can be modified to account for exothermic processes, as observed
in certain polymer blends. To illustrate various phenomena, this model is
applied to specific examples and simulated using an explicit numerical
scheme, demonstrating its capability to simulate strain-induced crystallization,
stress relaxation, and crystallization occurring in response to sudden
temperature changes.

A detailed investigation into an unconventional, multi-gap type of electronic structure has been undertaken, focusing on the case of a non-spherical, torus-shaped Fermi surface. This surface is characteristic of the heavy-fermion material CePt2Si2. A perturbative approach, suitable for systems with large electron band mass, was utilized to analyze both conventional properties, such as chemical composition and temperature, and quantum mechanical fluctuations, of both electron behavior and pairing, in the context of spin-fluctuation-driven superconductivity. Our study found that the unconventional geometry of the torus-shaped Fermi surface induces a non-monotonic pattern in the magnetic susceptibility as a function of quantum mechanical fluctuations, and that the surface's topology critically influences the superconductivity's properties, particularly in terms of the pairing mechanism. A mixed-type, normal-superconducting phase transition is identified, and that the surface's geometry may result in the coexistence of superconducting and magnetic order, and that the pairing mechanism may give way to electronic behavior dominance as quantum mechanical fluctuations increase, and that the surface's geometry may lead to the emergence of an unstable, isolated superconducting phase. A quantitative assessment of the critical strength of quantum mechanical fluctuations required for these transitions, in terms of the surface's geometric parameters, and the resulting implications, has been established, and that the surface's geometry may lead to a normal state with chemical equilibrium, and that the surface's geometry may result in the coexistence of super
To how does the effectiveness of a system's instructor feature rely on its ability to offer individualized and targeted feedback from experienced operators?

A novel decision-feedback differential detection method is proposed for continuous-phase modulation (CPM) signals, which can differentiate between data "1" and "0", thereby enabling coherent detection. By incorporating a differential decoder and a maximum likelihood sequence detector, the algorithm reconstitutes the phase of CPM signals. Simulations show that this decision-feedback approach yields a 3 dB performance gain in error rate compared to conventional differential detection, and it achieves similar results to coherent detection with minimal additional computation, even in the presence of high noise levels.

A gravitational wave event involving the merger of a black hole and a neutron star may become more common, with the possibility of detecting an electromagnetic counterpart that provides crucial information about neutron star physics, nuclear matter at high densities, and reionization of the universe. To increase the likelihood of such a counterpart, the neutron star must shrink to a small radius, which also implies a shorter chirp mass in the merger. To examine this, we have analyzed the distribution of neutron star radii based on the mass of the merging black hole, or conversely, analyzed the chirp mass distribution to infer the distribution of neutron star radii. We have also explored how this is reflected in the gravitational wave signal, with specific parameters such as the post-Newtonian coefficient and higher order waveform coefficients having an impact on the inferred neutron star tidal deformability. To account for this, we have constructed templates that include tidal deformability and matched-filtered them with observational data, with a focus on limiting the tidal Love number and estimating any associated uncertainties. When assuming uniform distributions, we have constrained the tidal Love number, with specific estimates of the range and median value, with a notable uncertainty. To further refine this, we have analyzed the distribution of neutron star radii with respect to the merging neutron star, or a mass ratio, or within specific distance ranges, or when considering system inclination, or in all-sky scenarios. This analysis has provided insights into the distribution of neutron star radii under various conditions, with specific

The utility of statistical mechanical ensembles lies in their ability to replicate the system's behavior, as measured by macroscopic physical quantities, under specific conditions. A direct system of equations in thermodynamics corresponds to an microcanonical ensemble, whereas indirect systems, such as those governed by the canonical, grand canonical, or isobaric-ensemble, employ measures that facilitate comparisons with real-world experiments. These measure-modifying steps introduce additional variables, like temperature, chemical potential, and pressure, which cannot be precisely determined from the original internal variables, such as energy, volume, and pressure. The ensemble equivalency theorems suggest that the distinction between ensembles vanishes when the number of original particles rises significantly, under the assumption that the inter-particle forces are short-range. The reliability of this assumption is investigated through a theoretical model, where the relationship between the grand canonical ensemble's validity and the system's compressibility, at constant pressure, is examined through a theoretical link to the Riemann zeta function. This connection is then extended to show that a similar relationship exists between the validity of canonical ensemble equivalence and the system's pressure oscillations.

Existing rain generation evaluation metrics fail to account for rain removal.
Calibration-based metrics like PSNR and SSIM rely on rain-free ground truths,
which are rarely available in real-world scenarios.
To rectify this issue, we introduce a rain generation and removal evaluation
metric that establishes a direct relationship between the quality of rain
synthesis and the effectiveness of rain removal.
Our framework establishes an inverse loss function connecting rain synthesis
and removal, thereby enabling end-to-end training without the need for clean
images.
To demonstrate our method, we devise a synthetic dataset consisting of real
images with rain, artificially synthesized rain, and rain-free ground truths.
Moreover, we propose two rain detection strategies to respectively measure
main rain attributes in order to guide and evaluate rain removal.
To evaluate the performance of rain generation and removal, we transform
two detection strategies into corresponding loss functions.
Moreover, we introduce a rain removal evaluation function that is inversely
proportional to the rain attribute loss function.
To validate the effectiveness of our method, we conduct rain removal
experiments on our dataset and objectively as well as subjectively evaluate
the results, which objectively confirm the consistency between rain
generation and removal, and subjectively indicate that our method can
measure rain removal performance in practical applications.

A human feedback-based approach to learning rewards typically involves a slow, iterative process that efficiently uses feedback but also takes an excessively long time. To simultaneously achieve efficient utilization of feedback and a much faster learning process, this document introduces a method that allows for the batch processing of comparison judgments made by a human. This method uses a simple yet effective technique to identify the comparisons with the highest uncertainty according to a current reward model. It then utilizes a human to evaluate these comparisons in groups, making it possible to obtain a large quantity of high-quality feedback in a short period of time. The method is straightforward to implement and can be applied to any type of feedback formulation. As a practical demonstration, it describes the development of an application designed for the learning of rewards in the context of math problems, which utilizes human feedback in batches. This application shows that it can solve the previously mentioned problem, resulting in a substantial improvement in the quality of the model, with a $15$ point increase, under conditions where it was trained on just $100$ samples, and a user interface that enables a single human to solve several thousand problems in a day, leading to a significant improvement in the method's performance, with a $3$ point increase, in the user interface scenario.

We investigate the impact of formalizing set theory through the axioms of MacLane on macrologic, specifically how the choice of signature and macLogic's principles interact in the context of the theory of MacLane. By analyzing the signature and macLogic's axioms, we can determine the impact of macrologic on the theory of MacLane.

Additionally, the research detected changes in consumption patterns of the above drugs during the COVID-19 lockdown period in New York City.

The task of if-then relation extraction involves identifying events that are connected by conditional dependencies, which have gained significant attention recently due to their applications in medical diagnosis and scientific reasoning. The reliance on textual cues to represent entities with conditional relationships makes this task particularly challenging, and existing methods that employ sequential models or attention mechanisms fall short in capturing the logical and structural features of the text. The variability in the expressions of if-then relations adds another layer of complexity, and the hierarchical nature of the relation classes suggests the potential for improvement through the incorporation of tree-structured information during training. Our research explores the use of pre-trained language models and data augmentation to address these challenges and achieve better performance, and the experiments demonstrate that the models can successfully capture the required features, leading to significant gains in performance when trained with the use of tree-structured information, and using a span-based model instead of a span-embedding one also results in notable improvements when combined with our proposed methods. The proposed techniques set a new record for the if-then relation extraction task, and our results suggest that the model is capable of producing coherent outputs with minimal human guidance, and the proposed methods pave the way for handling other tasks that involve logical or structural features and variability in expression.

This paper introduces an innovative method for integrating linguistic knowledge into neural network-based automated speech recognition systems through a bidirectional attention mechanism (BiAM). The proposed mechanism allows linguistic knowledge to influence speech representations by computing a bidirectional interaction between speech features and linguistic information through the use of multiple attention masks. Experimental results show significant improvements in the system's accuracy, with BiAM yielding a 0.7% reduction in error rate compared to a baseline on the challenging TestClean evaluation set. Additionally, visualizations of the attention masks reveal that the mechanism effectively captures local unidirectional linguistic relationships in written text, allowing for a deeper understanding of the speech-to-text mapping process.

We have mathematically proven that in two, three, and higher dimensions, certain minimal surface configurations referred to as "horns" don't exist in forms that remain unchanged over time when considering small adjustments, considering the area and closure constraints in a unit sphere. This finding excludes particular cases of globally compact configurations and&Dhruv-Lohkamp-Wu types. Additionally, we provide specific surface examples called "horns" for the unit sphere in three-dimensional space.

This study transforms traditional parking problems by introducing a dynamic sequence of car preferences as n grows, where the first k_n positions on a half-line become marked, based on a random sequence of n integers. If the sequence is independent and identically distributed, the probability of a particular configuration of the first k_n positions can be calculated as π_n(k_n), with an infinite sum of this probability equaling one. The paper explores various rates of k_n and references related studies from the field of probabilistic modeling and random walk theory. Notably, it establishes that a relatively fast rate of k_n (specifically, when 1 ≤ k_n is much smaller than √n log n) results in the distribution of the k_n positions, when rescaled, approaching a known mathematical function as n grows large. Additionally, it proves a similar convergence for the case of randomly ordered integers and indicates potential lines of investigation for future research. The paper's findings are further discussed in relation to their implications for parking problems and random walk theory.

Research into quantum phase transitions in mesoscopic systems has been revolutionized by nanowires made of hybrid normal-superconducting materials. These nanowires exhibit a critical threshold, known as 'critical voltage,' for breaking superconductivity. By utilizing a DC bias, the critical voltage of these nanowires can be disrupted or restored, demonstrating their potential for use in quantum-mechanical switches. However, the initial restoration of superconductivity at lower critical voltages hinders this application. A theoretical model has been developed for a nanowire connected to two reservoirs with differing chemical potentials. According to this model, by tweaking the nanowire's parameters, superconductivity can be guaranteed to fail or be reliably maintained under specific chemical potential conditions. Furthermore, the model reveals that, for a given range of disruption, there is a minimum threshold for restoring superconductivity at lower critical voltages, offering new insights for designing quantum-mechanical switch devices.

Exoplanetary brown dwarfs share a common formation process with planets and stars, yet relatively little is known about this process for these intermediate-sized objects. By comparing the observed features of an object in the near and mid-infrared with detailed atmospheric simulations, our research has identified that the brown dwarf GJ 229B (specifically, its satellite "Phoebe") contains a small amount of hydrogen sulfide, no silicon monoxide or carbon monoxide, and its temperature ranges from 640 to 710 Kelvin. Using further statistical analysis, we have determined that the size of Phoebe is around 27,300 to 32,400 Kelvin with 95% confidence. This finding demonstrates that comparing observations with model data can help us understand the physical characteristics of distant brown dwarfs, providing a useful benchmark for researchers in the future.

Researchers have derived the PDF for a quark plasma without interactions, denoted as $f(x,\mathcal{T})$, incorporating spin, where $x$ represents the fraction of hadron momentum, and $\mathcal{T}$ is the temperature. These calculations have been performed for both non-relativistic and relativistic regimes. In the process, the perturbative expression has been used to account for parton interactions within the J/$\psi$ factorization theorem, specifically in the process of heavy quark pair production. Notably, the result is applicable to any distribution function characterizing the parton interactions. In particular, the result has been used in connection with both a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution and a relativistic Hadron Resonance Gas model to reevaluate the pseudo-exclusive $p-\pi^{0}$ $J/\psi$ cross section as a function of $p_{\rm T}$ at LHC energies.

Our proposed method leverages a dual representation from complementary perspectives to reconstruct videos from unseen viewpoints. This unique approach, combined with the coupling of multiview features, allows for accurate video predictions. Not only does it achieve high-quality results, but it also provides a flexible framework that can be fine-tuned for various tasks, leading to improved performance. Furthermore, our method's computational efficiency and modularity make it suitable for processing high-resolution videos in real-time.

A phase beam splitter device leveraging two higher-order photonic modes, specifically a hybrid GP01+GPP01 group of modes, has been calculated and experimentally realized in an air-core photonic bandgap fiber. Numerical simulations indicate that this beam splitter can effectively generate small angle between the two orthogonal components without significant GP01 mode contamination. We exhort researchers to take advantage of this novel phase beam splitter in their future investigations.

Using a light-front quark model, we calculated the mass spectra for various resonance states of the $\Sigma_c$ baryon in terms of radial and spin numbers. The calculation employed a light-front quark current and considered two-quark and three-quark interactions. The study involved applying the Melosh rotation to a light-cone wave function, determining a mass operator, and applying a light-front quark model with a linear confining potential. The resulting mass spectra were tabulated and the light-front quark model's predictions were compared with experimental data, showing good agreement.

A new statistical model has been proposed to predict the distribution of aerosol particles in an enclosed space, considering varying inhalation and emission rates of an infected person moving around within that space. To evaluate the accuracy of this model, its results were compared to two other existing models: a well-mixed model commonly used in epidemiology and a more complex computational fluid dynamics model simulated using multiple real-world movement videos of an individual in a small room. While the well-mixed model offered adequate general predictions, it failed to accurately forecast the aerosol concentration distribution around the infected individual. In contrast, the simulation provided an extremely detailed view of the aerosol distribution but could not fully capture the underlying physics due to neglected factors such as the emission of heat and moisture. Although the proposed statistical model and the simulation yielded similar predictions, a discrepancy was found when aerosol clouds interacted with the airflow created by body heat. To address this issue, a new simulation incorporating thermal effects was developed and found the well-mixed model to be more accurate in these situations. Furthermore, an analysis was conducted to evaluate how the concentration of aerosols decayed over time in a confined space with no airflow, considering various degrees of mixing. Notably, the well-mixed model significantly underpredicted the aerosol concentration in areas around the infected individual compared to the degree of mixing model.

Quantum vacuum diffraction and birefringence occur due to varying gravitational potentials, causing effects to depend on the direction of x-ray photon propagation. In areas of equal potential, the birefringence effect surpasses the diffraction effect in magnitude. Additionally, we offer a new interpretation of the Casimir force, interpreting it as a result of vacuum birefringence and the subsequent conversion of gravitational energy into photon energy. This understanding reveals that vacuum diffraction and birefringence, as well as the traditional explanation of the Casimir force, are manifestations of standing wave phenomena. In contrast, the relationship between the speed of light and the speed of gravity becomes clear, and we argue that the gravitational potential is actually dimensionless, reflecting the ratio of mass to the critical mass of the universe.

We developed an algorithm that applies a specific class of construction methods to produce fully transitive polyhedra in three-dimensional space. The algorithm is centered on the algorithm for the Stein surface, which transforms torus embeddings into complex structures known as Stein surfaces within three complex dimensions. The algorithm for the polyhedron is based on combinatorial transformations called elementary moves. The algorithm for the Stein surface confines its operations to combine two complex-dimensional surfaces and decompose a complex three-dimensional space into those surfaces and complex one-holes.

Copy-protection, a notion safeguarding the ability to replicate black-box access to a target function despite repeated repetition, is generally believed to be unachievable for any non-trivial function without specific assumptions about the function class. While previous research has shown that certain cryptographic primitives like public-key encryption and digital signatures can be copy-protected without additional assumptions, it was also established that other principles such as leakage-resilience and updatable encryption are fundamentally flawed if copy-protected. Although some schemes exist for protecting cloning when a certain amount of private key information is leaked, it has been proven that no fully leakage-resilient or updatable schemes exist encryptions for unlearnable functions without assuming an independent random source, or for cloning protection where the leaked information is presented as an adversarial choice. This research demonstrates that unclonable encryption, specifically scheme that excludes cloning access when the two shares are combined an arbitrary manner even when the two users are adversaries, is possible and that unclonable encryption is equivalent to a copy-protected scheme for unlearnable functions in the random oracle model. Furthermore, the study provides an unclonable encryption scheme achieving forward secrecy, which was previously believed to be unachievable.

A method has been developed to modify codes used in a channel, enabling a receiver to detect unauthorized transmitters as they attempt to send a different message than the one they actually sent. This technique is applicable to any channel code and does not require the receiver to have knowledge about how to encode messages. It achieves this by combining a code with an extractor protocol, which can be effective even in channels affected by noise. Additionally, the method remains functional when applied to systems susceptible to man-in-the-middle attacks, by designating a specific party to control the encoding process and sharing a secret with the receiver. This approach has potential applications in modifying existing authentication systems, such as those used in power-line communications and wireless networks.

Atomically thin layers of transition metal dichalcogenides have properties that are highly desirable for next-generation valleytronics applications. These layers are characterized by an indirect bandgap in the valence band that can be converted to a direct bandgap at the $\Gamma$ point through valley polarization. Achieving gauge and spin polarization in these materials is essential for their functionality. Lattice relaxation and electron filling in the conduction band of moose two layers in a twisted configuration were analyzed using a first-principles approach to answer this goal. It was found that lattice and doping adjustments can lead to significant changes in the valley and spin characteristics of moose two layers, resulting in highly plasmonic behavior at specific frequencies and doping levels and at specific frequency ranges in undoped regions.

This paper presents several key results related to almost conformal Ricci solitons on a manifold. Initially, we establish criteria for an almost conformal Ricci soliton to be classified as an almost conformal gradient Ricci soliton. Subsequently, we show that on a manifold with a nonnegative almost conformal Ricci soliton, the almost conformal factor must be constant. Additionally, we derive the formula for the scalar curvature's evolution over time when the soliton is almost conformal Ricci flow.

Massive outflows, or magnetospheres, formed by interacting winds from stars and their surrounding planets or planets, have formed since the early days of the solar system. These structures formed from the collision of opposing winds not only protect the star or planet from further exposure to the wind, but also significantly influence how planets are heated and magnetic fields are generated, ultimately leading to the emission of particles that can be observed as jets. In a fascinating comparison, researchers are now using a similar process to the one that forms the solar wind to explain the powerful outflows, or magnetospheres, formed from the collision of opposing winds from the binary star system II Per and its surrounding stars, and the massive outflows, or magnetospheres, formed from the opposing winds from the binary star system Gamma Cassiopeiae and its surrounding planets, and the massive outflows, or magnetospheres, formed from the opposing winds from the binary star system Beta Pictoris and its surrounding planets, and the massive outflows, or magnetospheres, formed from the opposing winds from the binary star system Trappist-1 and its surrounding planets, and the outflows, or magnetospheres, formed from the opposing winds from the binary star system B5088 and its surrounding planets, and the massive outflows, or magnetospheres, formed from the opposing winds from the binary star system V471 Tau and its surrounding planets, and the massive outflows, or magnetospheres,

We've created thin-film stacks of Cobalt and Bismuth, with four periods, using magnetic transport techniques to measure their electrical properties. Our research shows that Bi layers primarily determine the Hall effect's behavior through a diffusive process, while Co layers influence the Hall coefficient via the ordinary Hall effect. In fact, the extrinsic Kaneyoshi Hall effect within our Cobastallite structure is about 10 times more significant than its pure Bismuth counterpart. The Bi layers also serve as barriers that isolate the Kaneyoshi Hall effect in the Central Co layer, resulting in a 4 times more pronounced effect compared to the outer Co layers. Our findings imply that thin Bi layers can extend the reach of the Hall effect into adjacent ferromagnetic materials, making it possible to manipulate and measure the Hall effect in thin magnetic films with greater efficiency.

In a recent study, researchers analyzed the problem of finding time-periodic solutions to a unique, irreducible potential in N-dimensional space that contains no singularities. This study examines two cases: when a particle is free from obstacles and when it encounters an arbitrarily shaped obstacle in N-dimensional space, based on the time-dependent fractional Schrödinger equation. They prove that for any given potential parameters $\alpha$ and $q$ greater than two, this equation has at least one solution with a given energy level, using variational methods. Additionally, they employ inequality techniques specific to fractional derivatives to ensure the solutions are well-behaved and non-singular. For the case with an obstacle present, they utilize the method of reflection to find a solution with prescribed asymptotic behavior at infinity.

The choice of p-norm in measuring the distance between input data significantly influences a classifier's decision and can cause models to make incorrect predictions for nearby inputs. This characteristic of modern classification models contradicts the principles used by humans, which typically rely on evaluating risks through average losses and describe data distances via a Gaussian distribution's Euclidean distance. To address these concerns, our study investigates the effects of training a neural network with a bounded Lipschitz constant under various p-norms (including p=1, 2, and 3) and demonstrates that certain p-norms can increase classifi- cation accuracy while maintaining stability for a broader range of inputs, providing theoretical bounds and empirical evidence to support these findings.

Human comprehension and production of language are thought to be guided by the sentence structure's hierarchy. Although modern deep learning models have made considerable advances in understanding the linear dependencies within sentences, their capacity to grasp the hierarchical nature of the syntax remains unclear. This research reveals that these models, which include recurrent neural networks and transformer-based architectures, possess an implicit capacity to capture the hierarchical nature of the syntax by means of a non-referential understanding. This implicit grasp is assessed by introducing sentence pairs with differing degrees of alignment to the hierarchy, then measuring the degree to which the model's internal knowledge is aligned with the syntax of the sentences. This analysis reveals that these models' implicit grasp of the syntax is aligned with the hierarchical nature of the grammar, outperforming a random baseline by a significant margin of 0.22 in F1-score. This has significant implications for the use of these models in language tasks, as well as for further research into the nature of sentence comprehension and production.

Researchers analyzed the far-ultraviolet light from the star HD 806060 and the subsequent ionization and temperature of the planet HD80606 b using a detailed model of the interaction between the two. The temperature of the planet was found to vary significantly, dropping below 500 Kelvin at a distance of 40 days and rising to over 1000 Kelvin at the closest approach. The model's predictions aligned well with observational spectrographic data, allowing the estimation of the molecular and atomic compositions of the planet's atmosphere. The analysis revealed the presence of highly ionized species such as Fe+ and Mg+ and suggested the existence of possible weaker lines of Ti+, Na+, Si+, H2O, and CO. The researchers also hypothesized the potential for a temporary ionization trail left by the planet as it moves through the stellar wind, which may be observable for an extended period after the closest approach.

Wearable technology with feedback has the potential to provide effective
homework exercises that promote healthy behaviors, but the lack of motivation
to complete these tasks is an issue. Introducing game elements may enhance
rehabilitation and physical therapy programs by balancing practice,
engagement, and enjoyment. However, establishing suitable interaction settings
to achieve this balance is necessary. This research project automatically finds
these optimal points through an analysis of user behavior and feedback in the
form of ratings. Using a motivationally driven interface for upper trunk
rehabilitation as an example, our method identifies key feedback elements that
users want, as well as extreme values of the search parameters that are
uncomfortable or boring. Subsequent tests can focus on these areas to
ultimately determine the optimal settings that maximize users' desire for
motivation and provide valuable insights into the algorithm's reliability
and applicability.

This research compares the geometrically nonlinear elasticity and linearised elasticity models to understanding brittle fracture energies, examining both finite and infinite strain scenarios. By building on Bauman's work, we establish consistent estimates that bridge the gap between two types of energy models, also yielding an idealised model ideal for direct computation. For infinite strain, we derive comparable results under mild assumptions and additional outcomes in higher dimensions, building upon Hancherl's approach. This yield on infinite strain relies on minimal assumptions, largely eschewing the need for high regularity found in prior research including Faraco-Muller-Schmidt, Kirchheim-Maz'ya and Woyczynski. If certain rate-independent hysteresis behavior is present, we show that the nonlinear elasticity model can be idealised by its linearised counterpart. This is demonstrated under both large and infinite strain conditions. A key prerequisite for this idealisation is the absence of negative stiffness behavior, which often characterises materials exhibiting brittle behavior. This research is carried out with an underlying assumption of rate-independent dissipation.

The Standard Model includes several families of particles, with the third family being the quarks and leptons. A type of leptoquark, specifically a vector one, could be present in the first or second family and its presence could be detected in the Large Hadron Collider by looking for the production of two jets and a single neutrino or the total amount of missing energy and the amount of energy that is not detected. Although the current limitations of the LHC allowed the exclusion of vector leptoquarks with a mass of two leptoquark masses greater than 1.4 Tebb, the prediction of such a search required approximations that were one loop accurate, or NLO. A new approach, specifically one that combines perturbation theory with particle physics simulations, could be used to make more precise predictions for the process of vector leptoquark detection. As a result, a more precise prediction, one that takes into account the effects of the strong force, could be used to lower the mass limit of vector leptoquarks from 1.4 Tebb to 1.3 Tebb, effectively closing the gap between theoretical predictions and experimental evidence.

Researchers are proposing an integrated deep neural network (DNN) system with regularisation technology that would enable the production of high-quality PET images from low-dose scans while also incorporating complementary information from MRI data. The suggested approach utilizes a multi-stage framework in which the initial stage generates a preliminary PET image from a PET MRI ratio map and a low-dose PET scan, followed by an intermediate stage that combines this ratio map with a PET MRI-DNN difference map to create an enhanced PET image. The suggestion involves employing a single-stage deep neural network (DNN) model that includes the multi-stage framework as its component, which would enable it to learn how to combine low-dose PET scans, MRI data, and regularisation to produce high-quality PET images from single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) scans or PET scans with limited counts. Simulations and clinical trials are used to validate the effectiveness of this approach.

The rise of personalization in media presents both a chance to individualize news presentation and a threat to user privacy. Investigating this issue through the lens of information visualization and experience design, we administered an online survey to 500 US participants who were asked about their preferences and concerns regarding personalized news algorithms. The results revealed a widespread desire for tailoring to individual tastes among participants, yet varied perceptions on the associated privacy risks. In addition, age influenced users' expectations from personalized news platforms, while browsing history had an impact on their privacy settings. This research can contribute to the development of visualization techniques that prioritize user needs in designing engaging, personalized news interfaces while protecting users' privacy.

To align with Centering Theory, a neural coreference modeling approach is proposed that's tested and found to be beneficial. The approach involves capturing sentence-level context within the neural model, leveraging the existing context that's typically used in coreference decisions. A new evaluation framework is also introduced to assess the model's ability to incorporate contextual information. The evaluation framework is applied to ten neural coreference models, revealing that the models' performance does not necessarily match the theoretical expectations. Furthermore, the results show that adding more contextual information leads to a decline in the models' performance, as well as a similar phenomenon when the distance between the focusing and background units increases. To address these issues, two novel architectural designs are proposed that aim to better capture the core behavior of Centering Theory. The first design, a Neural Focus-Background Estimator (N-FBE), assigns centering attributes to the focus and background vectors, while the second design, a Neural Focus-Background Estimator (N-FBE), implements a neural network to predict the next focus vector given the current focus and background entities. Both models are found to significantly outperform the baseline models on the evaluation framework. The N-FBE and N-FBE models are discovered to almost entirely match the theoretical assumptions of Centering Theory, a marked improvement from the baseline models that showed little coreference-like behavior.

We developed a new algorithm that can be efficiently tailored to various types of directed acyclic graphs by leveraging their treewidth. Our approach builds on a recently developed framework that allows for efficient transfer of directed algorithms to graphs with hierarchical structures. The new algorithm successfully applies a directed treewidth parameterized algorithm in scenarios where the algorithm's runtime can be managed by a specific polynomial function of the treewidth. As a practical demonstration, we designed a novel method to solve the k-vertex deletion problem with a significantly optimized runtime when applied to graphs where the treewidth is low, achieving a substantial improvement in the exponent of k in the runtime. This method relies on utilizing the connectivity properties identified in the previous work and results in a highly effective algorithm that can be efficiently adapted to various types of directed acyclic graphs.

Using optimization to configure complex systems offers multiple advantages.
First, using an optimal objective function to guide configuration processes allows
humans to understand and compare the systems' performance relative to their
desired goals.
Moreover, the use of objective metrics accelerates the evaluation
process of various systems and software, including difficult-to-assess biological
systems and audio outputs.
To illustrate these benefits, we have chosen two diverse examples: evaluating
the effectiveness of political policies and comparing sound effects used in
sports broadcasts.
In the former case, a policy assessment platform leverages optimization to
generate, visualize, and summarize the effects of multiple configurations across
various performance indicators, thus facilitating the evaluation process and
identifying areas for further analysis.
To speed up sound effect evaluations, we employed Bayesian optimization
to compare different configurations used in the British Grand Prix broadcast,
comparing outputs with professional commentators and those without commentary.
Results revealed that optimization-based evaluations reveal quantitative
patterns that human assessors might overlook, thus facilitating more efficient
and focused feedback processes.
To accelerate sound effect evaluations, we observed a significant reduction in
time consumption, thus enabling the comparison of a larger number of
configurations.

A major challenge in understanding quantum chaos and operator growth is the complex structure of the Lie algebra generated by time-evolving operators. By leveraging the concept of logical qubits, we develop a tractable approach to studying this complexity. Assuming that the logical qubit's properties remain unchanged under local unitary transformations, or that it encodes a topological phase, our symmetry-based strategy can be applied. Utilizing this method, we analyze the underlying patterns of growth for both gapped systems and systems with localized defects within the Toric code, where the logical qubit possesses symmetries akin to those of a spin-1/2 on the sphere. Furthermore, our framework enables a precise computation of the average growth rate using both SU(2) invariance and full unitary group invarance, yielding results that align with previously obtained results through entanglement and charge operators. By extending the growth rate calculation to include spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet, we identify a systematic pattern in the results. Ultimately, by incorporating the underlying symmetries of the Hamiltonian, our approach can yield detailed insights into the operator growth rate by leveraging the specific properties of the spin and U(N) invariance of various Hamiltonians.

In location estimation techniques based on WiFi, the initial step typically involves mapping the entire coverage area into a virtual space comprising all recorded WiFi fingerprints. However, using conventional distance measures to determine the position of a new WiFi fingerprint within this space often yields inaccurate results due to the non-Euclidean nature of WiFi signal propagation. To overcome this limitation, this study applies machine learning to generate distance metrics that yield superior results compared to traditional approaches. Specifically, it focuses on modeling the Euclidean distance between fingerprints at the same location but with different signal strengths. By analyzing this model, key locations and their relative importances are identified, and the model can be used to estimate the distance between any two fingerprints. To further refine this model, it incorporates the unique characteristics of individual locations, allowing it to account for variations in the distribution of signal strengths. Moreover, it allows for the derivation of a distance metric between any two fingerprints. Lastly, this model can be adjusted to minimize the Euclidean distance between locations with similar WiFi fingerprint distributions, a crucial step in locations based multilateral localization.

According to the Kardiashvili-Olson framework, the maximum possible energy output a Type II civilization could generate from nuclear fusion is $10^{15}$ watts per square meter. However, by utilizing particle beams and directing them at obstacles to create shockwaves, it is possible to exponentially increase this energy output, resulting in a maximum possible energy output of $10^{17}$ watts per square meter from geothermal energy and $10^{19}$ watts per square meter from chemical energy. On the other hand, by converting the entire energy released from converting planetary masses into energy through the process of mass-energy equivalence, it is possible a Type II civilization could exponentially increase this energy output by a factor of $10^{20}$, thus making chemical energy the most luminous energy source among those considered.

Peer-to-peer (P2P) technology has been widely applied to create decentralized and scalable systems, including real network performance monitoring. By sharing raw measurement data between neighboring network nodes, this approach reduces the need for excessive redundancy and expense. Leveraging P2P technology, P2Ppro monitors service level agreements (SLAs) by allowing network operators to define performance goals and share measurement data among users. To tackle the vast amounts of exchanged data, distributed algorithms utilize local processing to minimize storage requirements, presenting no central bottlenecks. This method enables efficient monitoring of real-world SLAs even as more participants are added, thanks to the decentralized nature of the system.

In multi-pass energy recovery linacs, a unique filling pattern is utilized in the RF structure to prevent interactions between counter-propagating beams. The arrangement of this pattern may impact beam-rf interactions and determine the threshold current where instability begins, ultimately influencing waste power and its distribution within the linac. A general framework is established to evaluate the threshold current, beam-RF standing waves, and waste power for any pattern configuration. Furthermore, the specificity of the proposed two-fill two-pass energy recovery linac design is analyzed within this framework, showcasing improved threshold currents, beam-RF standing waves, and waste power distribution.

The cross section of neutrons interacting with scintillator material has been measured directly for the first time in a high-energy range, between 98 and 688 MeV, using the SEU-N experiment at the NUCOLAR facility. To carry out this measurement, the neutron beam was modified with deuterons as incident particles and two detection systems: the primary was the SEU neutron detector and the secondary was the SEU missing energy detector which helped estimate the properties of the interacting neutrons. To correctly interpret the results from the neutron energy detection system, Monte Carlo simulations using the GEANT4 package were utilized to create a neutron energy spectrum that could be compared with the actual data obtained from the experiment. This allowed for the derivation of the total neutron cross section by applying the missing mass method to remove background contributions. The findings showed a gradual increase in the neutron cross section as the neutron energy increased, which aligned with the predictions made by several theoretical models and could not be explained by the bipolar proton-neutron structure found in the nuclear wave function.

Comet comets are known to contain water ice, yet the optimal conditions for their formation remain unclear. The sticking forces of particles vary greatly in the presence of water ice, leading to uncertainties in the timeline of planet formation within the solar system's icy region. To address this issue, researchers addressed the formation timescale of planetesimals in the outer solar system by sticking forces alone, sticking and sliding within the icy system. To tackle this challenge, they constructed a two-dimensional model that incorporated temperature, rotation rate, sticking, granular hydrodynamics, and hydrothermal processes, then integrated it with a disc model to address the formation timescale of planetesimals in the outer solar system. They found a notable increase in sticking forces in very cold temperatures above 150 Kelvin, which led to the identification of an optimal temperature range for planetesimal formation (between 100 and 50 Kelvin), regardless of the temperature at which the water vapor from the surrounding gas returned to the solid phase. This model suggested that the ideal location for planetesimal formation was in the water ice line, which moved inward over time due to the decreasing amount of ice in the surrounding gas. This model also predicted that comet-forming bodies formed in the outer solar system during the first few million years, while the water ice line had not yet moved significantly inside the Earth's orbit.

The Package fda in R is part of the tools available for conducting local Fisher discriminant analysis of multivariate data, covering both its standard and extended forms. It is located within the contributed package area of the R installation.

A key challenge in developing robot skills through imitation learning is dealing with complex environmental constraints. Real-world applications often involve nonlinear, discontinuous constraints that create significant mathematical difficulties. To address this issue, we develop a novel conical value function approximation that provides a precise tool for solving and describing these problems. Building on this, we propose constrained imitation learning, an efficient learning framework based on this approximation. Numerical tests demonstrate its effectiveness in solving highly challenging skill learning tasks with complex, nonlinear constraints that many existing methods struggle to handle.

Inspired by the Witten hexagon, a dual conformal symmetry approach was adopted to study the four-loop six-gluon soft anomalous dimension (CEV) within $ \text{N=4}$ super Yang-Mills theory (SYM) and QCD. Initially, a hypothesis was made that the CEV can be derived from finite four-loop amplitudes in the soft limit. This assumption was validated to a considerable extent, with only minor deviations found, which can be attributed to collinear limits. Furthermore, the exact values for the four-loop CEV in both SYM and QCD were found, with the results indicating a specific structure involving zeta values. Additionally, the obtained CEV results can be seen as a particular form of a more general equation, with coefficients determined by group theory values and previous lower-loop findings.

A study is conducted to examine the topological characteristics of a superconducting state in a material with spin-orbit coupling and $s$-wave symmetry, with photo-induced superconductivity being an example. The approach utilizes a generalization of the Li-Hubbard transformation to account for spin-orbit coupling and map the super-Hamiltonian to an effective Hamiltonian with broken symmetry. The results show that the superconducting state with spin-orbit coupling maintains a non-trivial topological property, with the effective Hamiltonian being equivalent to the Berezinskii-Hosehough-Topper model. Furthermore, the effective chemical potential in the transformation reveals that the superconducting gap's opening on the Fermi surface is driven by the shift of the normal chemical potential, rather than opening on the original Fermi surface.

Vortex lattice patterns in $d$-wave superconductors near the transition point have been observed to have an unexpected shape, which is reminiscent of a square lattice with diagonal stripes. This finding contradicts earlier studies that simulated $d$-wave order and confirmed their results with various symmetries, which showed vortex lattices that were aligned with the axes of the Fermi surface. However, when researchers simulated $d$-wave superconductivity near a van Hove singularity, they found that the vortex lattice aligned with the diagonals of the square Fermi surface, which is consistent with experimental data. Moreover, both particle-hole and particle-hole and particle-hole symmetries near a van Hove singularity produce similar vortex lattice alignments. This suggests that heavy metals such as HgBa$_2$CuO$_4$ may be close to a van Hove singularity, which is one of the possible explanations for their large hole doping and high critical temperature.

Our research delves into the freeness energy of stretching on long brushes with a scalar extension, taking into account the curvature and optical thickness of the surface, using a self-consistent field approach. We break down the total freeness energy into parts, including those affected by the curvature and optical thickness of the surface, and then use the mean field approximation to calculate the mean field energy. A combination of theoretical methods allows us to resolve the potential field without needing additional assumptions, resulting in a more accurate representation of the brush's behavior, including its possible multilayer structure, particularly in cases of multicomponent brushes.

Graphs embedded in a given distance measure have been used to study their geometric properties within a specific space.
This investigation focuses on a local measure of dimension known as the metric dimension.
We establish a relationship between the dimensions of a graph and its equivalent embedded form.
Moreover, we identify a specific threshold; below this value, the embedded graph has the same dimension as the original graph,
while the dimension increases without limit as values above this threshold are reached.
This limit is proven to be at least as great as a certain dimension known as the intrinsic dimension.

When comparing the long-term variability of active galactic nuclei, the extended time frames necessitate either continuous monitoring or inconsistent sampling. The massive data collection generated by observing the Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Mission presents both an opportunity and a challenge in this analysis. By utilizing the Swift-BAT 9-year light curves in the 14-190 keV energy range, the researchers were able to conduct an extensive statistical study of 1444 soft X-ray variabilities over the course of a decade. The challenges of a heterogeneous sample were resolved through the application of bootstrap resampling, allowing for the calculation of confidence intervals in the 644 cases where the variability amplitude could be precisely measured. The results indicate that the BAT sample's distribution of logarithmic variability amplitude follows a normal distribution with a mean of 0.36 dex. Furthermore, the research discovered that the BAT sample's mean logarithmic variability amplitude is comparable to that of the radio BATON sample, even though the BATON sample's energy range is much lower.

Bipartite matching and directed graph assignments under weights have significant implications for valuation structures, which in turn can have profound effects on the quality of social welfare approximation, even in scenarios involving numerous agents and items. Specifically, our research highlights that approximating valuations can lead to substantial losses in welfare, even when utilizing advanced techniques like exponential algorithms and polynomial-time algorithms for certain graph types. To address this issue, we develop a new method to limit the size of these valuations, which can be efficiently computed via a flexible algorithm. This technique has the potential to yield crucial bounds on approximation issues for market mechanisms that currently receive less research attention, such as the design of mechanisms for matching and graph assignments.

This study examines various methods used to analyze point spread functions (PSFs) with implications for multiple fields, including binary asteroid research, multiple object detection within the telescope's field of view, and the identification of candidates from wide-field surveys. Specifically, we investigate strategies for both time-domain and spatial domain analyses of the PSF, evaluating their effectiveness in detecting subtle features, such as secondary components in the image plane, and assessing their computational efficiency. Moreover, we discuss the utilization of the residual image as a diagnostic point spread function (D-PSF) and outline potential approaches for score function optimization that could prove beneficial in multi-object classification and detection tasks. Ultimately, our goal is to provide a framework for researchers using the James Webb Space Telescope and other high-resolution instruments with sufficient field of view to efficiently identify objects of interest, such as nearby exoplanets, and minimize the need for targeted follow-up observations with dedicated instruments.

Researchers in economics and related disciplines often study peer effects in networks, but available datasets typically lack information about network structures. This paper presents an innovative technique for estimating peer effects and uncovering hidden network connections by utilizing existing data on behaviors and covariates. The proposed method relies on formulating a spatial model of peer interactions and developing a novel statistical framework to validate the robustness of its assumptions. The framework enables researchers to non-parametrically test specific network properties and provides estimators for actual network connections. As network data can be expensive to obtain, the framework serves as a powerful tool for inferring hidden network structures based on behavioral data alone. The paper illustrates the effectiveness of this approach by examining exclusive eating patterns among female students in a university dormitory, revealing the existence of hidden clusters and cluster sizes. The results demonstrate how the framework can be used to test the independence of actions, discover network structures, and map specific network connections within a case study.

In this study, we introduce several chain rule formulas for variable-order fractional operators based on the Riemann-Liouville approach, addressing both semi-linear and fully non-linear cases with multiple terms. Initially, we examine a collection of chain rule formulas for operator combinations such as $\alpha(t)\,\vartheta_{0+}^\alpha f$ and $\alpha(t)\,\vartheta_{0+}^\alpha f + \beta(t)\,\vartheta_{0+}^\beta f$. Subsequently, we derive new, distinct chain rule formulas for the variable-order Riemann-Liouville fractional derivative, acknowledging the operators' non-local characteristics. Furthermore, we explore applications of these results in the context of time-dependent fractional differential equations, answering specific questions regarding point source problems and obtain a novel variable-order Kelvin's formula.

The performance gap between an optimally Bayesian detector and a suboptimal one in multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) detection is computationally prohibitive to know. Researchers have investigated various methods, yet their effectiveness often depends heavily on specific system parameters, making it difficult to generalize their performance, especially at high data rates. In this work, a universally applicable lower bound is proposed for the performance deficit of linear detectors in MIMO systems with known channel conditions, valid for any detection algorithm and channel statistical model. This bound's value is mostly unaffected by signal-to-noise ratio, providing a valuable benchmark for evaluating linear detectors' performance, which was verified numerically and illustrated in certain cases.

A new package for processing galaxy spectra has been developed in Python using astropy, allowing the derivation of basic physical properties from raw spectra. This package enables a comparison to the Balmer Diagnostic Diagram for ionized gas and determines physical properties such as [OIII] emission ratio, ionized gas density, and ionization state. It is sufficient for obtaining these properties when analyzing a substantial number of low-signal-to-noise-ratio galaxy spectra. The package demonstrates its capability by analyzing an SMGC sample from the GAMA survey using both low- and high-resolution spectra. It is clear that even with low-resolution spectra, a significant proportion of the variance in physical properties can be recovered for a wide range of galaxies. Moreover, an almost linear relationship is discovered between the equivalent width of H$\beta$ and the equivalent width of [OIII], indicating the potential to derive a wide variety of physical properties with minimal data.

Western Central Africa's breakup from Gondwana around 150 Ma significantly impacted the region's passive margin evolution and sediment accumulation, with variations in current and subsurface data indicating complex breakup processes. Three distinct phases of rupture are evident in the region's major basins, with the initial phase characterized by a northeast-southwest directed extension, followed by rapid release during the second stage. A third stage involved a more moderate extension directed towards the southeast, resulting in the formation of the Congo-Angola gap. This multi-stage extension influenced sediment supply and the development of coastal features, with high sediment supply promoting the growth of marginal features, while low supply led to a lack of such features. Increased transport of heavy minerals during high sediment supply periods promoted the formation of submarine cones and channels, while low supply led to the deposition of turbidites in distal basinal areas.

Our new unsupervised pre-training framework for segmentation is called Contrast-Disentanglement Aggregation (ContrastDA). It has been designed to tackle key issues in self-supervised learning methods that tend to over-segmentation and focus too much on local features. The model has two novel principles proposed to address these problems: for one principle, ContrastDA uses contrastive learning to differentiate and separate features within the same image; the second principle suggests learning multi-scale feature points across different levels of granularity to capture more localized information. These two principles are combined into a unified framework with contrastive learning at both coarse and fine granularities, utilizing an aggregation module to fuse multi-scale features and transfer information between them. Our experiments show that contrastable training points are generated with improved segmentation performance; the model has been successfully tested on popular datasets such as Cityscapes and ADE20k, and has outperformed current state-of-the-art unsupervised pre-training methods while requiring only minimal learning parameters.

The capacity for collaborative problem solving between humans and machines has significant potential when both parties engage effectively through shared communication. This study proposes integrating a theory of mind concept into goal-directed communication frameworks to enhance communication efficiency within collaborative tasks. Building on this idea, a new communication model is developed and implemented in a collaborative game environment where partners must coordinate to collect scattered resources. The results show that utilizing the theory of mind-based communication model leads to improved goal attainment when collaborating with an unknown partner, compared to other communication models and no communication at all.

Recent techniques using machine learning and computational linguistics have shown great promise in leveraging linguistic patterns within text to reveal underlying cognitive properties within the brain. This research builds upon a previous study by leveraging a modified version of BERT through a negative sampling method to investigate linguistic changes within individual words. By fine-tuning pre-trained models on specific language tasks, researchers have consistently discovered that latent representations of words reflect shifts in their meanings over time. These meaning changes can occur on a continuum and are often indicated by arrows that depict the increase or decrease in a given signal within a word's vector representation. In this study, we leveraged large corpora and a LEXICAL SIMILARITY dataset to identify pairs of contexts that evoke different meanings within the same word, often referred to as "lexically similar" pairs. By examining these pairs, we developed a novel, data-driven, and cognitively motivated search strategy that employs a binary classifier to identify pairs that exhibit a given meaning change within a word's vector representation. This strategy was applied to a diverse set of 24 words that exhibit polysemy, and as a result, researchers were able to uncover pairs of contexts that evoke new meanings within these words, often stemming from historical meaning shifts within the English language. This study demonstrates the potential of leveraging machine learning to reveal the polysemous nature of words within our language, and it reveals that machine learning models can capture the dynamic and ever-changing nature of meaning within individual words. Building upon the concept of partons within hadrons and their corresponding transverse movements, we develop two key functions. These include the correlator of transverse densities and the average squared displacements of partons, which are directly connected to the TMD PDFs. The functions are designed to be universal, process-dependent, and accessible through experiment, particularly in semi-inclusive processes involving leading twist, single polarization, or double polarization. Furthermore, explicit connections are established with the collinear PDFs, including their twists, as well as with the Sivers and Boer-Mulders functions.

This study focuses on the role of knotting depth in altering the folding behavior of proteins formed into trefoil and figure-of-eight knots.  It finds that shallowly knotted proteins exhibit multiple folding pathways, with one involving a distinct metastable state, whereas deeply knotted proteins fold directly without forming this state.  Molecular dynamics simulations in an idealized environment are used to identify the mechanisms behind these varying folding pathways and provide an energetic map of the potential energy landscape.  It is concluded that the degree of knotting in proteins directly influences their folding mechanisms by determining the folding pathway in response to different temperatures.

Under these conditions, given any irrationality pattern in the second-degree cohomology, there is a formation of infinitely many mutually disjoint, closed Lagrangian submanifolds whose collective sum equals the relaxed form. The irrationality condition is only required within the first-degree cohomology. Furthermore, for simply connected compact symplectic manifolds, infinitely many mutually disjoint, closed Lagrangian submanifolds can be found whose collective sum equals any given irrationality pattern in the second-degree cohomology, based on a result of Entov and Polymay. This construction is not constructively proven.

In models featuring both the kaon and kaon-vacuum condensates, the mass of a typically massless Nambu-Goldstone boson, such as the axion, can be given substance. We show that a framework describing the QCD phase transition, known as the kaon condensation model, is capable of incorporating both condensates and explaining the mass-generation mechanism for this boson within it. Furthermore, we investigate various implications of this model, including constraints on the axion-fracton interaction constant, potential solutions to the axion isocurvature constraint, and the possibility of a detectable axion-dominated component with a non-Gaussian distribution.

Deep insertions, or disruptions, are used to test the robustness of models, but the current evaluation methods have flaws that overestimate a model's ability to generalize and remain resistant to attacks. To address this issue, researchers developed a new way to evaluate model stability by incorporating counterfactual data created by their disruption generation method. They then demonstrated that training models with this counterfactual data increases model resilience and prevents overestimation of model performance. In fact, using their method to generate and evaluate counterfactual examples resulted in models that were less prone to disruption, with some models achieving up to a 35-point decrease in accuracy when evaluated with these counterfactual examples, compared to just an 18-point decrease when evaluated with original examples.

Neighborhood sum-distinguishing and color-based total chromatic numbers of equitable coloring in circulant graphs $C_n(2,1)$ are investigated in this study, with a neighborhood condition established and the exact sum-distinguishing colors identified for certain types of circulant graphs $C_n(2,1)$.

We've developed a technique for growing a type of carbon-rich compound called BiScO$_3$ on single-crystal plates of nickel that have been carefully matched to graphene using a process known as lattice-thermal expansion mismatch. This technique is based on controlling the flow of atoms during deposition without chemical breakdown. When we carefully analyzed the atomic structure and electrical properties of BiScO$_3$ using techniques such as X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy, we found BiScO$_3$ to be monolithic, without any structural damage or conductive pathways. This success required clean surfaces on the nickel and careful control of the surface where atoms are deposited to ensure BiScO$_3$ was formed rather than another carbon-rich compound called Ni$_3$ScO$_7$. An important finding from our research is that there are specific points where the surface where atoms are deposited wants BiScO$_3$ and other points that want Ni$_3$ScO$_7$, and that we can influence which one forms by adjusting the temperature at which we grow the material. This gives us the ability to create different atomic structures within the same material by forming different types of structures side by side, and that we can control their size and arrangement.

Using the transform of Wolf, we establish a method for determining the rank of lineary codes through the use of a basis, making it accessible. This approach is specifically applied to codesexamined using the transform of Wolf, resulting in the formulation of bounds for rank of lineary codes in the transform of Wolf. These boundaries are significant, as they provide a framework for code design. We also provide an example to demonstrate the calculation of rank for a code examined using the transform of Wolf. Building on this, we establish the distance covered by lineary codes in the transform of Wolf, as well as an upper boundary for the size of lineary codes in the transform of Wolf that meet certain distance requirements.

Research on polymer injection into the oil industry is being carried using a new numerical method that models the complex interaction between polymer and oil in areas of high turbulence. The model uses a specific function to describe polymer behavior, which includes four key factors, and incorporates two types of mathematical models to describe oil and polymer dynamics. A key feature of this research is the development of a new numerical method, which utilizes surface tension to prevent instability and accurately simulate the polymer and oil dynamics. The results of this research show that the model accurately predicts the polymer injection profile and the formation of a distinct polymer layer, which becomes thinner as the model's factors change. The research also reveals that the model's polymer injection profile is significantly impacted by the model's factors, which highlights the importance of choosing the right polymer injection profile for increased oil recovery. The research is being carried in a two-dimensional, horizontal well model and yields promising results, which suggest the accuracy of the model's polymer and oil dynamics simulation.

A significant challenge in training deep neural networks is the high cost of creating large, high-quality multi-label datasets. These data points, where several labels are associated with the same object, are particularly expensive to annotate. A novel strategy has been developed to accelerate the generation of synthetic multi-label data by leveraging readily available single-label data. The new strategy involves iteratively creating new data points through back-propagation, rather than relying on the physical properties of existing images. Rather than measuring the performance of this strategy against the vast number of possible real-world data distributions, it is evaluated by comparing it to the few available benchmark methods. The experimental results show that the new strategy yields superior performance, particularly in applications with many categories, where it outperforms the current best approach by a 2% margin, while also having a significantly lower annotation cost - just 1% of the instances needed.

This research paper investigates the energy dynamics of the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation within a two-dimensional, smoothly bordered region, focusing on its progressive transformation and eventual stabilization over time. The study confirms the presence of an energy dissipation law and demonstrates that the process's energy eventually stabilizes in a specific timeframe, given certain initial conditions. The findings are supported by rigorous mathematical proofs and theoretical analysis.
