Using detailed numerical hydrodynamics simulations, we determined the merger rates of Population III binary black holes and neutron star binaries to be influenced by stellar cluster properties. The merger rates peak at a redshift of 1.5, with an estimated 2.5 times 10^-5 per year per gigaparsec^3, and become  order of magnitude lower below and above this peak. The merger rates are most prevalent in regions with higher peak hydrogen mass densities within the range of 1.3 to 10 times 10^-7, and are found to be  several times higher in regions with higher pair instability supernovae fractions within these regions. The results highlight the importance of considering stellar cluster properties when studying Population III binary remnants, and the potential for future space telescopes to constrain the merger rates of these objects.

We have developed a Gamma-Ray Burst (GRB) simulator tailored for the Wide Field Survey Instrument (WFI) on the Swift satellite, utilizing actual data from the instrument's timing and trigger logic. To validate its functionality, we compared the simulator with real data for both X-ray and gamma-ray triggers. Our analysis of short-duration GRBs indicates that the simulator's time jitter is approximately 0.3 seconds, which is consistent with the time difference between trigger thresholds as determined from the timing data. Additionally, we found that the simulator's variable intensity feature accurately replicates GRB characteristics, with implications for identifying potential x-ray and gamma-ray bursts within the data.

A previously established result by Fryer and Rueda-Rohland indicates that for power series functions f belonging to a specific function space BMOA_p, with a range of 1 < p < 2, the weak compactness of the function is closely associated with the strong compactness of a related operator T_g, within a different function space B_p, again with 1 < p < 2. Building upon this prior work, two additional questions have been completely answered. First, it was proven for functions g in the analytic algebra A, that the operator T_g is strongly compact within the B_p space if and only if the related operator is near the closure of the diagonal operators, again within the B_p space, with 1 < p < 2. Moreover, it was also established for functions g in the BMOA_q, with a specific function q, that the operator T_g is weakly compact within the B_p space if and only if a related operator is near the closure of the diagonal operators, again within the B_p space, with 1 < p, q < 2.

To measure the growth of knowledge within a field of study, we need information that's universally acknowledged within that field's community. This concept, known as a Quantitative Index of Knowledge (KQI), can be operationalized using natural language queries and answered by structured data, such as knowledge graphs. Our research focuses on constructing a KQI for the field of NLP, specifically the TRENER graph, and developing tools to analyze the distribution of knowledge within scientific literature. This involves incorporating KQI construction as a metric when evaluating KGRs, effectively integrating the graph's content assessment into the SSGR evaluation framework. We've built a N-specific KQI graph, NLG, by adapting existing KGRs, and compared its structure to other KGRs to reveal the underlying distribution of knowledge within the NLG graph, including the phenomenon of knowledge linearization. Furthermore, we've developed a KQI construction cost function that is critical for balancing the KQI's granular detail. This cost function is determined through human input and can be integrated as a constraint during KGR evaluation frameworks, such as the SEEGRE framework.

Investigating a two-hop wireless communication system, we model an scenario in which an intermediate relay receives a signal transmitted by an originator node, with the relay's transmission being monitored by an eavesdropping ground station. We aim to develop optimal power allocation strategies for both transmission links to either maximize the system's data capacity or its security, without considering power constraints at the nodes. We A general approach is proposed to distribute power in a way that optimizes the system's performance, taking into account the possibility of unlimited power availability at the nodes. We also explore specific cases with limited power supply, as well as the impact of power distribution when considering increased complexity in power control, and compare the optimal end-to-end power allocation strategy to that of a single transmission.

A robust method for generating non-classical light sources and non-local quantum entanglement involves using integrated quantum emitters with topologically protected edge modes in photonic devices. These emitter-node systems can produce complex multi-photon states when interacting with edge modes, offering the potential to utilize them as quantum memory and facilitating non-local quantum entanglement. This research demonstrates that by interfacing emitters with edge modes in an electrostatic larix model, a significant depth of multi-emitter controllability can be achieved through the global and local gating, allowing for complex interactions and the generation of tailored quantum states. Specifically, we show that multi-emitter systems can interact via edge modes when global gating is used to bring energy levels into resonance, while precise control over relative energy resonances is enabled by local gating. This controllability is demonstrated through the use of material with quantum well and potential for inducible polarization. Furthermore, we utilize a rate equation model to exhibit that complex two-photon entanglement structures can be reliably generated with high fidelity when accounting for real-world losses.

This research focuses on how traffic lights impact decision-making for collaborative automated vehicles navigating urban intersections. We analyze the effectiveness of using publicly available traffic light information in decision-making processes, specifically looking at how connected vehicles respond to different signal configurations and prioritize information about approaching vehicles. Our findings, validated through real-world intersection scenarios, show that collaborative vehicles take into account traffic lights when developing travel plans, with significant effects observed during yellow and red phases. We also discovered that collaborative vehicles give more importance to the approach of emergency vehicles at all stages of the traffic light cycle.

Interactive learning techniques, like text-based training for alignment and classification, have shown great potential. However, their potential has been hindered by the lengthy simulation times needed for large datasets. To overcome this limitation, a super-efficient text-based exploration environment called TextWorldExpress has been developed. It allows for massively parallel simulations, achieving up to 1000 times faster processing speeds than the original TextWorld. By leveraging TextWorldExpress, researchers have been able to conduct a large-scale experiment using the RHLR dataset, performing thousands of samples per day and exploring a new application called interactive few-shot learning.

A new memory-oriented hardware design named FDHT-Mapper for tensor-hashed linear transformations has been devised, serving as a vital component in tensor decomposed model-oriented HPC systems. In contrast to conventional hardware, FDHT-Mapper achieves a significant reduction in memory access while maintaining high data throughput via an innovative tensor hash decomposition technique combined with a hierarchical memory structure. As a result, applications can be executed with fewer memory transfers, markedly enhancing overall performance and energy efficiency. To validate the FDHT-Mapper design, multiple real-world applications were utilized, demonstrating its ability to enhance performance when integrated into tensor-decomposed models. Implementing the FDHT-Mapper design for ScaLAPACK's TRSM and TSMQ routines yielded substantial performance gains of up to $3.36\times$ and $2.24\times$ respectively, yielding best-case performance improvements of $2.24\times$ in energy efficiency when incorporating BLAS operations. Furthermore, incorporating the FDHT-Mapper design into a tensor-decomposed model for an AI workload resulted in energy efficiency gains of $2.24\times$ best-case performance improvements.

Current trends in NLP emphasize using massive datasets, yet the emphasis on efficient learning with smaller data sets is becoming increasingly important. We've investigated a wide range of data augmentation techniques that are commonly employed in other fields but haven't been commonly applied to NLR so far. Our study explores various techniques such as task-specific, language-specific and grammar-specific augmentations, as well as ones that linguistically preserve meaning. By conducting thorough experiments across four distinct aspects of linguistic preservation and obtaining human validation through crowdsourcing, we used a thorough evaluation framework to assess the effect of our 13 different augmentations on four different tasks using the TREC dataset. Our results, obtained with as little as five neural network training runs per experiment, demonstrate that certain methodologies, including graph-based and semantic-based approaches, can effectively enhance NLP performance with minimal data. Notably, we found that these approaches outperformed other methods like paraphrasing and translation, particularly in low-data scenarios, thus proving valuable for efficient NLP learning.

For theories with two derivatives that break conformal symmetry, specifically with negative cosmological constant, I develop a quantitative self-measure for dark energy, termed 'self-binding energy'. This definition relies on the distinction between bulk and boundary energy in the context of AdS/CFT, utilizing the Casimir effect to calculate the difference in vacuum energies. I demonstrate that this definition is physically meaningful by showing that the stability of dark energy balls is governed by it, and that the quantity appears in the formulation of the Weak Gravity Conjecture for AdS. With the case of Einstein gravity, the definition becomes computable from the boundary CFT data, and I find that, under certain assumptions, positive self-binding energy is required for the validity of the Weak Gravity Conjecture in AdS. A related analysis is also conducted in dS space, albeit with limited success.

A new method for estimating multiple target states within quantum simulations has been introduced. This technique involves representing the collective set of target states with a small space where each state within the space is an eigenstate of the model Hamiltonian. By utilizing the Quantum Phase Estimation and projecting out the corresponding quantities from the target observables, the parameters of the Hamiltonian and the initial states can be determined more effectively. A key advantage of this approach is its ability to provide robust estimates even when the initial states are not completely orthogonal, which is beneficial in scenarios such as modeling dynamic processes in quantum systems. The effectiveness of this method has been demonstrated with simulations of multiple quantum states, where it outperformed traditional methods in terms of accuracy and stability.

Let's consider a univariate polynomial ring $S$ with coefficients in a field $K$ of characteristic $p > 0$. Denote the ideal of $S$ as $\mathfrak{a}$. Given an integer $c$ in $S$, a positive integer $e$, and an element $x$ in $S$, we define the local cohomology module $H^{1}_{\mathfrak{a}}(x/c)^{(e)}$ by twisting it $e$ times. It has been demonstrated that for sufficiently large values of $e$, the zero submodule of local cohomology $H^{1}_{\mathfrak{a}}(x/c)^{(e)}$ is independent of the parameter $e$. 

Let $I$ be an ideal in $S$ and let $x$ be a nonzerodivisor in $S$. A significant result established by Tucker and Vasconcelos states that there exists an ideal $I'$ in $S$ such that for any integer $e$, $H^{1}_{\mathfrak{a}}(x/I)^{(e)}$ is isomorphic to $H^{1}_{\mathfrak{a}}(x/I')$. Furthermore, in sections 5-7, we examine specific families of ideals in $S$ to provide explicit descriptions of $I'$. These descriptions are based on $\mathbb{F}_q$ and enable us

In the European energy market, grid operators must ensure a all-or-none order requirement for participation in the dispatch market, which may lead to unnecessary costs and inefficiencies. We examine the strategic implications of mandatory, flexible, and optional bidding on market efficiency, relying on a comprehensive dispatch market model that accounts for multiple grid constraints. Our analysis indicates that optional bidding promotes over-procurement by the grid operator, whereas flexible bidding encourages over-investment in generation capacity. Surprisingly, a grid operator can minimize system costs by implementing an optional bidding mechanism, which is also socially optimal in certain scenarios. We validate these theoretical findings using a numerical model based on the German electricity market.

A key finding in this research is that for a field of rational functions over an algebraic integer algebra with bounded norm, any finite group can be realized as a Galois group with specific properties of being generated by two elements meeting certain polynomial conditions. This conclusion is independent of the characteristic of the underlying algebraic number algebra. Additionally, in cases where the algebra is algebraic, it demonstrates that almost all finite groups appear as Galois groups with increasing frequency. This appears to be the first instance of studying Galois groups in function fields associated with algebraic number algebras, and it has implications for previous conjectures, including a relation to the polynomial analogue of the Bateman-Horn conjecture and an application of Minasker's conjecture.

The search for the Higgs boson at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) with an energy level of 7 TeV relies on advanced statistical methods to distinguish weak signals from prominent background noise. To improve the sensitivity of the search, it is essential to accurately estimate background levels, particularly in the region near the Higgs boson's mass. Given the difficulty of modeling certain background processes precisely, it is proposed to utilize an external constraint on the top quark pair production cross-section as a means to refine background predictions. This strategy was tested during the analysis of top quark pair data obtained from the CMS collaboration's 2011 dataset, which comprised 2 point-like signals at invariant masses of 112 and 226 GeV, leading to the rejection of the Standard Model Higgs boson hypothesis at a 2.6 sigma level, and ultimately confirming the existence of top quark resonances, also known as tetraquarks, within the mass range of 630-860 GeV, each with an anisotropy of less than 8 percent.

Investigating the Standard Model's extended scalar sectors requires a comprehensive understanding of the Higgsstrahlung process, which encompasses both di-boson resonant scattering and non-resonant di-photon scattering. We propose a novel approach to test these extensions by leveraging precise measurements of the diphoton decay rate and asymptotic freedom in the electroweak theory. We specifically assess the non-resonant di-photon scattering contribution, aspect unique to the SM Higgs boson. We demonstrate that even with current LHC data, limitations on the $\gamma\gamma$ decay rate can be translated into more stringent direct limits on the colorless scalar spectrum, outperforming previous indirect constraints derived from the precisely measured electroweak oblique parameters, S and T. We further predict that a similar analysis will yield equivalent benefits in the upcoming High Luminosity LHC, despite any added colorless scalars affecting the $\gamma\gamma$ cross section through virtual loops. We suggest that in the future, $\gamma\gamma$ cross section measurements will provide more precise limits on the scalar spectrum than process-related approaches, offering an exceptional tool for searching for new physics with next-generation colliders.

This study focuses on the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex (NPSV), a rarely observed phenomenon at Saturn's north pole which differs significantly from the polar stratospheric features seen at the planet's south pole during its Saturnian summer. The NPSV is characterized by a cold polar cap, marked by amorphous cloud formations and ice crystals within the stratosphere. Within this research, a comprehensive exploration is undertaken into various aspects including temperature and circulation patterns, as well as chemical and thermal precursors within the north polar mesosphere and stratosphere, as the North Pole enters its Saturnian summer. By combining observations from long-wavelength radio echoes with computerized simulations (3D GPS) and radiative-convection models, the REX program acquired temperature and circulation data, whereas radio observations and computer simulations indicated that circulation and temperature at the NPSV behave in contrast to the Extended Vortex observed at Saturn's south pole. Furthermore, radiative-convection models attribute the formation of a permanent cold cap in the NPSV to insufficient solar heating and limited circulation of warm air from higher altitudes.

Recent research has shown that the Kermack-McKendrick epidemic model can be connected to the Schrödinger equation through an asymptotic approximation, where time tends to infinity, in a complex, singular limit involving the appearance of $i$ as a parameter. In this paper, we consider the Schrödinger equation as a standalone, approximate model and in doing so, we prove the solution will reach infinity in a finite amount of time for both its nonlinear focus-compact variants. This result includes the case where there is no boundary present, in which instance, we derive an existing, nonlinear discrete equation as a byproduct of the study. Moreover, we establish that in the presence of a boundary, the solution will always vanish in a finite amount of time or at the spatial location furthest from the boundary in both focus-compact Schrödinger variants. These outcomes are surprising, since the standard ways of proving the solution will collapse in the presence of a boundary or become singular in its absence for this type of equation typically involve events occurring at very high frequencies present in the Schrödinger equation, which involve infinite coefficients when the parameter $e$ approaches zero. This sort of behavior is absent in the focus-compact Schrödinger equation, which causes the high frequency coefficients to become negligible rather than infinite in the limit as $e$ approaches zero.

This paper introduces an analogy between commutative algebra in characteristic zero and positive characteristic, providing specific instances and a key theorem to support the conceptual framework for those cases in characteristic positive. The main contribution is a proof that certain properties hold in characteristic zero based on the behavior in positive characteristic, given a set of conditions and a key condition derived from the Newton polytope of the underlying function. The theorem is used to demonstrate the effectiveness of the approach through an existing example, offering a more concise proof of a previously established result. The new proof implies the validity of a hypothesis regarding the existence of a certain basis for a module, providing a more general understanding of the relationship between commutative algebra in characteristic zero and positive characteristic. The new proof is a significant contribution to the field, as it relies solely on the structure of the underlying module and its definition through the Newton polytope. The research is motivated by the field of positive characteristic commutative algebra and its application to rational dynamics in non-Archimedean analytic spaces. The characteristic-zero approach is a novel framework that builds on the principles of patching techniques and provides a basis for further research in the field.

A comprehensive examination of the spectral weight distribution in complex many-body systems is broken down by our work, which effectively serves as a metal-insulator indicator. Utilizing a unique visualization technique, we map the spectral weight distribution of a two-dimensional photonability model across its entire parameter space and compare these findings with theoretical predictions from the Hartroft approximation and the diagrammatic self-consistency approach. Our analysis uncovers a distinct alteration in the distribution pattern at the boundary between metallic and insulating states, confirming previous suggestions that the 'sum rule violations' could act as a reliable marker for this transition. Moreover, we identify an accompanying high-energy shift that outlines the transition boundary and discloses insulating characterizations present in the vicinity of the transition point. Our full visualization of the spectral weight distribution provides a route to anticipate the transition without resorting to the conventional methods like calculating the gap or analyzing the self-energy.

Using the su(2,1) algebra, we develop a precise analytical approach to address the quantity invariance profile issue. This methodology yields an exact analytical solution for the quantity invariance profile, which is then applied to create a new, highly non-linear quantum state within the one-dimensional su(2,1) double dark-soliton framework. Specifically, we create a quantum state composed of two dark-soliton components in a one-dimensional su(2,1) double dark-soliton model that exhibits a finite, quantity invariance profile between the two solitons. This quantity invariance profile is characterized by a "valley" and is described by Bessel functions. Furthermore, we derive an equation of motion for this quantum state that involves interaction parameters, and through numerical simulations, we investigate the behavior of this state as it evolves and demonstrate that it maintains its structural integrity for a significant duration. This method can also be extended to other models containing multiple one-dimensional dark-soliton components.

The paper builds on previous work concerning symmetric vector bundles by exploring symplectical double vector bundles, which are symplectical structures on vector bundles that are compatible with their underlying linear morphism. We then extend this concept to symplectical symmetric double vector bundles, which are symplectical structures on symmetric vector bundles that are compatible with their underlying linear morphism. This paper also investigates some fundamental properties of these types of bundles and provides examples to illustrate their characteristics.

Lied algebra theory utilizes nilorbit theory extensively, with significant contributions from various authors. Before moving on, it's important to examine the connection between Kirillov's measure and geometric measure defined on orbits within the dual of a Lie algebra for triangularizable matrices as explored in this paper. Moreover, the notion of nilorbit can be expanded beyond the gl.n. setting, and we establish the relation between Kirillov's measure and geometric measure for all triangularizable matrices. Nonetheless, we notice that the absolute value in Kirillov's measure formula seems unnecessary.

A new algorithm for x-ray spectrum recovery from single-shot measurements is described. The algorithm's effectiveness in retrieving the spectrum is enhanced with prior knowledge about the photon energy distribution. Used in conjunction with statistical phase retrieval techniques, the new algorithm has the potential to improve spectrum and sample density matrix recovery. A simulation demonstrates the efficiency of this approach in preventing the propagation of measurement errors and the propagation of artifacts.

Quantum error correcting codes inspired by statistical mechanics have a major drawback: their disordered nature makes decoding challenging. To address this issue, we propose adapting techniques from disordered statistical mechanics to decode these codes, an idea first successfully applied in a recent study for the Shor code. To broaden this approach's applicability, we develop a general framework based on the belief message passing algorithm for classical disordered systems, which we apply to a few quantum codes that can be reduced to classical problems and one code with a inherently disordered defect configuration, all of which were previously unsolved or required ad-hoc solutions.

Researchers have examined the electronic properties of quantum-well structures, consisting of tellurene vacuum dielectric layers sandwiched between tellurium semimetal layers. Tellurene's large lattice constant and adjustable carrier effective mass make it an ideal strain-engineering material. Studies utilizing a four-band k$\cdot$ p model reveal that a quantum well with tellurene dielectric can develop a non-minimal gap through strain engineering, whereas tellurium semimetal layers contribute little to gap formation due to their heavy mass. By applying tensile strain, the valence and conduction band edges shift to specific spin-split states, indicating potential for valley-polarized injection. Calculations indicate that a 6 nm well width achieves a significant gap of approximately 200 meV under 1.2% strain, offering new possibilities for valley-tron applications using quantum-well devices.

The 2D, 3D MRSPSE flow simulation model addresses the interaction between multiple scales of matrix and fractures, incorporating effects of flow path blockages within fractures.  A key component of this model is the Dirac-$\beta$ function, which effectively models blocking fractures by capturing their non-monotonic properties and providing a generalized form of fractional calculus.  To simulate the complex process of pore clogging in three dimensions, we extend the existing 1D, 2D MRSPSE approach to 3D by utilizing the 3D Riemann-Liouville operator to account for blocking fractures.  A primary advantage of extending to 3D is the ability to model 3D geometries, including rectangular boxes and cylindrical shapes.  To demonstrate the practical application and computational efficiency of 3D MRSPSE, we present analytical derivations, numerical tests, and comparative examples with the conventional 3D model with linear kernels.

A new variant of a spin-trap device has been discovered that exhibits two distinct states with different high and low electrical resistances. The switch between these states can be influenced by a magnetic field and demonstrates unique properties not seen in conventional spin-valve devices. Specifically, the critical exchange field required to switch the device's resistance is much lower than that required to switch a typical spin-valve, allowing for more efficient operation at low exchange fields. Further analysis using first-principles calculations has highlighted the significance of a thin nonmagnetic barrier and optimal layer thicknesses for achieving the desired spin-trap behavior. This multi-stable spin-trap holds potential as a novel memory element controlled by a magnetic field that can operate with low energy requirements.

When making a decision, living organisms and automated systems must balance collecting relevant information with leveraging existing knowledge to choose among alternatives. The setting of decision-making under uncertainty captures this challenge. In the context of multi-arm bandit problems with multiple possible interpretations of observed data, we demonstrate how pre-existing beliefs and incentives can be unified within a decision-making framework guided by utility functions. We show that optimal policies can be formulated using value of information and utility functions, which we then apply to simple models to reveal the role of risk, reward sensitivity, and ambiguity in shaping the relationship between information seeking, exploration, and exploitation.

The choice of a particular linguistic path is influenced by the semantic and pragmatic connections between words in a text, whether adjacent or not, which are encoded through discourse markers. To explore this encoding, a new, openly accessible dataset called DiscSense has been created. DiscSense focuses on identifying specific pairs of predicates within sentences that are linked by a wide range of discourse markers and annotates the semantic and pragmatic relationships between them, as well as the markers used to convey those relationships. This annotation goes above and beyond existing resources, such as DoPrAs, by including 15 new categories of causal relations and 11 additional categories of temporal relations, as well as a range of other marker- specific relations that do not fall into these categories. To support research into the complex field of using pairs of words to convey meaning, DiscSense provides examples for 284 distinct categories of meaning- encoding relations, including those caused by a cause, those that occur over time, and those that occur simultaneously.

A distinct energy barrier exists for nonradiative decay in single Pr^3+ ions, but not in groups of Pr^3+ ions, according to a model based on the Mott-Seitz framework. This finding is explained by the model's ability to capture the movement of the Pr^3+ ion within its potential well, which is absent from other theoretical models. The energy barrier is also found to vary with group size, consistency with a 'r^4' dependence. This variation arises as the group potential moves closer to the crystal lattice site, diminishing any asymmetry in the potential well. This model can be applied to any Pr^3+ ion system within a group, regardless of the specific local symmetry, as demonstrated with four different systems in Lu_2O_3.

A new algorithm for training multilayer perceptrons has been developed with an alternative error calculation method that does not involve traditional forward and backward error propagation. This proposed algorithm is being tested for its effectiveness and efficiency in various scenarios to compare its performance against standard error propagation-based methods used in current applications.

A key feature of a certain model involving magnetic interactions is its underlying symmetry, which permits the use of homotopy theory to classify different magnetic configurations, including those of p-fold skwrm type. The structure and arrangement of these p-fold skwrm configurations are dictated by the homotopy properties of the model's target space. In cases where the model lacks sufficient symmetry, a specific topology may give rise to both point-like and vortex-like features within a single p-fold skwrm. Additionally, an analytical method has been established to determine the magnetic energy of p-fold skwrm configurations, which has a direct impact on their stability.

A comprehensive examination of HF and DFT-HF convergence is conducted as a function of electron-electron Coulomb interaction magnitude (k) at various k levels, utilizing models with differing single-particle energy level spacings. It is discovered that when k surpasses a specific threshold, HF and DFT-HF solutions demonstrate increased stability. Thorough k analysis is performed for three distinct sets of single-particle energy level differences and reveals that convergence Ratchets described by K-Dynamical Mean-Sfield Theory (KDMFT) can be linked to underlying HF physics that follow consistent patterns as a function of k. Furthermore, our study indicates that KDMFT's fundamental assumptions are supported by its k-dependency being primarily governed by electron-electron Coulomb forces.

This study investigates the phenomenon of explosive synchronization transitioning from first-order to S-shaped curves within complex networks that exhibit dynamic and structural disorganization. We developed an analytical framework to analyze minimal models of complex networks and established a numerical approach for their complete solution. This approach allows us to differentiate between the effects of dynamical and structural disorder. Our numerical results suggest that significant factors in determining the type of hysteresis are the coupling mismatch and disorder in synchronization order. Our model is applicable to a wide range of complex systems, including those composed of pendulums, lasers, and neural networks with diverse and dynamic connections.

In low-rong approximation and optimization, we often deal with non-convex problems of the form $min f(W_1W_2)$, where $f$ is the objective function. The question of whether the geodesic strong convexity and smoothness properties, as well as the Bachen curvature of such factorized objectives can be predicted based on the properties of $f$ is crucial. Most previous studies have approached this topic by making assumptions about the properties of $W_1$ and $W_2$ without considering their relationship with $f$. This paper, however, removes these assumptions and instead focuses on analyzing Neural Networks, a widely used application area. The analysis is carried out under the Riemannian geometry of the domain, and it assumes that $f$ is restricted strongly convex and smooth. The paper provides formulas for the strong convexity, smoothness, and Bachen curvature of such factorized objectives, and the paper's analysis is tailored to applications with square inputs and outputs. The results of this paper are expected to have a positive impact on the design of efficient and globally optimal algorithms for training Neural Networks.

The strong chromatic edge coloring of a graph is related to identifying the minimum number of colors needed for edge coloring such that every pair of vertices is separated by a specified distance. In 1990, Faudree and Gyárfás made a conjecture about strong edge-coloring in graphs with limited vertex degrees. They proposed that graphs with specific maximum degrees require a minimum number of colors in edge coloring. This study investigates bipartite graphs with a maximum degree of 3 and tests these requirements, both confirming and exceeding the proposed color numbers. Additionally, new lower bound formulas are established for graphs with higher maximum degrees, along with corresponding examples.

Using a novel approach through graph theory, we establish several key features of Dirichlet L-functions at whole number inputs, particularly Gauss sums and their combinations, as well as identities observed in quadratic fields.

Researchers propose an innovative idea to discover non-Gaussian features in the primordial gravitational-wave background that can reveal the existence of massive particles in the early universe. These particles can create clusters of gravitational waves, which become more visible as their mass increases and their interaction with the cosmological horizon causes their non-Gaussian characteristics to be amplified and potentially observable today. A similar effect may also be seen as a side note, based on the power spectrum of scalar perturbations. This research estimates the feasibility of detecting these features using current and upcoming large-scale observations, assuming a standard inflationary model, which raises the possibility of gaining valuable insights into heavy particles in the post-recombination universe if further research confirms their existence.

We have derived a minimal model to capture the snowman-like effect observed in the research of Swartz et al., which reveals the underlying cause of unexpected swimming behaviors and shape-altered propulsion seen in helical swimmers. Underwater, these swimmers exhibit twisted movements, influenced significantly by their unique double-helical design. Our model identifies unanticipated consequences of this configuration, specifically a forward-leaning swimming posture and an unbalanced rotation that varies with the swimmer's geometry. Surprisingly, certain designs could even result in reverse rotation. To address these issues, we conducted simulations using a more advanced hydrodynamic framework, discovering that snowman-like patterns arise from a combination of factors, including structural vibrations and fluid dynamics that counter traditional principles like reciprocity. Furthermore, our research indicates that non-uniform swimmers experience additional challenges, presenting opportunities to explore innovative design concepts, such as controlling motion through asymmetric vibrations induced by unique shapes, and modeling biological swimmers with their spiral houses.

This study employs genetic algorithms through a co-evolutionary approach, where the population is divided into two, with each individual in one group interacting with those in the other, necessitating a fundamental change to reach a stable Nash Equilibrium. It leverages Albrecht's analytical framework to investigate two learning mechanisms - a random trial method and a rational evaluation process - and implements a rigorous mathematical simulation. Results reveal that with a fixed learning parameter $\tau$, the expected distance to the Nash Equilibrium is consistently higher under social learning than individual learning, particularly in large-scale scenarios, due to reduced variability in social learning. Additionally, increasing $\tau$ leads to a rise in expected distance to the Nash Equilibrium for both learning methods. However, a comparative analysis of specific algorithm implementations - Majority for social learning and BestResponse for individual learning - shows the former often yields smaller expected distances to the equilibrium, in contrast to the latter's generally larger expected distances, as opposed to findings in standard evolutionary algorithms where expected distances are typically similar or the majority expected distance is smaller.

To protect users on open platforms, effective monitoring requires the rapid identification of threats in high volumes of data. One method to achieve this is automatically extracting key security concepts from user inputs and discussions. This study focuses on improving the accuracy of such extraction systems by testing various configurations of the Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory model for use in a text classification model. The study aims to optimize the BLM-based system by exploring different implementations and input methods, ultimately selecting the most effective configuration for the application. The research is constrained to the French language and SECReVite dataset, but the findings can be adapted to other languages and datasets with minor modifications.

We've developed an integrated model that combines the CF and AB models, simulating individuals with two opposing opinions while also accounting for magnetic interactions. Averaging over different configurations, we've determined key metrics like the average magnetization and its fluctuations for a simple variant of the model that only considers magnetic interactions. For this variant, we've discovered that the average magnetization squared in the opinion network is four times smaller than in a purely interaction-based network. Similarly, we've found that the magnetic interaction strength is equivalent in the model, regardless of the presence of opposing opinions, but it results in the magnetic temperature being four times higher than in a purely interaction-based network.

The COVID-19 virus is transmitted through respiratory droplets that vary in size, with the droplet composition influenced by the person's physiology, the surrounding environment, and external forces such as the airflow in a room. To understand how infection spreads, it is necessary to account for the different droplet sizes, which also contribute to the different aerosol concentrations people are exposed to. Although research has been conducted to develop mathematical models that account for various factors, the difficulty of modeling the different droplet sizes and their interaction with their environments presents a challenge. This study aims to create and experimentally validate computational models that simulate infection transmission through air in different settings, including the airflow in a classroom and the different droplet sizes. The results show that the model can accurately predict infection distribution in different parts of a classroom, with the model's accuracy improved by including the different droplet sizes. The study also highlights the difficulty of modeling infection transmission in different settings and the need for further research to develop more accurate models.

Inverse and ill-posed problems are complex mathematical challenges with numerous critical applications, such as CT image reconstruction, solving heat equations from boundary measurements, and Compressed Sensing. In this research, we explore the utilization of neural networks, a cutting-edge technology that has solved many optimization problems, as potential solutions to these challenging problems. In fact, most current implementations of neural networks, designed for processing image data, address inverse problems. Due to their widespread adoption and diverse applications, there is a growing interest in developing efficient algorithms for training them. Although recent studies have proven the effectiveness of neural networks, most of these works focus on specific types of problems, resulting in the absence of comprehensive algorithms that can handle both inverse and ill-posed problems within the context of a unified framework. This research proposes an innovative approach to learning physical priors within neural networks, enabling the solution to multiple problems, including multi-problem formulations with various right-hand sides, data sources, and control parameters. This universal solver is applied to typical problems such as the Coefficient Identification Problem, PDE image reconstruction, and Compressed Sensing. We begin by formulating a unified framework encompassing these problems within a multi-input single-output setting and introducing a universal neural network architecture. This new architecture learns a universal decoder to generate multiple outputs, a universal encoder, and a universal optimizer. This work demonstrates the uniqueness and stability of the 0-minimum of such a universal solver and provides a theoretical foundation for the universal architecture using $\Gamma$

Let W be a weight function assigning positive integers to the vertices of an oriented graph G, and let I_Eg(W) represent its weighted edge ideal. Our analysis demonstrates that the equality I_Eg(W)^s = I_Eg(W)^{(s)} holds for all positive integers s if and only if the graph G belongs to one of two specific configurations, thereby characterizing the graphs where the ordinary and symbolic powers of weighted edge ideals are equal. Furthermore, we examine G's path-like structures, and determine the sets of s for which I_Eg(W)^s = I_Eg(W)^{(s)} in both isolated and non-isolated cases.

Building upon the work in arXiv:2109.06666, this paper extends a method for calculating partition functions of SU(N) Lie groups, previously introduced in the context of U(N) in JHEP10(2021)201, this paper presents the general formula for SU(N) the exact part of which had been derived already in the case of (N, n) = (2, 2) in NuPhB942111016.

A silent data corruption, also known as a silent corruption or bit rot, is a well-documented drawback of modern computer technology caused by data that is modified but produces no audible warning. In the context of neural network training, this issue arises when backpropagation propagates incorrect gradients due to a bug in the learning process. This paper presents an in-depth analysis of silent data corruptions and proposes non-uniform range restriction methods to prevent them. The author explores the causes of silent data corruptions and provides a detailed examination of their origins. The paper then compares various definitions of silent data corruptions and offers a range restriction approach to stop their propagation. The author also investigates the limitations of this method and offers an expanded range restriction technique to address them. The proposed method is called upon in the context of correct data propagation during neural network training. An example is provided to illustrate the implementation of range restriction in PyTorch. The author argues that range restriction can be a valuable tool for identifying and fixing bugs in network training workflows. The proposed range restriction method is found to be beneficial in detecting and preventing silent data corruptions, including an investigation of the data's value and distribution both before and after the backward pass. The author concludes that range restriction can be a valuable data monitoring tool for detecting and preventing silent data corruptions. The proposed range restriction method is found to be effective in this role.

Secret service and clearing, also known as netting, involve offsetting mutual obligations between multiple parties to minimize overall payments. Here, we explore the potential of graph algorithms in resolving netting challenges, with a focus on achieving anonymous and secure solutions. By presenting a variant of the classic All-Pairs Shortest Paths problem, we define a customizable debt function adaptable to various monetary scenarios. Our approach utilizes the Ellipswarm meta-heuristic in combination with an exact algorithm, yielding optimal or near-optimal results. A critical aspect of this research is the integration of graph techniques to address netting challenges through peer-to-peer communication, ensuring privacy and authenticity without the need for trusted servers or central coordination.

We explore the Jordanian twist in detail, focusing on both its basic form and a broader application. Through our analysis, we establish that a wide range of Jordanian twists can be derived, focusing on algebra and coalgebra structures within the context of quantum groups. Specifically, we demonstrate that the deformed Jordanian twist preserves the YBE under specific conditions, and this preserves an exponential form. Our findings reveal that the deformed Jordanian twist is related to its original non-exponential form through an automorphism, and it is coordinate-independent, with specific expressions in various coordinate systems. Moreover, we investigate the coproduct in the context of Jordanian twist and demonstrate that the deformed Jordanian twist drives a monoidal structure on the category of its representation, with specific focus on the Drinfel'd quantum adjoint action and its connection to the deformed Jordanian twist.

A new approach for name tagging in low-resource languages has been proposed, combining the advantages of graph-based methods and pattern-matching techniques. 
This model, which is called an improved graph pattern matching model (IGPM), was designed to tackle the limitations of graph-based and pattern-matching models separately. 
IGPM utilizes a rule-based system to extract a graph pattern matrix that is input to a graph algorithm which is called the IBM. 
To enhance the model's performance, IBM was improved through graph structure analysis, position-dependent scores generated by an iterative classifier, and an iterative matrix multiplication operation. 
To test the IPGM model's effectiveness, it was evaluated on the MSRA and TUCO Chinese name tagging datasets as well as an extended English dataset called EN-NBT. 
The results showed that the IPGM model significantly outperformed other name tagging models and achieved a 5.376% increase in F-score on the EN-NBT test set.

Researchers have examined how particles produced in the same-type collisions correlate with each other across different collision scales (pp, pPb, and PbPb collisions at specific center-of-mass energies). They found that certain particle ratios follow a pattern when the collision scales change: specifically, the $D_s^{--}/D_s^-$ and $B_s^{--}/B_s^-$ ratios increase in smaller collisions but show no distinct pattern in larger collisions, while the $K^-/K^+$ and $B^-/B^+$ ratios follow the same pattern in both types of collisions. These observations are compared to theoretical models (AMPT and vMC) that simulate the different collision types. The researchers suggest that the unusual behavior of some particle ratios could be a signature of the color glass condensate and the absence of chemical equilibrium in the partonic phase, rather than chemical non-equilibrium in hadronic phase.

This study investigates dialogue state tracking models trained on datasets with inaccurate labels. We assess the dialogue state tracking model's performance under two conditions: one involving a training dataset with incorrect labels and another with a test dataset with inaccurate labels. To investigate the impact of inaccuracy in both scenarios, we investigate model training using the MultiWOZ 2.0 and a newly created dataset called MWoZ-noisy, which consists of inaccurate labels. As it turns out, dialogue state tracking models struggle to learn from noisy labels due to their inability to accurately infer dialogue states from user utterances. We also experiment with a contrastive learning approach that ranks utterances as similar or different based on their ability to infer dialogue states. This method demonstrates superior performance in both scenarios and achieves similar performance to models trained with accurate labels.

We integrate complex network theory and differential equations to study how the layout of urban environments, specifically Athens, influences collective actions. Our research demonstrates that spatial configurations and physical settings can significantly impact events that occur simultaneously across different locations within a city, rather than just individual psychological effects. By incorporating a practical detection mechanism that models the spread of information, we illustrate that certain urban patterns can either stifle or accelerate civil unrest, depending on their complexity.

To evaluate the reliability of the Prospector framework in estimating star formation rates for quasars, researchers analyzed the $\beta$ luminosity relation, which reflects the average steeper slope and narrower distribution of quasars compared to the general stellar population. By comparing the computed distributions with observed quasium data, it was found that models based on the Kalman filter produce distributions that are too narrow, whereas the models produced by Prospector accurately match the diversity of stellar populations seen in the scatter, highlighting the effectiveness of Prospector in capturing the variability present in the star formation rates.

Given a set of polynomials that form a sum of squares, we can identify the maximum number of polynomials in such a representation by examining the rank of matrices within the Gram spectrahedron. However, not all Gram matrices corresponding to SOS decompositions are created equal - some allow for 'cancellations of squares', leading to an inflated count of squares that aren't genuinely necessary. To address this limitation, we propose a method to minimize the number of squares in a existing SOS decomposition, by formulating an LP-DCC problem and providing an algorithm with a projected graph linear programming approach.

u$ collaboration has compiled a comprehensive set of constraints on various theories, specifically focusing on families of neutrinos, dark energy, neutrino sterile states, and dark Higgs bosons. The primary goal is to detect neutrino interaction cross-section deviations, quantify CKM unitality beyond current understanding, search for neutrino-scattering processes, and identify the presence of dark Higgs bosons and neutrino sterile states by analyzing neutrino interaction rates, searching for missing $K^0$-$ ar{K}^0$ oscillations, and conducting a thorough investigation of TLVH scattering processes. The project has unique capabilities to probe theories in several regions, specifically FASER$

We have developed a symbolic decision procedure to check language containment between regular expressions. This procedure is based on the construction of deterministic finite automata from regular expressions using Brzozowski's operator, along with the development of simplified expressions that maintain equivalence to the original expressions. By combining operator alternative construction, automata determinization via the Thompson automaton, the application of Brzozowski's operator, expression minimization, and reversed construction, we can check containment by comparing the canonical representations of regular expressions. This approach allows us to verify that one regular expression denotes a subset of another, with the ability to provide a counter-example if the containment does not hold.

This paper is the first to address the challenge of Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) using-captured video streams without any preprocessed data. Traditional VIO approaches typically rely on meticulously calibrated and processed sensor data, including algorithmically aligned and registered images, as well as temporally filtered and integrated inertial measurements. In order to explore the potential of end-to-end learnable VIO systems, researchers usually employ synthetic data for both training and testing, while assessing performance on real data requires the introduction of external tools, including Gaussian Process Regressors and Decision Trees. As a result, it has been found that these models perform poorly when exposed to real-world scenarios, leading to the conclusion that the current approach to VIO is best served by a hybrid system that incorporates traditional and deep learning-based components. As the first end-to-end VIO system to process raw sensor data, the proposed model is able to achieve comparable or superior performance to state-of-the-art VIO algorithms on the KITTI and TUM datasets. In order to evaluate the proposed model, researchers compared its performance to multiple VIO approaches and found that it performs best in terms of both accuracy and robustness.

Like understanding an ultra-strong magnet as the combination of weaker magnetic forces, higher-order Weyl semimetels may possess a unique form of "geometry" - square-root topology - that emerges from more complex underlying patterns in three-dimensional space. This novel topology could potentially be observed through the unusual behavior of charge carriers, which would serve as a tangible manifestation of this phenomenon.

This study focuses on a numerically efficient method for solving incomplete data problems, particularly effective when dealing with incomplete boundary information. Utilizing a high-resolution method for completing Hamilton-Jacobi equations, we implemented a nonlinear explicit scheme for solving the incomplete data problem. To accurately resolve the equation, we used edge finite elements to discretize the equation, avoiding spurious oscillations. To validate the proposed approach and simulation results, two examples are provided: the first involving the reconstruction of a potential function from scattered electron tomography, and the second involving the reconstruction of a vector field from scattered magnetic measurements, both reconstructed from scattered data.

The derivative of the highest weight vector in the highest weight module of the simple affine Lie superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$ is demonstrated to generate a parafermion vertex operator algebra, with an identified submodule that forms an instance of a Lie superalgebra weight module, characterized by a specific index. Through analysis, the $osp(1|2n)$ module is shown to be constructed from the parafermion vertex operator algebra by applying creation operators, with an established set of idempotents in the endomorphism ring enabling decomposition of the module into irreducible components. Furthermore, upon setting a parameter to infinity, a limit is defined within the category of weight modules, with modules exhibiting properties related to the simple Boody-Chevalley-Quantized (BQ) algebra.

When building intelligent systems, there's often a necessity to integrate multiple trained components into a singular, highly-trained system. However, knowledge transfer techniques frequently struggle to pinpoint which parts of the source models are genuinely beneficial, especially when multiple teachers are involved, as they also introduce noisy labels. This issue becomes particularly prominent in knowledge amalgamation using sequence-to-sequence models, such as those employed in summarizing, paraphrasing, and translation tasks. To tackle this issue, we propose an innovative knowledge transfer method based on identifying the most relevant knowledge within the teacher models. By incorporating a novel technique called the Masked Cross-Entropy Loss, we can generate saliency masks that highlight which parts of the teacher labels are valuable. As a result, our method not only filters out noisy labels but also discovers and utilizes underlying valuable knowledge. In knowledge distillation, our approach outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods, while in knowledge amalgamation, it achieves superior results compared to frequent techniques and represents a substantial enhancement over state-of-the-art student training methods. Notably, with just one teacher, our method yields a precise improvement of 1.2%, while with multiple teachers, it achieves a significant gain of 1.4%.

Internal brain systems sustain our spatial awareness, memory and navigation skills, with the hippocampal-entorhinal network at their core. Location-sensitive neurons called 'grid cells' within the inner layer of the subiculum of the entorhinal cortex receive spatial inputs from the hippocampus which then influence grid patterns in the subiculum. Although grid cells are highly sensitive to external stimuli such as visual and olfactory cues, very little is known about where their sensory inputs originate, or how their grid patterns are affected by these inputs. A dissection study using acute slices of the entorhinal cortex-hippocampus found that grid pattern generation is driven by specific types of neurons called 'ORC' within the subiculum. A study using optogenetics to stimulate ORC showed that grid pattern production can be altered at will, suggesting that the entorhinal cortex-hippocampus might play a crucial role in how the brain uses and integrates spatial information from various parts of the brain.

Research on slowly rotating stars like the Sun reveals recurring patterns in their activity cycles, and this study explores conditions under which magnetic cycles can arise in these stars. By combining existing models with observational data on stellar rotation and activity, researchers investigate the impact of kinematic and helical turbulence on magnetic field regeneration. Results show that in non-helical turbulence scenarios, regenerating magnetic fields require significant rotation rates or helicity, and this regulation effects magnetic field occurrence in stars. Specifically, regenerating fields are more prevalent in intermediate and fast rotators while non-active or weakly active stars correspond to slow rotators, and this study discusses potential applications of this reasoning to categorizing stellar behavior and analyzing rotation-activity correlations among various stars.

According to M. Stoll's conjecture from 2009, there's an infinite variety of Galois field extensions using the symmetric group S4, where specific elliptic curves won't increase in rank. Building on previous research, we've found 135 fresh instances confirming this idea, or at least matching its spirit. In addition, we've identified specific instances utilizing the GL2–abc height function, as well as several distinct projects utilizing the GL2–satellite method to detect S4 quartic extensions in great numbers, resulting in discoveries of over a million such extensions up to conductor 5.6 million, with some potentially reaching as high as 12 million.

During quantum quenches, the generates irreversible entropy can be used as a dynamic order parameter, providing a versatile approach to explore nonequilibrium physics. We have developed an original strategy to compute a lower bound of irreversible entropy production via quantum quench, incorporating both Quench Turbulence and holographic scenarios. By analyzing both nonequilibrium entropy and temperature changes, we have discovered that the entropy production lower bound closely mirrors the variations in nonequilibrium temperature for a specific range of quenches, characterized by a sudden increase in temperature. This approach is achieved by formulating the nonequilibrium temperature through the equilibrium free energy and utilizing the second law of thermodynamics to estimate the irreversible entropy production.

We investigate non-unitary dynamics, specifically quantum operations $\mathcal{E}(t)$ that result from tracing out a quantum system's interaction with an environment, given unitary evolution of the combined system. It is shown that a class of quantum operations, often utilized to model open quantum dynamics, results from appropriate initialization of both the system and environment. The operations in question require the initial state to be uncorrelated. However, they lose derivability when quantum operations are applied repeatedly, given that the environment is a finite-dimensional Hilbert space. Surprisingly, the time at which quantum operations depart from their unitary evolution origin, i.e., the distinguishability time, is unrelated to when deviations become unavoidable due to insufficient dimensionality, i.e., the unavoidable divergence time. Moreover, a direct correlation is found between time-twirling and quantum operations that result from such model, even when there is no precise relationship between the two times mentioned above. This connection is further explored in detail in this research.

A nondegenerate regular simplex with vertices within the unit cube in R_n is being studied, with recent research determining its minimum possible diameter for given dimension. This paper addresses the question of interpolation at the vertices of such a simplex by establishing an equivalent condition for a given regular simplex to be inscribed in the unit cube in R_n. A general algorithm is also provided to construct such a simplex for interpolation nodes that can be factored by the dimension dimension plus one.

We've analyzed the carrier concentration in etched silicon and found significant variations in the silicon's top nanometers. The method for determining carrier concentration involved utilizing an optical etching technique, manipulating the silicon substrate's thickness, and analyzing the result with ellipsometry. The carrier concentration could be manipulated by altering the etching process parameters, and it was observed that etched silicon had approximately 10 times more carriers than typical silicon. The carrier type could also be customized as long as the etching process was controlled. However, the carrier mobility was seen to vary within the silicon's top few nanometers and was seen to be around 100 cm^2/V at the surface, which was not as limited as expected. The mobility was limited to around 350 cm^2/V at a depth of around 10 nm. We attributed this to reduced scattering of the valence band due to the reduced disorder of the etching process, which resulted in single-crystalline like behavior. This outcome is significant for the performance of silicon-based transistors, which could now have higher conductivity by increasing the carrier density, which could offset the reduced mobility.

In this work, we extend several key concepts from rational homotopy theory to the realm of homotopy K-theory. Specifically, we investigate cdh descent and Milnor excision for twisted homotopy K-theory, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of the twisted Karoubi-Villamayor K-theory as a model, enabling us to prove split short exact sequences for homotopy K-theory and twisted Karoubi-Villamayor K-theory.

Modeling an planet's complete system, encompassing its shape, atmospheric conditions, and internal workings, over extended periods presents significant challenges. Despite its essential role in defining an planet's ultimate form, atmospheric evolution is infrequently given more than basic considerations, usually limited to surface temperature and gravity. This is problematic given the prevalent and frequently substantial activity of a planet's interior. We propose incorporating a volatile cycle between the interior and surface to more thoroughly explore this issue. This approach involves introducing variable components representing chemical compounds with varying degrees of volatility. These compounds, which include water and CO2, regulate the volume of a planet's atmosphere, influencing its thermal properties and ultimately the planet's overall evolution. Incorporating this volatile cycle into the model results in a valuable feedback loop that impacts both the interior and atmospheric conditions, which in turn affects geological activity and mass loss, leading to a more comprehensive variable interaction cycle. We established a computational framework for volatile cycle evolution by integrating it with variable introduction/elimination mechanisms and simulated various evolutionary cycles with varying degrees of volatility. The results show various valuable Faint-Biased Stars can support prolonged existence and potentially habitable conditions, which provides a surprising insight into the potential for extended habitability of such stars.

To understand the production of methane from biodegradable waste, we studied how mass-selected ions like ethylene and propylene react with 1,2-propanediol (PDO) and 1,3-PDO. When ionizing at 70 eV, adding PDO to a hydrocarbon ion increases the amount of CH3+ formed, but this effect varies depending on the parent ion. For example, CH3+ formation is more common when methyl cations can result from the direct loss of water molecules from the adduct ions, but less so when cations are formed by loss of the intact PDO molecule. CH3+ is particularly prevalent when reacting with 1,2-PDO, but not when reacting with 1,3-PDO, likely due to the different molecular structures of the two PDOs. This difference results in different decomposition pathways, leading to different primary losses of larger neutral molecules, such as C3H5+ in the 1,2-PDO adducts, but not in the 1,3-PDO adducts. This indicates that ionization structure plays a significant role in mass spectrometry analysis of biodegradation, and that mass selection may not accurately reflect what is actually ionized.

Recent advancements in quantum hardware and computing have facilitated the synergy of tensor networks (TNs) and parametrized quantum circuits (PQCs). By leveraging quantum devices for simulating and engineering both TNs and PQCs, researchers have discovered a valuable partnership. The mapping of quantum states from both domains establishes a profound connection, enabling the utilization of TN algorithms in quantum computation and serving as a benchmark for developing efficient TN algorithms through quantum implementations. In this context, we review the current state of quantum algorithms for working with TNs, with a focus on the benefits and challenges this collaboration offers to both TNs and PQCs. The algorithms' capabilities in learning complex patterns through quantum processes and the potential for developing quantum-inspired TN algorithms are highlighted, alongside emerging research directions in the field.

Graph neural networks are graph-based algorithms that excel at managing dependent data, such as graphs of neural activity in the brain, and are being investigated for their potential to classify tissue representations in the brain that separate healthy tissue from cancerous areas. Researchers are now in the process of comparing GNNs to traditional machine learning methods to determine which approach is most effective at distinguishing cerebral tumors, particularly in a dataset consisting of MRI brain scans labeled as normal, with astrocytoma tumors, or with glioblastoma tumors. The study is anticipating valuable insights into the relationship between neural activity patterns and tumor classification, potentially contributing to a deeper understanding of neural activity's role in cancer diagnosis.

In multivariate point processes, the inclusion of interaction effects, like those seen in the nonlinear Hawkes process, can be challenging due to their impact on the distribution and estimation of parameters. We developed a novel multistep least squares algorithm for parameter estimation in the nonlinear Hawkes process, an algorithm that notably bypasses the need to determine the intricate integral equation associated with the cumulative intensity. Our method's performance, when compared to established estimation techniques, shows superior results in various data sets, providing a significant improvement in efficiency and reliability.

The Public-domain Fast Multipole Method (pFMMLib) is a C++ library for the Fast Multipole Method (FMM) that's specifically optimized for computational applications in astrophysics and physics, particularly in calculating gravitational forces. pFMMLib is available free of charge under the terms of the GPL license version 2 or a later version.

Deep learning methods for guiding treatment planning have been successfully used, but their effectiveness is hindered by the need for time-consuming and expensive evaluation processes. To tackle this problem, models incorporating semi-supervised and domain adaptation techniques aim to create more accurate and efficient treatment plans using fewer labeled data. However, most existing approaches struggle to function across different anatomical domains due to significant functional differences and varied label guidance. To address these limitations, we propose an innovative framework called Contrastive Semi-supervised learning for Cross Anatomy Domain Adaptation (CS-CADA). The CS-CADA learning framework integrates guided contrastive learning, pseudo-label guided contrastive learning, and a network guided by semi-supervised and domain adaptation mechanisms. The proposed framework employs guided and Pseudo-label guided contrastive learning to generate high-quality pseudo labels, facilitate the alignment of semantic features across different domains, and enhance feature representation. The experimental results from studies using public datasets confirm that CS-CADA yields improved segmentation performance compared to existing methods.

We investigate the BRS symmetry within the supergravity theory in three spatial dimensions and demonstrate that its global nature can be comprehended through the analysis of BRS symmetry itself. Moreover, we claim that studying the BRS symmetry serves as an essential prerequisite for quantizing supergravity. To support this assertion, we examine the algebra of BRS charges in supersymmetric theories, specifically addressing the anomaly problem. Additionally, we investigate the implications of our approach on the anomaly issue by comparing the results of two distinct methodologies: cohomology of the complex of local BRS charges and the algebra of global BRS charges derived from the former. As a practical illustration, we apply this logic to the model containing the gravitino field in three spatial dimensions.

Researchers have long hypothesized that using a plasma waveplate inside a laser cavity could enhance the polarization conversion efficiency needed to produce circularly polarized femtosecond pulses. These advanced pulses possess unique magnetic properties, which may provide a superior alternative to traditional ferromagnetic materials that absorb significant amounts of light. The feasibility of this plasma waveplate approach has been evaluated, which involved a computational model that accounts for multiple light reflections within the plasma and laser cavity. The model indicates that the plasma plate must be quite thick, which in turn depends on the strength of the magnetic field, which is influenced by the magnetic field strength and electron density. It is estimated that for typical parameters, the required plasma plate would need to be around 75 micrometers thick, which is larger than usual ferromagnetic layers. However, if the plasma's group velocity matches the speed of light, the required thickness could be reduced to approximately 30 micrometers. If such a plasma waveplate proves effective, it would provide a novel and highly controllable method for generating intense circularly polarized light within a few weeks' time.

A comprehensive examination of the potential for two-Higgs doublet models of the type-II, which extend the Standard Model, is presented, with a focus on the impact of the Higgs sector on the electric dipole moment of the tau. We identify and analyze the primary factors influencing the electric dipole moment of the tau within this framework and discuss the applicable limits imposed by existing tau physics constraints. Moreover, we assess the significance of considering five-body decays of B mesons in upholding flavor changing tau physics. Finally, we predict the magnitude of the electric dipole moment of the tau in type-II two-Higgs doublet models and discuss the implications for future experiments.

Rank metric codes are renowned for their robust error correction capabilities,
typically exhibiting strong performance around rate 1/2 and weaker performance at
higher rates. This article reveals that the intricate structure of the rank metric
can be mapped onto an information-theoretic framework, showing distinct
characteristics for rates below 1/2 and above 1/2. We emphasize that rank metric
codes above rate 1/2 essentially correspond to a combination of nested systems, often
used in achieving high reliability in communication over fading channels. This
structure provides a more precise basis for developing codes above rate 1/2 that
retain desirable properties of good rank metric codes, rather than merely relying
on the observation that such codes can be viewed as projections of higher-rate
codes. This new perspective underlies our main finding, that the widely employed
rank metric convolution codes are actually equivalent to nested networks in the
newly defined sense. This notable equivalence enables a complete characterization
of their duality and maximum rank distance properties.

We investigate the operator product expansion (Poisson bracket) of current OPE blocks in two-dimensional field theory, which is linked to geodesic operators in the anti-de Sitter spaces of two and one dimensions. Through a study of the double commutator of current OPE blocks in the anti-de Sitter space of two dimensions, we gain insight into the correlation functions involving four points in the anti-de Sitter space of two dimensions. By examining the relationship between the conserved current two-point functions in the boundary conformal field theory and anti-de Sitter space of two-dimensional geodesic operators, we can determine the single-trace two-point functions in the boundary conformal field theory from the bulk theory with anti-de Sitter space of two dimensions. Additionally, a comparison is made with the case where the bulk theory with anti-de Sitter space of three dimensions is considered, revealing a difference in the structure of the double commutator of the current OPE blocks in the anti-de Sitter space of three dimensions when expressed in terms of the AdS$_3$ geodesic operators.

A recent study by Komatsu,, 20099 suggested that neural network methods and traditional estimators have similar efficacy for lensing reconstruction. This finding was further investigated and confirmed with a different neural network architecture that generally outperformed the traditional estimator. It was also discovered that a key factor in lensing reconstruction performance is how well the chosen method models the likelihood function, and that results from both neural network and traditional approaches can be improved by combining them with the likelihood function provided by the MAXLIK code (Komatsu+98). This factorization concept was applied to a probabilistic neural network that models both the data likelihood and the prior, and its connection to maximum a posteriori estimation was explored.

This paper provides a concise overview of combinatorial differential geometry, an interdisciplinary field with roots in the pioneering work of Gelfand and MacPherson. Their collaborative efforts ultimately led to the development of the category of combinatorial differential manifolds and its associated tangent functor. Before their groundbreaking contributions, combinatorial differential geometry was explored by various mathematicians who laid the foundation for its further study. The paper then delves into the proof of Kelly's characterization of combinatorial differential geometry, demonstrating its equivalence to Cartesian differential categories, and kelly2019combinatorial all the way through the more recent demonstrated equivalence.

The remnant of a type II supernova, known as Cas A, contains Fe~26 as evidence from isotopic spectroscopy. Fe~26's presence indicates Type II supernovae have the capacity to generate iron group elements through electron capture processes during core collapse, even when an iron core is not fully formed. However, the precise mechanism for producing this ~26 is still not fully understood. We analyzed the Ni/~26 and Ni/Co ratio in SN~2020jfo, a Type II supernova with electron capture origin ~26 and Ni/~26 and Ni/Co ratio in SN~2020jfo are electron capture nucleosynthesis is the main producer of iron group elements in some Type II supernovae with collapsed iron cores. We found the Ni/Fe production ratio in SN~2020jfo is about 1.5 times greater than in another Type II supernova, RCW 103, suggesting a heavier stable isotope of Ni has a larger abundance in SN~2020jfo. The Ni/~26 and Ni/Co ratio in SN~2020jfo is about 1.5 to 2.5 times greater than solar values, while Ni/~26 and Ni/Co ratio in another Type II supernova, SN~2014J, is less than solar values.
