Using deep learning techniques, a neural network can effectively identify different segments of a complex lobster-eye optics system by analyzing the image's rotation angle. In a controlled laboratory setting, a cross-shaped image was rotated at various angles, and a neural network was trained to map these angles to corresponding segments. Surprisingly, the network performed optimally when trained and tested within a limited range of rotations, but generalizing to new, unseen angles resulted in incorrect predictions. This discrepancy led to the discovery of a unique non-linear relationship between angles and positions, ultimately allowing for a precise mathematical formula to be derived that accurately reflects this relationship.

Recently, level set methods have had success exploring the field of second-order fully nonlinear equations. Despite their practical success, a rigorous theoretical understanding of these methods for such equations has been largely absent. This research proposes an alternative level set formulation that enables the original problem's equivalence and utilizes novel tools from the theory of stochastic complementation to prove the comparative property within the viscosity framework.

Using hydrodynamical simulations, we investigate the impact of our universe's fine-tuned amplitude of initial scalar perturbations on the accuracy of predicting halo masses through $f_R$ modified gravity, with one of its key parameters closely aligned to $\Lambda$CDM. Our findings reveal that under the given constraints, a density-only model predicts halo masses much more precisely in $\Lambda$CDM than in modified gravity, notably with a significant discrepancy when considering the group of Shapley. Furthermore, we observe that halos containing live central stars are rarer in modified gravity due to enhanced potential wells, potentially contributing to the earlier formation of supermassive black holes and possible deviations in the observed stellar mass function at high redshifts.

Recently, separating mixed audio sources has become an important area of research.
This task typically involves multiple tasks, such as source separation, super-source
separation, and single-source separation. One notable area of single-source
separation research involves converting monophonic signals into polyphonic signals.
In this paper, we address the challenge of transforming a monophonic signal into a
polyphonic one, a task that has not been widely explored with deep learning methods.
Our work focuses on converting a monophonic piano recording into a polyphonic one,
achieved through the CNMF approach that employs non-negative matrix factorization
to model the time-frequency representation of the time-series recording.
To facilitate this task, we developed a semi-supervised CNMF method incorporating
time-frequency masking, continuous-time decomposition, and time-series post-processing.
Through comprehensive evaluations using three piano recordings in the MegaSeP dataset, we
demonstrate that our semi-supervised CNMF method outperforms leading low-rank factorization
techniques and supervised deep learning methods in piano transcription, representing a
novel approach to polyphonic sound reconstruction using CNMF factorization.

In analyses of rotating stars undergoing rotational instability, the approach is taken of tracking individual fluid fluid elements with consistent properties, such as mass, specific angular momentum, and velocity. This method diverges from conventional practices in stellar astrophysics, which typically assume a quasi-static equilibrium for each fluid fluid element. Researchers investigated the extent to which the non-equilibrium approach surpasses the equilibrium-based method in precision. It was found that deviations from equilibrium yield significant results, resulting in up to a 20 percent increase in internal energy when analyzing maximum stability models. This in turn affects predictions of accretion disk properties, showing that using the non-equilibrium approach results in emission lines that are orders of magnitude weaker than predicted with the equilibrium approach.

Acquiring labeled data is a costly and time-consuming process that can be
reduced through the use of active learning, which strategically selects data
for labeling. Despite the potential of active learning, existing methods often
neglect the crucial step of confirming the validity of their selected samples,
which can introduce label noise and compromise their performance. To address this
shortcoming, a novel active learning framework called ValidAL has been proposed,
which incorporates sample validity verification into the active learning
framework. Specifically, ValidAL focuses on identifying easily labelable samples
among the active learning candidates, assigns priority to difficult-to-label
regions, and optimizes the balance between the two to prevent model bias toward
noise during training. Experimental evaluations on various real-world image
datasets demonstrate that ValidAL significantly outperforms existing baseline
methods in terms of performance, achieving a substantial improvement of up to
8.5% and reducing label costs by as much as 88%. The source code for ValidAL can
be found at the following link: https://github.com/GaryZhang1995/ValidAL.

When neutron stars merge, both gravitational waves and electromagnetic radiation are released, leading to improved insights and data from combined observations. This paper conducts hypothetical analyses examining the effects of merging neutron stars under various conditions, assuming both a ground-based space telescope and the Einstein Telescope can see the events. It presents methods to combine data from gravitational waves and X-rays or radio waves, demonstrating how these methods can be used in actual cases. It presents several key findings, which include: typically, neutron star mergers result in radio waves, with about 1% becoming hypernovae or only 0.1% resulting in gamma-ray bursts, which have specific rates in certain mass ranges, the mass ranges affect the timing of the transitions, the events have specific characteristics that can differ based on their mass, the events may have abnormal parameters, and the results suggest that most radio events have low luminosities, which could be hard to detect, which could increase the challenges in finding the actual rate of these events, which currently may have limited sensitivity in certain time frames, which could be improved in the future, which could lead to better constraints on the ratio of radio to gravitational waves events, which typically have normal values, which could be used in various analyses, which have specific ratios that can be compared to other events, which could be more precise in certain mass ranges, which typically have specific characteristics, which could be better understood with greater sensitivity, which currently may have limited data in certain time frames, which could be improved in

Determining the effectiveness of treatments for chronic conditions, such as heart failure, relies heavily on non-clinical factors known as social determinants of health (SDOH). While SDOH are crucial, the unstructured nature of electronic health records (EHRs) presents a challenge in SDOH data extraction. To address this challenge, SDOH annotations in the MIMIC-IV notes have been utilized to train and evaluate machine learning models, specifically clinical note NLP pipelines, in extracting SDOH data automatically. This study assessed the ability of these models to accurately extract SDOH by training and testing them with different subsets of the MIMIC-IV notes and clinicians' labels as reference points. Furthermore, a heart failure patient population was identified from the EHR metadata, and a random forest classifier was employed to analyze SDOH data, treatment approaches, and care utilization between HF patients and the broader inpatient population. The study discovered that note content varies significantly based on the presence of certain SDOH such as food insecurity and homelessness, which has implications for NLP model performance. As a result, this research offers a framework for leveraging clinical notes to extract SDOH data and provides insight into the relationship between SDOH, care utilization, and care management program participation.

When studying active matter, incorporating non-conservative forces into models is a common practice. To better understand this, we've developed a novel framework for creating effective potentials and governing stochastic equations that account for internal states in systems driven outside of equilibrium. Applying this equilibrium-transduction framework to an idealized two-state model of a swimmer operating in a viscous environment, we determined the actual work required to move it between two fixed locations. Next, we analyzed the optimal switching strategy for this linear line drive, revealing that the cost-effective method involves frequent state switching at a particular rate, as increasing the rate of switching results in a proportional increase in switching costs. The effective potential we've defined for this system enables the comparison of distances between states in terms of statistical probability, which is an order of magnitude smaller than the physical distance between the system's positions. Alternatively, we derived a non-equilibrium free energy difference that is mathematically equivalent to the minimum minimum work required to move the system between two states, which is also applicable to calculating cycle work. Notably, if the system's internal switching is slow, not only does it need more energy to operate, but it is much closer to achieving equilibrium in each of its states.

The pandemic has produced lasting changes in urban environments, with restrictions and social distancing influencing how people interact within their communities. Due to increased digital connectivity, the long-term effects on community dynamics and human interactions remain unclear. To understand the multi-year, seasonal variations in urban encounters post-pandemic, researchers analyzed GPS and smartphone data in New York City from 2019 to 2021, alongside event data and mobility metrics. They found that urban encounters with strangers have shifted seasonally over time and that the diversity of interactions decreased in 2020 and 2021, with remaining differences from pre-pandemic patterns observed as late as summer 2021 and into summer 2021. However, urban encounter diversity began recovering by autumn 2021 and exhibited seasonal fluctuations once more during the 2021 calendar year. Although urban encounters with strangers did not fully align with overall mobility or spatial movement, they were correlated with local spatial mobility during the 2021 calendar year. Ultimately, this research underscores the significant, long-lasting impact of public health policies on urban encounters and highlights urban spaces' adaptability in promoting public health while maintaining social and seasonal dynamics.

A young stellar object, X Tori-1, in the Monoceros OB1 association, has a remarkable large-scale radio disc surrounding it, which poses a question about how it can exist without being disrupted by nearby massive stars or migrating objects within the surrounding gas ring. High-resolution observations of the 21-cm line have provided velocity maps of the gas ring, which, when analyzed using the Tremaine-Binney-Olin method, have revealed a distinct, narrow inner solid body orbiting X Tori-1 at a distance of 1400 AU, likely a star or brown dwarf. However, the presence of this object could threaten the stability of the inner solid body's gravitational forces, which, although sufficient to maintain the ring's circular orbit, may be exceeded, potentially disrupting the inner solid body, especially if it is not fully masslocked to X Tori-1. Alternatively, the inner solid body could be maintained in a stable state if it has a sufficiently high mass, which, while theoretically possible, is unlikely given the probable low mass of such a body. Regardless, the inner solid body could provide an ideal target for further observations, which have revealed the possibility of a nonKeplerian, slow precessing ring, which, although not fully explained, could reveal information about the motion of the inner solid body, which, in turn, could provide valuable information about the formation and evolution of gas rings around young stellar objects.

Given a scattering matrix and an asymptotic algebra for a broader class of locally algebraic quantum field theories, we demonstrate that a particular scattering theory can be reconstructed, at least formally. Under additional assumptions relevant to rational conformal field theories and their Bogoliubov transformations, our formal construction becomes rigorous.

A recent controversy has been fueled by claims regarding 5G cellular towers' potential harm to human health, necessitating an examination of exposure levels from these towers. Researchers have now developed modified models to estimate average 5G and pre-5G cell site power density in urban settings, incorporating the attenuating effects of buildings. Data from actual monitoring devices was used to validate a 5G model, resulting in average values that matched those of its predecessor, indicating no increased risk to public health from 5G. However, 5G small cells were found to have higher exposure potential compared to legacy cells in some studies.

This study explores methods to resolve periodic water surface profiles using only wave amplitude information, with applications including remote sensing and seiche lake restoration. The approach involves representing water surfaces as parametric curves and verifying their parametric convexity through envelope representation of breaking waves. A direct algorithm for parametric convex curve reconstruction is developed, and its effectiveness is demonstrated via numerical simulations and laboratory tests under various conditions.

Let X be a locally convex space that is not normable. To gain insight into the structure of differential forms on X, we aim to establish that the map from the collection of differential k-forms to the collection of alternating multilinear forms is surjective. However, previous research has primarily focused on sequence spaces that lack certain properties. In contrast, let X be a space equipped with a Bochner space norm, and let us demonstrate that the surface layer of X is homeomorphic to the surface of the associated associated sequence space, and moreover, the tangent spaces at the origin are also homeomorphic. Consequently, the surface layer of the associated sequence space is also homeomorphic to the surface layer of Bochner space, and the tangent spaces at the origin are also homeomorphic. Furthermore, let us demonstrate that any (k-1)-form in the associated sequence space can be represented as integral over the differential k-form in Bochner space. Consequently, any k-form in the associated sequence space is represented as sum of the differential of the (k-1)-form in the associated sequence space and the pull-back of k-form in Bochner space through the canonical linear map from the associated sequence space to Bochner space.

A novel system for autonomous navigation in empty environments has been developed and implemented on a mobile platform equipped with three-dimensional sonar sensors. The navigation strategy is divided into two independently operated layers: the primary control layer manages the movement of the platform using the sonar sensors to map the surroundings, while the secondary control layer takes over when obstacles are detected within a defined detection range. This obstacle-navigating module employs the same dynamics, sensors, and actuators as the primary control layer, utilizing the same path-planning algorithm but with real-time obstacle tracking and trajectory modification capabilities, thus enabling efficient navigation in close proximity to and within the obstacle's range.

Fake news detection is increasingly being addressed by algorithms that analyze text alone, yet the practical application of these systems falls short due to their inability to incorporate real-world false information. A critical first step in developing effective fake news detection tools is examining the impact of networking context on predictive performance. We found that incorporating contextual information into abundant text-based solutions results in a significant 6-10% drop in accuracy. To improve these results we devised a method that uses contextual data to identify and remove accounts with unusually high activity levels. This approach yields more than 10 times more frequent gains of over 5%, while yielding fewer than 0.1% probability of exceeding 10% gains in accuracy. We also observed our method to be particularly beneficial when applied to highly controversial subjects such as vaccinations, terrorism, and elections. Notably, contexts have a much less profound effect on model performance when spreading misinformation is aimed at.

This study formulates a generalized Landau theory, integrating system curvature, to explain first-order phase transitions and coexistence of phases within black holes using holographic duality. Within this framework, negative curvature accelerates system oscillations, reduces entropy, hastens the completion of the Suessdorf effect, and induces a latent heat indicator in the $T$-$S$ graph. Conversely, positive curvature accelerates the formation of black holes via the SUHKHL threshold, displays an inflection point in the entropy graph, and may result in the Heterodirectional Hysteresis. This theory is supported by calculations involving black strings, black holes, and suspensions in various bulk geometries, including asymptotically AdS spaces with both positive and negative dilaton potentials. Notably, only black strings exhibit features of an unstable localized mode, denoted as the hairy black hole, within regions of large positive curvature in domains with negative dilaton potential.

A precise optimal decoding strategy is devised for soft decision intersection decoders of low-density parity-check codes, yet its implementation is hindered by substantial computational complexity. A simpler, suboptimal decoding approach is proposed, and its performance is proven to converge to the optimal method as more check equations are considered. A theoretical lower bound is also established for this proposed approach. Given the lack of a practical measure of check node values, an innovative decoding order is proposed to enhance the suboptimal approach's performance. However, this proves challenging to determine in real-time. A heuristic solution is derived from check node degree and initial message reliability. Nevertheless, this leads to decreased performance and potentially unstable iterations. A novel inequality is also introduced to stabilize the approach's performance. Check node degrees are modified using this inequality to ensure balanced iteration convergence. This enhances the decoding order's performance and lowers the risk of instability. Although providing practical guidance, these methods yield suboptimal outcomes. The proposed approach is no longer guaranteed to converge and may fail to decode valid codewords. The proposed inequality provides an efficient, straightforward decoding order selection. It significantly lowers the complexity of check node operations by roughly an order of magnitude, with minimal performance degradation. Simulation results demonstrate that this approach lowers the complexity of check node operations by nearly tenfold, relative to a baseline approach.

In this work, the two-block first-order reformulation of the nonconvex and nonlipshitzian L1-PCA problem under rotational invariance is solved. We develop a general iterative proximal gradient algorithm for the two-block structured form with a specific two-step iteration process. The convergence to a Karush-Kuhn-Tucker point is theoretically guaranteed regardless of the first-order convex and strongly concave properties of the first and second blocks, respectively. Moreover, if both blocks possess these properties, we prove the convergence to a local optimum. The algorithm's two-block form can be expanded to various types of weighted L1-PCA problems with arbitrary weight matrices. A novel two-block multiplicative PCA problem is also addressed with this general algorithm. Numerical performance of the proposed algorithm is demonstrated through various numerical experiments.

An underexplored angle of validating crowdsourced annotation data involves using multiple, unrelated categories to validate the annotations of a single, unrelated category. In this research, we focus on validating the annotations in the Food-101 dataset by validating the annotations in the ImageNet dataset. A key observation made is that verifying all 101 Food-101 labels by verifying just 10 network nodes is possible, due to the hierarchical organization of the labels, which reduces the inter-class boundary values between neighboring labels. This observation enabled us to validate 99 out of 100 labels by examining 7 pairs of adjacent network nodes, with minimal inter-class boundary values. To gather valuable insights from the nodes' responses, we developed an inter-class probability distribution model, which is built upon the neural tangent kernel and is capable of capturing both the Nearest Neighbor and Nearest Neighbor Votes (NNV) votes, as well as the nodes' activation values, without incurring the computational cost of actually performing annotation work. This model allowed us to validate 36 label pairs in the Food-101 dataset with Nearest Neighbor accuracy (NNA) and Nav activation value accuracy (Nava) by validating 5 nodes by 10 times 10 times. A key finding made along the way is that the inter-class distance between adjacent network nodes in the data space is equal to the Hamming distance between their corresponding output codes, divided by 10 times

Quantum games involve two players with access to shared quantum memory, interacting through sequential quantum actions until the game ends, at which point a outcome is determined based on the stored memory content. A condition for winning a game is considered positional if the optimal strategy can be found through iterative comparison of current and previous states. Previous research has shown that certain types of positional winning conditions, including those that are 'half-positional', cannot be perfectly characterized by quantum games. In this research, we first confirm that the class of half-positional winning conditions is not closed under logical 'and' operations, and demonstrate that it equals the highest sub-class of the broader class of positional winning conditions. We also find that quantum games lack the ability to perfectly characterize 'strongly half-positional' winning conditions, and this issue persists even when restricting to a specific sub-class of half-positional winning conditions known as 'weakly half-positional' conditions. Additionally, we demonstrate that the class of half-positional winning conditions cannot be accurately represented by par games, and this inaccuracy arises even when considering the basic sub-class of 'weakly half-positional' conditions. Finally, we find that another class of 'prefix-independent' conditions cannot be accurately characterized by quantum games and this inability persists when considering a specific sub-class of these conditions known as 'prefix-independent half-positional' conditions.

We studied the X-ray spectra of three high-variable asynchronous polars - 
TL Cru, Chryseris and IC 405 using the XMM-Newton mission, discovering that their 
emission patterns differ significantly from those of standard polars. 
Comparing the X-ray spectra of asynchronous and non-asynchronous polars reveals 
that the former emit more heavily on line emission while the latter excceed 
line emission constraints. As the variability in asynchronous polars is 
particularly pronounced, it could potentially aid in understanding their 
mechanism of operation.

This paper outlines the solution strategy for a fluid-structure interaction problem, broken down into manageable parts. Within this framework, we use a linearized approach to handle structural displacement, incorporating rotation effects through the Antman-Sundal model. We detail a partitioned solution method, where fluid and structural problems are solved independently, focusing on non-overlapping grids that only intersect at the boundary. We employ high-order compact schemes for internal points in the fluid domain and a finite element approach for the structure, then illustrate the method with a cantilever beam example.

To effectively manage navigation in complex and dynamic environments, mobile robots require comprehensive world models. Traditionally, global metric maps have been used for this purpose, but they become inefficient as map size increases due to their representative of the entire surrounding area. In contrast, HiTMap represents a novel hierarchical attention-based world model that efficiently handles both small-local and large-global areas. Utilizing attention mechanisms, HiTMap predicts necessary navigation information from the entire map without explicitly extracting a local view, thereby allowing for efficient end-to-end learning of navigation policies directly from the hierarchical features and world model predictions. Evidence for HiTMap's superiority to conventional global metric maps has been provided through various evaluations in complex and dynamic settings, demonstrating its exceptional navigation performance. Furthermore, HiTMap's computational efficiency has been demonstrated, yielding notable speed improvements over traditional methods, particularly for larger environments.

Our research team developed a content moderation system to identify and remove online harassment, which leverages multiple advanced models and techniques such as multi-task learning, negative sample augmentation, and an innovative anomaly-aware attention mechanism for anomaly-aware text classification. To enhance the model's capabilities, we expanded the existing dataset for the T-rex Challenge and the Oxford Student Hub, and manually labeled newly acquired data to increase its size. The proposed anomaly-aware attention model, the proposed multi-layered ensemble framework, and the enhanced dataset were all designed to work together to improve the model's performance. The proposed system's effectiveness was demonstrated by a macro F1 score of 0.799 in the offline challenge and a macro F1 score of 0.685 in the online challenge.

The sensitivity of previous measurements of local magnetic fields was limited by the precision with which we could control magnetic fields at a global level. However, an experiment described here overcame this limitation at a microscopic scale, allowing us to detect and compensate for a local magnetic field as small as 130 picotesla, despite our ability to control fields globally to within one picotesla. This was accomplished using an atomic interferometer, in which we found the signal could be adjusted by varying the global field control during the experiment. As a result, we determined the local field while simultaneously measuring the atomic interference pattern, leading to a more accurately compensated local field and a six-fold decrease in noise in the final result. The technique presented here is directly applicable to atomic clocks and may help reduce a long-standing limitation in the precision of such devices.

A heterostructure combining an atomic layer of magnetic material and a host substrate can exhibit a controllable quantum anomaly known as the magnetocaloric effect. This effect, manifesting as a differential response in magnetic moment to changes in temperature for opposite spin states, can be manipulated to produce either an enhancement or suppression of a spin state's magnetic response to temperature. By tailoring a sample's composition, the magnetocaloric effect can be harnessed to create a variation in spin states' temperature dependence, which has implications for the design of spintronic devices that rely on precise control over a sample's magnetic properties.

An advanced statistical method, accounting for interdependencies in space and time, has been utilized to develop non-gaussian interface models and compute interface distribution slopes at various depths. These models have been applied to estimate the effectiveness of gap widths in modeling the transport of light in turbulent waters. In a collaborative effort with the Airgardi group, we have created non-local interface models and calculated the corresponding gap widths. In contrast to traditional local models, which assume interface behavior is independent of the water column above, our model incorporates a method measure that considers the dependence on the sediment column. The model's results have been found effective in predicting water visibility, as visibility values computed using our model's effectiveness gap widths were more accurate than those predicted by traditional local models. The effectiveness of a specific model model was further enhanced by introducing a non-local parameter that quantizes the degree of water column dependence. This parameter has been found valuable in distinguishing between model models with varying degrees of interdependence, and it has been proposed as a means of evaluating model performance. The advantage of the effectiveness gap width model over traditional local models lies in its ability to estimate a performance measure that can be empirically validated, providing a framework for evaluating model performance.

The calculus of constructions has served as a foundational framework for a significant number of contemporary programming languages and advanced studies in type theory over the past thirty years. This study delves into its historical development, showcasing its evolution and key milestones. As the calculus of constructions was born from the merging of two distinct theories - Perreault's calculus and Reynolds's system F - the calculation of its structural properties has a direct impact on its suitability for use as a foundation for modern programming languages and type theory.

blending quantum physics, mesoscopic physics, and electronics. This compact
review explores fundamental quantum electronics by utilizing advanced theories
from quantum many-body physics, including entanglement theories. A key aspect
covered here is the connection between electronic currents, charge correlations,
and quantum states, facilitated by Relaxed Entanglement Envariance (REE) and
other relevant concepts like unitary tricks, operator mobility, and operator
tanglement. This framework enables a demonstration of famous mesoscopic
phenomena, such as the Aharonov-Bohm effect, Landauer conductance, and
conductance quantization, as well as a novel analysis of their charge
backflow characteristics. Furthermore, we show that operator mobility can
serve as a general tool for predicting and inducing operator mobility between
any two locations. This capability is illustrated through discussions of the
Aharonov-Bohm effect, Landauer conductance, and quantization of conductance,
alongside an examination of operator mobility's relation to electromagnetic
potentials, fields, and charges. This analysis is also applied to a model
system that mimics a Bose-Einstein condensate formation through coherent
tunneling. Here, we show that both 'superfluidity' and 'rigidity' emerge as

A nonparametric approach to analyzing data consisting of identifiable components with varying weights from multiple source configurations is explored. This view, compatible with the Bayesian hierarchical framework, facilitates exploration of data through the use of scores that reflect both the number of relevant components and their associated weights in a coherent manner. Employing a Dirichlet process prior on component densities as proposed by Griffiths and Ghosh (2005) leads to a specification of scores for relevant components, along with associated weights in the retrieval of admixture weights that form an $L_1$-martingale, enabling the use of standard Bayesian inference techniques such as posterior sampling via Gibbs sampling. This framework is not limited to a specific parametric distribution, offering flexibility in modeling and analysis.

Building upon the four-point correlator of four twist-two operators, we extend the analysis to include two-loop anomalous dimensions of specific four-operator combinations. This extension involves calculating two-loop corrections, focusing on single-zero and double-zero polarization configurations. By applying the Kolmogorov equation and utilizing the Lorentzian OPE, we diagonalize the anomalous dimensions to recover the cusp type behavior observed in the corresponding single-operator anomalous dimensions. Notably, in the double-zero configuration, our calculation validates the recently proposed four-point correlator result from Constantinou, Gromov, Konechny, and Zamolodchikov. This validation utilizes the finite sum of four-loop anomalous gauge-invariant twist-four operator terms, building upon the three-loop results by Korchemsky and Radyushkin, as well as the two-loop results by Korchemsky, Korchemsky, and Musatov.

Next-Generation Safety Critical Advanced Racing with Self-Driving vehicles (DARS) is a groundbreaking technology that merges GPU computing and self-drive technology for a more immersive and engaging experience. The computational demands of DARS, involving multiple safety critical processes and self-drive algorithms, are substantial. Given the real-time constraints, with critical frequencies of 2kHz to 5kHz, DARS is highly computationally intensive. To optimize memory management in DARS, we have developed a new GPU memory management platform called DynaSOAr. Unlike conventional GPU memory managers that result in performance degradation, memory fragmentation, and excessive safety-critical task delays, DynaSOAr delivers exceptional performance, guarantees real-time determinism, handles memory efficiently, and supports flexible and dynamic memory allocation. To achieve this, DynaSOAr combines the speed of SOA data layout, dynamic memory management, and real-time memory allocation tracking. It leverages CPU and GPU coherence, optimizes cache usage, and minimizes latency. We have conducted comprehensive benchmarks comparing DynaSOAr to top GPU memory management solutions, showing significant performance gains of up to 2.47x. We also demonstrate the potential of DynaSOAr to streamline the safety-critical real-time racing software stack, reducing delays and improving overall performance by as much as 1.97x.

This paper delves into the structural properties of the generalized lower triangular fractional integral operator and its K-type under K-condition. We establish the boundedness characteristics of this operator and its K-type within the realm of generalized mixed Morrey spaces.

When Fe surface anods are covered with Fe surface adatoms or dimers, the spin-orbit coupling is altered, shifting the YSR state peak positions to different energies including ground state and excited state peaks. Implicit functions have gained popularity in segmentation tasks, particularly due to their ability to handle complex shapes at various resolutions. However, training implicit functions requires time-consuming data collection methods such as multi-planar slicing or manual annotation. In contrast, end-to-end implicit functions can be trained directly from single images, but these models often lack the precision needed for detailed medical imaging due to their limited implicit features.

In contrast, FourierMask proposes a novel approach by combining implicit functions with a Fourier-based encoding layer, allowing it to produce high-resolution segmentation masks with exceptional detail. By leveraging this innovative technique, FourierMask was able to generate impressive segmentations of complex medical images, including rabbit kidneys and human kidneys with accompanying tumors, using 2D and 3D single images respectively. 

FourierMask's innovative design allows it to excel at segmentation tasks by combining implicit functions with a Fourier-based encoding layer, which enables it to handle complex shapes and structures with ease. Its impressive performance was demonstrated through the successful segmentation of complex medical images, particularily 2D rabbit kidneys and 3D tumors-kidneys, which were generated with high levels of detail using only 224 training images. 

By utilizing a compact network structure, FourierMask was able to achieve both high accuracy and efficiency, with inference times as fast as 0.02 seconds per image. Its innovative approach was able to handle complex medical images with ease, particularly tumorous kidneys, which were generated with high levels of detail and accuracy

Recent research by Khuri, Lee, and Tataru into the complete characterization of the discovery of complete bounded minimal disks in R^3 has implications for the understanding and complete description of the bounded spectrum of the Schrodinger operator on specific submanifolds in R^4. The paper expands on this duality between bounded minimal discs and bounded spectral characteristics. It proposes conjectures that a specific family of bounded minimal discs in R^3 will fully capture a given bounded spectral range, and at least one bounded minimal disc will always be present to match a specific starting point in the spectrum. The validity of these proposals would provide a crucial step in addressing the complete, bounded spectral characterization of certain submanifolds in R^4. The article also summarizes the existing knowledge of bounded minimal discs in R^3 and explores the connection between the complete characterization of bounded minimal discs in R^3 and the complete, bounded spectral characterization of certain submanifolds in R^4.

Wind-driven clouds often obstruct the view of the polar night aerosol "veiled core."
Researchers utilized high-resolution satellite images to map the three-dimensional structure of these clouds.
Three distinct methods were employed to analyze the clouds' morphology, with two additional methods used to assess their complexity.
Three case studies demonstrated that the "veiled core" appears as an independently formed aerosol feature, while the clouds themselves result from the interaction of air masses and ocean currents.
The clouds exhibit a flat, sheet-like structure with thickness variations arising from wind patterns and currents.
The analysis also revealed that the clouds display signs of fractal behavior, while the aerosol "veiled core" displays a more uniform, power-law distribution.

A Tilted Two-color Laser (TTL) with an extremely thin, low-density outer layer can significantly modify the distribution of electrons in the plasma's backside, leading to a deeper potential well and a higher concentration of ions upon the arrival of a subsequent ultrashort laser pulse. -3. When a TTL pulse consisting of two counterpropagating ultrashort laser pulses interacts with a thin plasma target, it can generate a highly monochromatic X-ray laser with an energy of hundreds of electron volts.

A rare find in exoplanet research is a system with multiple transiting mini-Neptunes within the habitable zone. To achieve this, planets must remain stable against gravitational perturbations, which would otherwise cause them to shift in position within the system. We utilized the method of transit timing variations to determine that these planets reside in a minimum energy configuration, located inside a stable regional boundary at approximately 0.35 times the distance from the central star as the outermost planet. This finding demonstrates that the stars systems hosting mini-Neptunes may be capable of maintaining stable, non-groundbreaking planetary arrangements.

Using first-principles electronic structure calculations, we investigated doping TiO2 with C and N to determine their location preferences and optimal configurations. Our results indicate that both elements favor occupying interstitial sites over substituting Ti or O atoms. Notably, 'anti-O' configurations are most stable among substitutional arrangements. Doping TiO2 with C or N generally leads to material type transitions, with most configurations being semiconducting except for two nonmagnetic interstitial cases and one magnetic one. However, all configurations display localized states near the Fermi level, affecting the material's optical properties by altering the TiO2 band gap. Additionally, magnetic moments arise in specific configurations due to unpaired d-electrons from adjacent O atoms.

A comprehensive search for flavor-changing neutral current (FCNC) semi-elastic processes in $t\bar{t}$ events has been conducted using 19.9 fb$^{-1}$ of pp collision data at $\sqrt{s}=13$ TeV from LHC experiments, which was also utilized to validate the amplitude run in the year 2016. A statistical likelihood method, incorporating both signal and background event likelihoods, was employed to derive confidence intervals for branching fraction limits or excess counts. A limit of $5.0 \times 10^{-2}$ has been set for the sum of flavor-changing neutral current decay branches of the top quark to down-type quarks, which is 1.5 times more precise than previously determined. No excess has been detected in any individual channel. A limit of $4.6 \times 10^{-2}$ has been set for $\\Gamma(t\to t\gamma)/\Gamma_{\\rm tot}$, which is 2.5 times more precise than previously determined. No excess has been found. The intra-cluster medium is currently being investigated for its potential to reveal dark matter through its spectral analysis using a new X-ray instrument, the X-ray Integral Field Unit (X-IFU). To demonstrate the instrument's capability in this field of study, researchers utilized an expansive, distant galaxy cluster to analyze the X-IFU's ability to probe the movement of gases within the cluster. With a unique data reduction software developed specifically for this analysis, the team was able to derive a robust measurement of the gas velocity dispersion, or turbulence, within the cluster. The resulting turbulence measurement of 365 kilometers per second is consistent with earlier findings, indicating the instrument's capability to provide meaningful measurements of dark matter's effects within galaxies.

By leveraging Erdos-Ko-Rado-style arguments and advanced graph theory, we establish a modified lower bound on edge-coloring requirements. Specifically, we prove that for any triangle-colored graph, the minimum number of colors required grows exponentially with a related parameter $\kappa$. Additionally, we examine the impact of adding constraints and consider strategies to enhance these bounds.

We investigated the three-dimensional density distribution in the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) using a newly created height-dependent velocity map. This model accounted for an anisotropic, ellipsoidal density structure, with orientations defined by best-fit angles and an anisotropy level. Additionally, a multi-fractal density model was employed to generate synthetic observations for a variety of density structure parameters. These synthetic data sets were then compared to the velocity maps through the correlation function and an optimization process, ultimately yielding an estimate of the anisotropy level and the anisotropy angle of the an ellipsoidal structure. Our study found that the anisotropy level increased with spatial scale, with a corresponding rise in the anisotropy angle, in contrast to previous studies that detected smaller anisotropy angles or no anisotropy at all, which diverged from our model's predictions. Furthermore, our results hinted that a highly elongated, filamentary structure might be present near the Sun, a region that has not been previously reported, with the observed elongation potentially explicable by the influence of inflowing streams, outflows, magnetic fields, and the gravitational potential on the formation of such structures.

Human face detection and recognition methods that require line-of-sight are being developed with an innovative, non-intrusive approach, focusing solely on the eyes. This groundbreaking concept utilizes an advanced face detection algorithm, combined with an eye-focused detector and an attention mechanism, to efficiently create link predictions and prioritize relevant regions. The proposed system offers two key advantages: first, it prioritizes a more accessible and accessible approach to face detection and recognition, focusing solely on the eyes; second, it provides an implicit spatial awareness, allowing the model to consider regional information while maintaining line-of-sight awareness. The system's performance was tested on three public datasets, where it demonstrated superior performance and faster performance than other methods.

Researchers studied how accurately we can determine the properties of a three-level atomic system, specifically the energy spacing between levels, in an open environment subject to various types of noise. They focused on two main tasks: calculating the energy difference and an angle representing the relationship between the different levels' energy spacings. 

To tackle these tasks, the team used a method called gradient descent and developed ways to simulate the noise channel and calculate the outcome measurements. They examined different types of noise models, including unitary channels such as dephasing and amplitude damping, as well as non-unitary channels like amplitude damping and phase damping. 

The team also investigated the tolerance to noise when calculating the energy difference and found that qutrits can be more robust to certain types of noise compared to qubits, particularly when calculating the relative phase phase angle. However, this advantage is not universal and depends on the specific noise model. 

The team's simulations demonstrated the effectiveness of their method by applying it to real-world data obtained from an experiment with a trapped calcium ion, and the results indicated that a qutrit system can accurately calculate energy differences even in the presence of multiple types of noise.

Our research involves the development of a method to calculate the spin polarization of positrons in a process where a virtual photon converts into a pair of particles, a positron and a proton. In the non-relativistic regime where the interaction between the particles is significant, our approach effectively achieves a degree of polarization in positrons in excess of 30%. The success of this level of polarization holds the potential to aid in measuring the fine-structure constant through precise observations of the 1s-2s transition in hydrogen-like ions and in determining the proton's charge radius through analyses of the Lamb shift in muonic hydrogen.

The given information comes from two sources: the first is the authors' original research, while the second originates from Daniel Wise's work. It presents an alternative, more straightforward proof of several key results:

    - Groups with rapidly growing polynomial diameter, including multiple nilpotent subgroups with distinct intersections with a bisection, have broad implications.
        * A hyperbolic isometry within these sections shares commensurable boundary paths.
        * Such groups possess a finite number of conjugacy classes within their convex hulls.
    The given proof also builds on Wise's diamond property, through a specific action on a tree with stabilizers possessing a specific dress. It is demonstrated that certain actions associated with specific graphs of groups and their modifications share the necessary properties to extend the dress of the tree action to a polynomial diameter. These results follow as direct consequences.

This research addresses the challenge of accurately measuring temperature with a high level of precision. We propose a novel method for calculating temperature based on the frequency variation of the positive branch oscillation in ring oscillators, which exhibits different slopes on rising and falling edges due to charge differences. The method makes use of these differences to detect and correct errors caused by process variations, as illustrated in Figure 1. An innovative circuit for temperature measurement has been designed and fabricated in 55nm CMOS technology. The circuit uses a ring oscillator, two unique types of frequency references, and mathematical models for slope analysis and temperature measurement. The proposed method achieves a high resolution and accuracy in temperature measurement, which exceeds the capabilities of conventional sensors. The proposed circuit successfully measures the temperature across a wide range, from ambient to body temperature, with a high level of precision and reliability.

For a stable equilibrium, the Toroidal-Kelboltzmann condition is necessary but not sufficient in the absence of mutual interaction between the toroidal and poloidal magnetic field components. However, when this interaction is considered, it can lead to an instability, especially when the mutual energy interaction exceeds a certain threshold. This cross-component interaction can be counteracted when the opposing components are balanced, possibly indicating the viability of long-term toroidal magnetic field maintenance in stars through stable mutual stabilization.

The concept of irreversibility in renormalization group (RG) trajectories within parameter space seems to be rooted in a deeper principle, potentially the emergence of a time-asymmetric arrow of time from time-symmetric underlying laws. As a starting point, we explore the connection between RG equations and fluid dynamics, with a view to finding a general metric that reflects the directionality of the RG flow. Building on this, we develop the holographic fluid/duality correspondence into a tool for calculating this metric, with specific applications to the AdS/CFT and DGP/RG multi-time formulations. Within this framework, we show that local scarring in CFT operator kernels corresponds to a form of turbulence within fluid dynamics.

When searching for music lyrics or audio, a search engine can significantly expedite the process compared to standard web searches. To enhance the search results, musiclyrics.com employs various NLP techniques and custom algorithms to process Bing's search outcomes from Spotify, Amazon, Apple Music, and Google Music. Furthermore, several examples have been shown to demonstrate the practical applications of musiclyrics.com in actual scenarios.

Given any topological groupoid and any topological group, we've developed a method to create a topological groupoid extension that corresponds to the given groupoid and group. Furthermore, the collection of these topological groupoid extensions can be related to a specific gerbe over the topological groupoid, where the underlying structure of the gerbe is a topological group, which is the given topological group.

To build a significant number of massive stars, molecular cores must remain and continue to grow over time. Although the typical lifetime of a molecular core is much shorter than that of a star cluster, the observation of massive star formation within relatively small, dynamic regions can be explained if the mass growth rate of molecular cores matches the mass accretion rate of the associated outflows. A study was conducted to test this hypothesis by analyzing the mass growth rates of four high-mass star-forming regions: W51e8, OB1/24, OL444, and S106. The analysis showed that the mass growth rates of three of these regions are extremely high, with two of them significantly in excess of the mass within their proposed feeding radii, suggesting that mass growth must be supplied from beyond these limits. By contrast, the mass growth rate of one region (S106) is moderate and aligns with the mass found within its feeding radius, but it may be an outlier as its mass growth appears to have already come to a halt, possibly due to a positive feedback mechanism from a newly formed O-type star. The formation of four massive stars within such a short timescale in the OMC-2/3 region can be understood if, like S106, they all formed within the same small, self-contained region.

The duality between G"odel algebras and certain distributive lattices has been utilized to represent finitely generated G"odel algebras through finite structures. Building on C"esarone and Fiore's 2019 work, this paper proposes a new category "D" of forests and demonstrates that it is equivalent to the category of G"odel algebras via dual equivalence. This equivalence is then used to present the elements of a finitely generated G"odel algebra as a forest in its corresponding dual lattice.

A point cloud LiDAR classification task is carried out on a 3D point cloud, where the context provided by neighboring points is key to a rich understanding of semantic information in 3D point clouds. Without adequate consideration of local geometry, classification performance is significantly hampered. In this work, we shift focus to extracting high-quality local features, incorporating not only coordinate features but also neighboring point labels. To achieve this, we introduce the neighbor attention network, which is capable of extracting feature coordinates and labeling neighbor points. The proposed network includes two novel network modules: the coordinate attention module and the neighbor attention module. In order to prevent label propagation errors, neighbor classification module is designed to classify neighbor points and incorporate classification labels into the network. To validate our approach, multiple experiments are carried out and performance is evaluated under different classification scenarios, including single-point, slice, and global classifications. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing methods in accuracy.

This study explores the preservation of posdefiniteness in zonal functions following applications of classical differentiation and integration methods. It establishes specific definitions and criteria, including an formula for spherical differentiation and proves deflation and inflation theorems. These proofs rely on the explicit definition of connection coefficients for zonal functions.

Recent studies have suggested a link between the directions of cosmic rays and the directions of neutrinos with energies in the hundreds of PeV range. Given the vastly different interaction strengths of these particles with matter, their propagation paths through the universe differ significantly. This discrepancy makes it more challenging to reconcile the observed correlation with the principle that high-energy cosmic rays cannot travel far through space. In this paper, we review our understanding of the correlation and utilize data from three neutrino detectors - IceCube, ANTARES and KM3NeT/NC2 - to conduct the first detailed statistical analysis of the correlation's significance. Our analysis indicates a 2.8-sigma excess that does not reach a statistically significant level. Looking ahead, the substantial improvement in statistics promised by the upcoming DeepSea v1 detector allows us to forecast that the correlation will be comprehensively tested within a couple of years.

Investigating the interplay between surface tension forces and viscous forces in liquid foams poses significant challenges due to their complex nature and multiple scales. To overcome these difficulties, we have developed a novel approach to assess the impact of viscosity on bursting dynamics, referred to as the 'roughness factor'. This factor embodies a distinct 'on-off' characteristic, indicative of the presence or absence of significant viscosity influence, and can be applied to various configurations and velocity models within liquid foams. Our findings demonstrate its efficacy in analyzing the bursting mechanisms of flat interfaces, wedge-shaped structures, and double wedges. Moreover, the roughness factor facilitates a clearer distinction between the effects of inertia and those of viscosity. When combined with ray theory, it offers a robust tool for examining the multifaceted physics of bursting foam structures.

Deep learning techniques have surpassed traditional methods in classification tasks using convolutional neural networks. Nonetheless, these advanced models are prone to making confident yet incorrect predictions. Enhancing classification models through ensembles has been proven to be a simple and effective technique. Nonetheless, developing high-performance ensembles remains a complex task. This study introduces the concept of automatic multi-week training to train robust ensemble models (MTF) for CNNs. The proposed approach leverages the versatility of PyTorch, a popular deep learning framework. By utilizing MTF, a straightforward and customizable procedure is established to create diverse ensemble models with the PyTorch framework. The simplicity of PyTorch enables the seamless integration of complex techniques, such as training uncertainty-aware models through ensembles, multi-task learning through task sampling, and meta-learning through the Monte Carlo dropout technique. By employing MTF and diverse training configurations, the optimal ensemble model is formed. The findings demonstrate that the proposed approach enhances the performance of CNNs and provides a robust baseline for the PyTorch framework, outperforming or matching SOTA methods in various applications and model settings. The source code and experiments are publicly accessible at https://github.com/zhengzhuangzhuang/mtf-baselines-.

When a rotating Hele-Shaw cell is filled with a liquid, membrane-enclosed fluid exhibiting varying inertia properties can create multiple stable states including star-shaped, concave and self-interverting configurations. This research reveals that memory is lost during a rotation-based filling process if the filling rate surpasses a critical threshold, corresponding to a minimum membrane tension requirement. It is found that higher angular velocities result in a critical radius of curvature that is reduced and may become zero, indicating a transition to a monolithic stable state. A reducing outer radius of rotation has a similar impact on the minimum membrane tension required to transition from a self-interverting to a monolithic stable state. A self-consistent, variable-angle model is used to explain the characteristics of a minified ISA. It also found that a specific range of angular velocities can cause a specific type of monolithic stable configuration.

A new interpretation of dissipated work in nonequilibrium thermodynamics has been posited, which can be interpreted as an average of intrastate work performed on a microstate during an irreversible process. According to this view, the internal work done on a microstate follows linear relations with changes in equilibrium variables, which serves as a definition of nonequilibrium variables like temperature, pressure, and chemical potential within a statistical mechanics framework. These definitions align with their equilibrium counterparts, and as a consequence, the dissipated work can be characterized as the average difference between nonequilibrium and equilibrium thermodynamic potentials over multiple simulations.

We utilized an advanced statistical state-to-state comparison state method to enhance the quantum state resolution of three dense spectral regions within cyclopentadiene, benzene, and fluorobenzene. High-resolution spectra were analyzed to determine the absolute and relative abundance ratios of cyclopentadiene to aromatic benzene ring species. The absorption feature at 888 nm in cyclopentadiene shows a 10 to 100 times greater CCH to CN derivatives abundance ratio than expected, in contrast to the 1 to 1 ratio observed in the 883 nm region of the benzene spectrum. Moreover, absorption features in the 835 nm region of the fluorobenzene spectrum reveal a CCH to CN derivatives abundance ratio of approximately 10 to 1. These increased CCH to CN derivatives abundance ratios in the aliphatic cyclopentadiene spectrum relative to the aromatic benzene and fluorobenzene spectra may reflect the stability and absorption differences between the CCH and CN derivatives of these species. This comparison highlights the importance of considering state-to-state relative abundance ratios in future spectral analyses and can inform future spectral interpretations of cyclopentadiene in planetary atmospheres.

The proposed approach enhances traditional attention mechanisms in neural machine translation by integrating look-ahead information into the look-back context that is used for decoding the current target word. This technique, named Comprehensively Decoding-directional attention, is introduced to minimize the inclusion of future words that can mislead current translation, with maximal-decreasing loss proposed to train the model. Comparisons on the WMT14 English-German and WMT15 French-German datasets demonstrate that our model outperforms the best previous attention models in terms of translation accuracy, with the best official score of 22.86 achieved in the WMT14 competition.

The European Grid Laboratory is dedicated to researching and developing grid and Pegasus computing technologies, with a focus on developing a user-centered approach for introducing these technologies. This document outlines the envisioned goals, challenges, and strategies associated with a user-centered approach, which involves user influence in roadmap planning, continuous support for user feedback, and regular user engagement. Additionally, it discusses the benefits and features provided by the European Grid Laboratory to achieve these objectives, including user involvement in roadmaps, regular user feedback, and multiple communication channels for user input.

A new class of anisotropic cosmological models based on Kosul connection has been introduced within this study, and their properties have been analyzed for a four-dimensional, anisotropic, flat-Friedman-Robertson-Walker universe. The model incorporates a specific coefficient of viscosity that varies both with time and the expansion rate of the universe, and it evolves from an initial singularity towards a final singularity. Matter within this model is composed of two fluids with differing equations of state, and the study reveals that the model exhibits past and future singularities, with both matter fluid densities becoming infinite at the singularity stages. The model also demonstrates that both expansion and shear rates increase as the model approaches the singularity, and the temperature of the universe follows a power-law relationship with the entropy scalar function. Additionally, barotropic fluid behavior dominates during both expansion and contraction phases, while non-barotropic fluid behavior emerges near the singularity, and the model satisfies the strong and weak energy conditions throughout its evolution.

Investigating how curiosity is influenced by peers remains a gap in research.
To promote further study in this area, we provide theoretical frameworks that
can inform future work on modeling and encouraging curiosity through social
interactions.

When utilizing non-conjugate models, the typical approach of calculating the full posterior distribution becomes prohibitively expensive for large datasets. Graph Matérn Gaussian processes, however, allow for the efficient estimation of approximate posteriors in mini-batch and non-conjugate settings, facilitating their application to generalized linear models, matrix factorization problems, and Bayesian neural networks. The researchers' initial evaluations confirm the validity and speed of this efficient approximate inference method. The efficient implementation of the algorithm can be further optimized through connections to the randomized numerical reconstruction of large linear systems.

Recent advancements in sensor technology and ridesourcing services have created an opportunity for using ridesourcing vehicles as a cost-effective solution for monitoring urban roads. This research reveals that utilizing ridesourcing vehicles for sensing purposes can reduce sensing coverage costs by up to 85% compared to fixed sensors, and achieving nearly 95% reliable sensing at low costs (by 4x) can be more efficient than traditional methods (by 9x). A new cross-layer optimization framework, consisting of a reliable sensing coverage determination module and a ridesourcing vehicle path planning module, is proposed to maximize sensing coverage with minimal delay and cost, taking advantage of ridesourcing vehicles' flexibility and road knowledge. Furthermore, an efficient algorithm named Extended KSP provides fast (with average 3x faster solution time) and reliable (achieved 90%+ reliability) road awareness of dynamic events such as road jams and accidents. Lastly, real-world validation using a dataset from San Francisco confirms the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed framework and algorithm.

Our study explores the implications of limits set by J/ψ invisible decays on dark matter interactions with tau lepton scattering, especially when J/ψ annihilation is mediated by a heavy, virtual particle in the case of scalar or pseudoscalar dark matter interactions. If J/ψ annihilation is responsible for the universe's mass distribution, our calculations show that the cross sections for dark matter scattering off nucleons must be below specific, very low thresholds - roughly 10^-43 cm^2 for pseudoscalar dark matter interactions and 10^-40 cm^2 for scalar dark matter interactions. These limits surpass the capabilities of existing experiments like J-PARC, JLab, and COMET in proton beam tests, jLab and Cometic in JLab, but can still be exceeded in tau beam tests, leaving room for further exploration. Moreover, we found that J/ψ invisible decays impose stricter constraints than other observations, such as J/ψ nuclear and nuclear anti-nuclear scattering, and big bang nucleosynthesis, in certain parameter spaces.

Recent research has shown that variable stepsize symmetric gradient discretizations can provide accurate and consistent solutions for time-dependent and elliptic problems. Building on this foundation, we develop and analyze the discrete version of the time-dependent Caglar-Lax equation using variable stepsize SGLMs, specifically focusing on nonuniform grids. First, we establish the convergence of the discrete method and then demonstrate a first-order error decrease in both $L^{\infty}$ and $L^{2}$ norms for the solution and its gradient. We also present numerical results to support our theoretical findings.

The Minimum MFSSA variation is successfully used for signal denoising, 
component extraction and component quantity estimation. 
However, its computational complexity hinders its application to large-scale 
problems. This paper introduces an improved minimum MFSSA 
denoising algorithm, which achieves a better balance between 
denoising effectiveness and computational efficiency thus enabling its 
practical use in component extraction and estimation. 
Furthermore, two distinct optimization methods are proposed for 
developing this new algorithm. Their validity is demonstrated through 
numerical experiments. The study also shows the algorithm's 
superiority over the original minimum MFSSA approach in changing the 
number of components and provides the formula for selecting the optimum 
denoising parameter based on a priori knowledge. Additionally, discusses 
potential applications of the minimum MFSSA 
variation in real-world scenarios, including temperature curve analysis and 
remote sensing image processing, and provides the new algorithm's 
implementation in the MATLAB toolbox.

Lack of reliability in scoring is often cited as a primary concern in essay evaluation, particularly when automated systems are used to assess large numbers of essays. Fortunately, advanced learning algorithms that generate automated scoring models typically exhibit consistent and stable performance patterns. Unfortunately, these models often react excessively to minor variations, indicating that they might display signs of both over-reactivity and consistent behavior. This phenomenon is further exacerbated by the fact that human scorers usually exhibit consistent performance patterns due to professional training and comparative scoring methods. However, the issue of over-reactivity and consistent behavior in automated scoring systems can be mitigated by incorporating diverse training targets and penalizing consistent behavior. This solution is inspired by biological mechanisms that prevent neural networks from becoming synchronized. As a result, the issue may also have practical implications for the development of more efficient scoring systems that can be used in real-world settings.

Independent and identically distributed increments with a mean of zero and variance one, denoted as $X_i$, generate a random walk $S_n$ for all non-negative integers $n$. The displacement of the walk at time $n$ can be expressed as $R_n = |a n + b n^2|$. We study the expected time $K_n$ spent by the random walk within the curve $R_n$. As $n$ grows large, we identify conditions under which $K_n$ is approximately equal to a specific asymptotic approximation, denoted as $f(n)$. Additionally, we define the probability $\mathbb{P}(K_n = f(n)(1 + O(1)))$ is found to be approximately equal to a specific expression, which can be expressed as a product of exponential and rational terms, which is based on the characteristics of the underlying distribution of the increments of the random walk, which is denoted as $\pi$ and is found to be one or zero, which is based on whether the increments of the random walk are symmetrically distributed or not.

The development of advanced and energy-efficient devices depends on
optimizing plasma sources, whose performance is directly influenced by parameters
such as electron temperature, atomic ion density, and neutral ion density within the
plasma. These parameters vary spatially and temporally, making their measurement
challenging and often requiring intrusive probes that can disrupt the plasma. To
overcome this issue, a non-invasive method based on a convolutional neural network
has been developed to map the intra-source distribution of plasma parameters, using only
a single Doppler-displaced optical emission spectrum as input. To validate this
approach, an array of simulations was configured to vary the gap between electrodes in
a radio-frequency discharge geometry. The method was shown to accurately recover
characteristic intra-source distances with a high degree of precision, demonstrating
potential applications in plasma control and monitoring.

The use of biological pesticides like entomopathogenic nematodes (EPNs) offers an alternative to chemical pesticides, which can have negative environmental side effects. EPNs naturally reduce insect populations through entomophagy and entomopathy, but their impact on the birth rate of target insects has not been previously considered. Our study develops a theoretical framework to investigate how EPNs influence both population size and birth rates of target insects, taking into account contact with infected nematodes, ingestion, and the resulting changes in survival, movement, and reproduction. Our theoretical predictions are validated using an alternative modeling approach and practical examples. Our findings reveal that contact with infected nematodes generally lowers the birth rate of target insects, but we also found that the mode of contact can result in increased birth rates, and that increased movement can lead to either increased or decreased birth rates, depending on the specific scenario. Our work underscores the importance of considering changes in movement and reproduction when studying dynamic processes in biological systems.

Nuclear target identification is crucial for the success of cancer therapy, and while pathologists perform this task manually, they are at risk of burnout due to increasing workloads. To address this issue, pathologists often rely on digital pathology technology, specifically computer-aided diagnosis (CAD), to enhance the efficiency and consistency of nucleus detection. To further improve CAD performance, researchers have recently shifted their focus to instance segmentation, and in this study, a novel deep learning architecture called a W-shaped network is proposed, drawing on the W-shaped expression in colorimetry as inspiration. Initially, a coarse segmentation map is created to divide the image into foreground and background regions. Then, a fine segmentation map is generated by processing the residual differences between the original image and the coarse segmentation map. Numerical experiments show that the W-shaped network's conversion of pathology images to "nuclear portraits" enhances network expression capabilities and improves automatic nucleus detection efficiency. In comparison to the current state-of-the-art methods, the W-shaped network's efficiency is comparable, and it exhibits better accuracy than its competitors.

This paper builds on the work of K. Ito, who established a formula for the rank of twists of local gamma factors associated with odd special orthogonal representations and complex numbers. We provide a more detailed analysis of these gamma factors, focusing on their behavior at odd special orthogonal and symplectic representations. Specifically, we derive formulas for the rank of these gamma factors twists, taking into account the isomorphism of the representations or their distinctiveness, as well as the position of critical points relative to integers.

A fundamental variation of the classic Hamiltonian path problem involves identifying all Hamiltonian paths within a given graph. Building on this, the Hamiltonian path index was proposed as a new measure for the longest list of non-repeating Hamiltonian paths starting and ending at fixed vertices in a graph. This paper experimentally investigates the Hamiltonian path index across various graph types, with a focus on sparse graphs such as trees and cycle graphs. The research suggests that the Hamiltonian path index may equal the number of possible starting vertices in certain classes of graphs, with a theoretical upper bound also established. Through analysis of directed cycles and tournaments, it is demonstrated that these structures contain diverse Hamiltonian paths with significantly different lengths between fixed end vertices.

COVID-19 patients frequently experience a shift from inflammatory to cell-damaging states induced by viral invasion. Observations suggest that certain anti-inflammatory medications may accelerate this cell-damaging process. Using light microscopes and electron microscopy, researchers found that dexamethasone could trigger an unstable form of cell death characterized by membrane blebbing. Furthermore, combining these medications with other cell-damaging agents resulted in membrane rupture. It has been proposed that certain cells undergoing this type of cell death could be primed for a more controlled form of cell death influenced by the body's immune system. The study also found increased cell damage in mice with COVID-19 after being given these medications. Researchers recommend that more in-depth studies, particularly clinical ones, are needed to fully understand the effect of these medications on cell damage and overall patient health.

By analyzing data patterns, machine learning algorithms can uncover previously unknown information, for instance, exogenous variables that have an impact on system behavior and influence the effectiveness of reinforcement learning policies. Although this ability to generate new, useful information is recognized, the resulting variables are often not easily interpretable because they typically take the form of complex mathematical combinations. In this research, we present a straightforward and actionable alternative that allows the discovery of these exogenous variables while ensuring their semantic clarity. Specifically, we modify the classical instrumental learning framework by introducing a set of constraints that push the framework towards finding near-optimal, sparse polynomial variables. We demonstrate the efficiency of this proposed method through theoretical convergence guarantees and simulation results, showing that it outperforms previous instrumental learning approaches in various scenarios.

The Michelson programming language is being utilized for developing Fireshade, a blockchain language with on-chain capability for off-chain computation and data transfer, featuring a gas-reduced transfer mechanism. To ensure the safety and soundness of this new system's security properties and sound accounting, a comprehensive static analysis tool, Michela, was designed, focusing on quantifying flow information and performing HELMHOLTZ compliance checks. This static analysis tool can validate Michelson programs by checking compliance with the HELMHOLTZ design principle, an logic-based specification that ensures correct accounting and security, and we demonstrate that Michela significantly enhances the verification of Michelson programs, as evidenced by the successful validation of the entire Fireshade implementation.

Recently, deep learning approaches like Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and fully connected Neural Networks have been reinterpreted as specific types of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) with particular graph structures. We extend this work by showing that any CNN or fully connected Neural Network has an equivalent GCN representation. We derive formulas to determine the edge weights in the underlying graph for the network to replicate its original behavior. We validate our methodology with a simple LeNet variant on the MNIST dataset and a more complex ResNet-18 model on the CIFAR-10 dataset, comparing their equivalent GCN versions.

A new holographic model is presented, linking the HC formulation to the CS theory in a rotating black hole background. We demonstrate the equivalence of the two models in terms of entropy and chemical potential in the given setting, but a discrepancy is found with the temperature comparison. We propose that the discrepancy arises due to the influence of the background on the global mode and and suggest that the chemical potential difference may also stem from this and confirm that it is indeed the case.

A novel approach to computing the fusion rules for non-invertible symmetries in field theories is presented, based on the concept of duality between (non)invertible symmetries and defect operators. Under the assumption that a given symmetry defect can be restored via a local operator, the central charge of any anomalous sector within its topological boundary theory can be computed using the topological defect's topological entanglement entropy. This is particularly useful in understanding the anomalous properties of non-invertible symmetries in well-studied theories such as Ising, $XY$, and $U(1)/Z_2$ models in $2+1$ dimensions.
